quarkus @DefaultBean conflicts with @Default SYNTHETIC
Ollama extension ChatModel registration error

entries.title: runtime Maven scope on a shared mock library silently expands CDI scan, breaking @DefaultBean suppression
entries.body:
runtime Maven scope on a shared mock library silently expands CDI scan, breaking @DefaultBean suppression

## Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` startup fails with `AmbiguousResolutionException` for an SPI type that has a `@DefaultBean` implementation:

```
Build failure: Build failed due to errors
  [error]: AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type
  GroupMembershipProvider and qualifiers [@Default]
    - CLASS bean [target=MockGroupMembershipProvider]
    - CLASS bean [target=NoOpGroupMembershipProvider]
```

The `@DefaultBean` on `NoOpGroupMembershipProvider` is not suppressing the ambiguity.

## Context

A shared library jar contains mock implementations alongside production code and is declared `<scope>runtime</scope>` in the consuming module's `pom.xml`. The scope was changed from `test` to `runtime` to satisfy a different CDI injection point at production build time. The side effect — bringing the mock into the CDI scan — was not anticipated.

## Root Cause

Maven's `runtime` scope is available at both production runtime AND test runtime. Quarkus CDI discovery scans all classpath entries at `@QuarkusTest` startup, including runtime-scoped jars. `@DefaultBean` suppression only activates when there is exactly one non-default bean. When two plain `@ApplicationScoped` beans implement the same interface, ArC raises ambiguity regardless of `@DefaultBean`.

## Fix

Exclude the unwanted mock from CDI scan in test `application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.example.platform.mock.MockGroupMembershipProvider
```

Add to `src/test/resources/application.properties`. Create the file if it doesn't exist. Apply to every module that uses runtime-scoped shared mock jars with `@QuarkusTest`.

## Why Non-Obvious

`@DefaultBean` reads as "there's always a winner." But `NoOpGroupMembershipProvider` is itself a plain `@ApplicationScoped` bean — it competes equally with the mock. The triggering scope change was made for a completely unrelated injection point, making the connection non-obvious. No compile-time warning; failure only surfaces at CDI container startup.

**See also:** [GE-20260604-81a6a6](GE-20260604-81a6a6.md) — @DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point lives in a different Maven module

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`AmbiguousResolutionException` @DefaultBean suppression
runtime Maven scope CDI scan
shared mock library scope runtime

entries.title: @DefaultBean implementations invisible to CDI when their supertype JAR has no Jandex index
entries.body:
@DefaultBean implementations invisible to CDI when their supertype JAR has no Jandex index

### Symptom

CDI reports "Unsatisfied dependency for type `Foo`" even though:
- A `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` implementation of `Foo` is on the compile classpath
- The implementing JAR contains a valid `META-INF/jandex.idx`
- The implementing class is listed in that index

### Context

A library JAR (`impl-lib`) provides `@DefaultBean class NoOpFoo implements Foo`. A separate JAR (`api-lib`) defines the `Foo` interface. `api-lib` ships without a Jandex index. A downstream module depends on both (directly or transitively).

Quarkus ARC processes the Jandex index of `impl-lib` and finds `NoOpFoo`. When it tries to validate the bean — checking the type hierarchy, qualifiers, and injection points — it needs to read metadata about `Foo` from its defining JAR. Because `api-lib` has no Jandex index, ARC cannot resolve the supertype and silently discards `NoOpFoo` from the CDI graph.

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC bean discovery is index-driven. All types involved in a bean's type hierarchy must be present in **some** Jandex index for the bean to be fully resolved. It is not sufficient for the implementing JAR to have an index — the interface-defining JAR must also be indexed.

### Fix

Add the Jandex plugin to the API JAR's build:

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>io.smallrye</groupId>
  <artifactId>jandex-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>make-index</id>
      <goals><goal>jandex</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

Or, if you cannot modify the API JAR, force-index it in the consuming module's test config:

```properties
quarkus.index-dependency.my-api.group-id=com.example
quarkus.index-dependency.my-api.artifact-id=my-api
```

Note: `quarkus.index-dependency` is a build-time property and must be set in `application.properties`, not via `QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("Unsatisfied dependency") points at the missing bean, not at the missing index. The implementing class is visually present in the JAR, correctly annotated, and listed in that JAR's Jandex index — all the obvious checks pass. The missing piece is in a completely different JAR.

### Alternative root cause — stale SNAPSHOT cache

The same symptom appears when the API JAR **does** have a Jandex index but the locally cached SNAPSHOT predates the commit that added the new types. This happens when:

1. `api-lib` is updated to add new interface types and a CI run publishes a fresh SNAPSHOT
2. A consuming module refreshes its SNAPSHOT dependency (e.g. `casehub-ledger`) but not `api-lib`
3. The local cache holds an old `api-lib` SNAPSHOT whose index doesn't yet list the new types

**Diagnosis:** check the JAR timestamp in `~/.m2/repository/`. If it's older than the CI run that added the types, refresh:
```bash
mvn install -DskipTests -f ~/path/to/api-lib/pom.xml
```

When refreshing a SNAPSHOT dependency chain (e.g. `casehub-ledger`), always refresh its upstreams (e.g. `casehub-platform`) if the ledger has added dependencies on new platform types.

**See also:** [GE-20260523-afab1d](GE-20260523-afab1d.md) — @ApplicationScoped bean in JAR bytecode invisible to Quarkus ARC without Jandex index | [GE-20260523-20046c](GE-20260523-20046c.md) — %prod.quarkus.index-dependency limits JAR indexing to production

**See also:** [GE-20260609-18a0b1](GE-20260609-18a0b1.md) — quarkus.index-dependency for a JAR with jandex.idx double-scans it (the reverse problem)

**See also:** [GE-20260610-204ddb](GE-20260610-204ddb.md) — stale core module jar breaks CDI resolution — symptom mimics missing @DefaultBean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Unsatisfied dependency for type `Foo`" is a common CDI error, but the root cause is often overlooked.
Unsatisfied dependency for type `Foo` Jandex index

entries.title: @DefaultBean is superseded by any non-@DefaultBean in @QuarkusTest — test CDI default is not @DefaultBean
entries.body:
@DefaultBean is superseded by any non-@DefaultBean in @QuarkusTest — test CDI default is not @DefaultBean

### Symptom

A `@QuarkusTest` that defines a recording/mock bean (`@ApplicationScoped`) alongside a
`@DefaultBean` for the same interface finds the recording bean is the CDI default — not
the `@DefaultBean`. Test assertions like "no explicit factory configured → InMemory used"
fail because the recording bean supersedes the `@DefaultBean`.

### Context

When a test class defines an inner `@ApplicationScoped` bean for the same SPI interface
that has a `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` implementation elsewhere, Quarkus ARC treats
the non-`@DefaultBean` as higher priority. `@DefaultBean` means "yield to any other bean
for this type" — it is the fallback, not the default.

This surfaces in tests that:
1. Add a recording/spy bean to observe calls (e.g. `RecordingCaseContextStoreFactory`)
2. Also have the production `@DefaultBean` on the classpath (e.g. `InMemoryCaseContextStoreFactory`)
3. Assert that the "default" path uses the `@DefaultBean`

### Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC is semantically "use this only if no other bean qualifies."
Any `@ApplicationScoped` bean without `@DefaultBean` is a "real" bean that takes precedence.
When `EngineStrategyResolver` discovers beans via `Instance<>`, the non-`@DefaultBean` appears
as the default strategy — `InjectableBean.isDefaultBean()` returns false for it, so the
resolver treats it as an explicit override.

### Fix

Do not assert that a `@DefaultBean` is used when a non-`@DefaultBean` for the same interface
is also in the CDI context. Instead:

1. Assert on the **outcome** (case starts and completes) rather than which factory was selected
2. Or use `@Alternative @Priority(1)` for the recording bean — alternatives are only active
   when explicitly selected, not when merely present on the classpath

### Why this is non-obvious

The mental model "no config → default bean" is natural but wrong in CDI. `@DefaultBean`
doesn't mean "this is the default" — it means "this is the fallback when nothing else
exists." The presence of ANY non-`@DefaultBean` bean for the same type silently changes
which bean is the CDI default, even if the non-`@DefaultBean` was added for a completely
different purpose (testing, recording, spying).

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus test default bean
@DefaultBean superseded by non-@DefaultBean
recording bean supersedes @DefaultBean

entries.title: @DefaultBean on @Produces method makes the produced bean default — placing it on the class does not
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans, leaving CDI ambiguity unresolved
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans, leaving CDI ambiguity unresolved

### Symptom

27 "Ambiguous dependencies for type `CurrentPrincipal`" ARC deployment errors at `quarkus:build`. Three `@Default` beans competing; you have the problematic one in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Build broken.

### Context

Multiple `@Default` beans satisfy the same injection type. You add the "intended winner" to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` expecting it to take priority. The entry is accepted silently — no warning, no error — but the ambiguity persists exactly as before.

### What was tried

Added the non-`@Alternative` class to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Quarkus did not reject the entry; the config appeared correct. But all 27 errors remained on the next build.

### Root cause

`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is designed for beans annotated `@Alternative`. For non-`@Alternative` beans, Quarkus accepts the config entry silently (no validation, no warning) but does nothing with it — the bean is already active as a `@Default` and needs no "selection." The other `@Default` competitors are unaffected. Since CDI ambiguity requires exactly one unambiguous `@Default` winner, adding the non-`@Alternative` to `selected-alternatives` achieves nothing.

### Fix

Do not put non-`@Alternative` beans in `selected-alternatives`. To resolve `@Default` ambiguity when you cannot change the competing beans' annotations (they live in upstream dependency JARs), add the losing beans to `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` instead:

```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.example.CompetingBeanA,\
  io.example.CompetingBeanB
```

The intended winner survives; excluded beans are not visible to CDI at all.

### Why this is non-obvious

`selected-alternatives` is the documented mechanism for activating a preferred CDI bean. Nothing in the Quarkus docs or ARC error output warns that the listed class must itself be `@Alternative`. The config entry is accepted, the bean is already live, so the fix "looks applied" — yet the 27 errors persist unchanged.

**See also:** [GE-20260524-2b587e](GE-20260524-2b587e.md) — `selected-alternatives` does not activate `@Alternative` beans during `quarkus:build` (related but distinct failure mode)

**See also:** [GE-20260616-036128](GE-20260616-036128.md) — casehub-ledger JpaActorTrustScoreRepository is @Alternative — must be explicitly selected

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement: base class NOT NULL fails despite subclass field being set
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement: base class NOT NULL fails despite subclass field being set

### Symptom

`org.hibernate.PropertyValueException: not-null property references a null or transient value for entity CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId`

The test code explicitly sets `cle.tenancyId = "test-tenant"`. Java field access confirms the value is set. The error is impossible — except it isn't.

### Context

JPA JOINED inheritance with a base class (`LedgerEntry`) and subclass (`CaseLedgerEntry`). Both declare a `tenancyId` field with `@Column(name = "tenancy_id", nullable = false)`. In JOINED inheritance, these map to separate columns on separate tables (`ledger_entry.tenancy_id` and `case_ledger_entry.tenancy_id`).

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Setting `tenancyId` on the entity before calling `save()` — still fails
2. Using `em.persist()` directly instead of the repository's `save()` — still fails
3. Setting the base field via reflection workaround — works but is wrong
4. Clean rebuild (`mvn clean`) to rule out stale bytecode — still fails

### Root cause

Java field shadowing creates two separate fields: `LedgerEntry.tenancyId` and `CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId`. They share the same name but are different fields in the JVM.

Hibernate bytecode enhancement (active by default in Quarkus 3.x) intercepts field access on entity classes. When code does `cle.tenancyId = "value"`, the enhancement transparently routes to the subclass field. When code does `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId`, the enhancement ALSO routes to the subclass field — making the shadowing invisible to Java code.

But `em.persist()` reads field values via reflection on the actual declared fields. `LedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId")` reads the base class field — which was never set (all writes were routed to the subclass by enhancement). The `nullable = false` constraint on the base table column fires.

### Diagnostic

```java
CaseLedgerEntry cle = new CaseLedgerEntry();
cle.tenancyId = "from-subclass";

// Java access (enhanced — both route to subclass):
cle.tenancyId                           → "from-subclass"
((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId           → "from-subclass"

// Reflection (raw — reveals the actual field state):
CaseLedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId").get(cle) → "from-subclass"
LedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId").get(cle)     → null  // THE BUG
```

### Fix

Remove the shadowing field from the subclass. JPA JOINED inheritance maps the base class field to the base table automatically — the subclass does not need its own declaration.

```java
// BEFORE (broken):
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    @Column(name = "tenancy_id", nullable = false)
    public String tenancyId;  // SHADOWS LedgerEntry.tenancyId
}

// AFTER (correct):
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    // tenancyId inherited from LedgerEntry — no shadowing
}
```

Migration: drop the `tenancy_id` column from the join table (it's redundant with `ledger_entry.tenancy_id`).

### Why this is non-obvious

Hibernate's bytecode enhancement makes the shadowing completely invisible to Java code. Both `cle.tenancyId` and `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId` return the same value. The error message names the subclass entity but the actual null is on the base class — and you can't see it without reflection. The symptom appears impossible: "the field is null but I literally just set it."

### Why this fix

Removing the shadowing field is the only correct fix. Workarounds (setting the base field via reflection, using a special save method) are fragile — they couple application code to JPA internals and break when the entity hierarchy changes. The field belongs on the base class; the subclass inherits it.

### Alternatives considered

- **Reflection workaround in test helpers** — sets the base field directly. Works but couples tests to the field shadowing structure and masks the underlying design bug.
- **Setting both fields explicitly** — impossible via normal Java code because enhancement intercepts the access. Would require reflection on every write path.
- **Hibernate `@Access(AccessType.PROPERTY)` with getter/setter** — might route correctly but changes the access strategy for all fields and is a much larger change.

### Caveats

- This only triggers when bytecode enhancement is active. Without enhancement (e.g. plain Hibernate outside Quarkus), both `cle.tenancyId` and `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId` access their respective declared fields — the shadowing is visible and the developer would naturally set both.
- The fix requires a Flyway migration to drop the redundant column from the join table.

**See also:** [GE-20260609-58e5d9](GE-20260609-58e5d9.md) — JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
cle.tenancyId = "test-tenant";
em.persist(cle);

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping — setting child field leaves parent nullable=false column null
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping — setting child field leaves parent nullable=false column null

## Context

A JPA JOINED inheritance hierarchy where the child entity redeclares a field already declared in
the parent entity — both with `@Column(nullable = false)`. The child table gets a denormalized copy
of the column (e.g. for a local index to avoid joins). This pattern is intentional for performance
but creates a hidden trap for external writers.

Example from casehub platform:
- `LedgerEntry.tenancyId @Column(name="tenancy_id", nullable=false)` — in `ledger_entry` table
- `CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId @Column(name="tenancy_id", nullable=false, length=64)` — in `case_ledger_entry` table

## Symptom

```
org.hibernate.PropertyValueException: not-null property references a null or transient value
  for entity io.casehub.ledger.model.CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId
```

Thrown even though the code explicitly sets `entry.tenancyId = "tenant-1"` before calling
`em.persist()`. The value is visibly non-null; the error says it is null.

## Root cause

Java field access is statically resolved by the reference type at compile time. When `entry`
is declared as `CaseLedgerEntry`:

```java
entry.tenancyId = value;   // resolves to CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId (shadow field)
```

This writes to the child's own field (mapped to `case_ledger_entry.tenancy_id`). The parent's
field `LedgerEntry.tenancyId` (mapped to `ledger_entry.tenancy_id`, also `nullable=false`) is
never written. Hibernate's nullability check validates BOTH the child's property AND the parent's
property — the parent's property is null → `PropertyValueException`.

## Fix

Set both fields explicitly from any external code that touches the entity:

```java
entry.tenancyId = tenancyId;                    // CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId (case_ledger_entry)
((LedgerEntry) entry).tenancyId = tenancyId;    // LedgerEntry.tenancyId (ledger_entry)
```

The explicit cast forces the Java compiler to emit `PUTFIELD LedgerEntry.tenancyId` — a
separate bytecode instruction targeting the parent class's field declaration, distinct from
the child's shadow field.

The correct long-term fix: remove the field redeclaration from the child entity. Use a
`@SecondaryTable` or a Hibernate `@Formula` to maintain the index without the shadow field.

## Why this is non-obvious

The call site `entry.tenancyId = value` looks complete. The entity compiles and CDI-deploys
without warnings. The failure surfaces at `em.persist()` with a message naming the child entity
and property — which ARE set — not the parent entity and property — which are NOT set.

The Hibernate nullability check message `entity CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId` refers to the
property-path in the entity class hierarchy, not the Java field that is actually null. This
leads to the investigation going in the wrong direction (inspecting the child's field assignment
rather than the parent's).

Any code that uses direct field access from outside the entity (common in JPA entities without
getters/setters) is silently broken when this pattern is in play. Only tests that actually
perform a database persist — not those that simply assign and read back — will catch it.

**See also:** [GE-20260612-1f4ed8](GE-20260612-1f4ed8.md) — JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement causes NOT NULL failure

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId null property exception
LedgerEntry tenancyId shadow field
JPA JOINED inheritance nullability conflict

entries.title: JOINED inheritance silently breaks when parent @Entity becomes @MappedSuperclass
entries.body:
JOINED inheritance silently breaks when parent @Entity becomes @MappedSuperclass

## Symptom

After a library refactoring where `LedgerEntry` moved from `@Entity` (runtime module) to `@MappedSuperclass` (API module), JPQL queries using `FROM LedgerEntry` silently stop returning subclass instances. No compile error, no runtime exception — queries return empty result sets or reduced counts. Seven tests failed with symptoms like `expected: <1> but was: <0>` (attestation count) and `Expected size: 2 but was: 1` (cross-dtype query).

## Context

A library (casehub-ledger) refactored its JPA entity hierarchy:

**Before:**
```
LedgerEntry (@Entity, @Inheritance(JOINED), @Table("ledger_entry"))
  └── MessageLedgerEntry (@Entity, @DiscriminatorValue("QHORUS_MESSAGE"))
```

**After:**
```
LedgerEntry (@MappedSuperclass)  ← moved to API module
  ├── JpaLedgerEntry (@Entity, @Inheritance(JOINED), @Table("ledger_entry"))  ← new runtime class
  │     └── PlainLedgerEntry, ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry
  └── MessageLedgerEntry (@Entity, @DiscriminatorValue("QHORUS_MESSAGE"))  ← still extends LedgerEntry!
```

`MessageLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry` compiled fine because `@MappedSuperclass` is a valid JPA supertype. But it became a standalone entity — not a JOINED subclass of `JpaLedgerEntry`.

## What was tried (didn't work)

1. Fixed import statements (`LedgerEntry` → `api.model.LedgerEntry`) — compilation fixed but tests still failed
2. Fixed `LedgerAttestation` entity creation (separate gotcha: GE-20260705-2a5555) — attestation tests still failed
3. Added debug logging to attestation path — no output because the code path wasn't reached (the entry lookup returned empty)
4. Checked tenancy consistency — correct

## Root cause

With `@MappedSuperclass`, `MessageLedgerEntry` inherits field mappings but does NOT participate in the JOINED inheritance tree rooted at `JpaLedgerEntry`. JPA treats it as a completely separate entity type.

Consequences:
- `FROM LedgerEntry` (which maps to the `JpaLedgerEntry` entity name) does NOT include `MessageLedgerEntry`
- `findEntryById(UUID)` returns `Optional.empty()` for `MessageLedgerEntry` records
- `findBySubjectId(UUID)` skips `MessageLedgerEntry` rows entirely
- Cross-dtype sequence tests fail because only `JpaLedgerEntry` subtypes are counted
- Attestation writes fail because the COMMAND entry can't be found for the causal link

## Fix

Change the parent class from `@MappedSuperclass` to the `@Entity`:

```java
// Before (broken):
import io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry;
public class MessageLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry { ... }

// After (correct):
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry;
public class MessageLedgerEntry extends JpaLedgerEntry { ... }
```

The subclass now participates in JOINED inheritance, gets `@PrePersist` (id, occurredAt), entity listeners (trace, identity), and appears in polymorphic queries.

## Why this is non-obvious

1. **No compile error** — `@MappedSuperclass` is a valid JPA supertype; `extends LedgerEntry` compiles and the `@Entity` annotation on the subclass is valid
2. **No runtime error** — JPA silently creates a standalone entity table; no warning that JOINED inheritance is broken
3. **Partial functionality** — direct queries on `MessageLedgerEntry` still work; only polymorphic queries through the parent type fail
4. **The import looks correct** — `io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry` is the canonical API type; using it feels right
5. **7 tests failed with misleading symptoms** — "expected 1 attestation got 0" doesn't point at an inheritance problem

### Alternatives considered

- Keep `LedgerEntry` as `@Entity` in the API module — would preserve JOINED inheritance but violates the API module's "no JPA entity, no Hibernate dependency" rule
- Add a compile-time check that subclasses of `@MappedSuperclass` are not `@DiscriminatorValue`-annotated — not available in standard JPA/Hibernate

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
LedgerEntry @MappedSuperclass JPQL queries
JpaLedgerEntry @Entity JOINED inheritance
@Entity @MappedSuperclass inheritance silent breaks

entries.title: ReactiveMessageLedgerEntryRepository.findLatestByCorrelationId queries LedgerEntry.subjectId, not MessageLedgerEntry.channelId — seeds with only channelId set return silently empty
entries.body:
ReactiveMessageLedgerEntryRepository.findLatestByCorrelationId queries LedgerEntry.subjectId, not MessageLedgerEntry.channelId — seeds with only channelId set return silently empty

### Symptom

An integration test seeds a `MessageLedgerEntry` and calls `findLatestByCorrelationId(channelId, correlationId, tenancyId)`. The method returns `Optional.empty()` even though the entry exists. No error is thrown.

### Root cause

The JPQL query is:

```java
"subjectId = ?1 AND correlationId = ?2 AND tenancyId = ?3 AND messageType IN ('COMMAND','HANDOFF')"
```

The first parameter is bound to `channelId` (the UUID you pass), but the query filters on `LedgerEntry.subjectId` — the inherited field from the base `ledger_entry` table. `MessageLedgerEntry` also has its own `channelId` column (`message_ledger_entry.channel_id`), but that column is NOT referenced in this query.

When seeding, both `entry.subjectId` and `entry.channelId` must be set to the same channel UUID. Setting only `entry.channelId` leaves `subjectId` null, failing the `subjectId = ?1` predicate silently.

Additionally, `messageType` must be `"COMMAND"` or `"HANDOFF"` — any other type is filtered out.

### Fix

When seeding `MessageLedgerEntry` for this query path, set both fields explicitly:

```java
MessageLedgerEntry entry = new MessageLedgerEntry();
entry.subjectId = channelId;   // ← required: used in JPQL query
entry.channelId = channelId;   // ← kept for consistency and channelId column
entry.correlationId = correlationId;
entry.messageType = "COMMAND"; // ← must be COMMAND or HANDOFF
entry.tenancyId = TenancyConstants.DEFAULT_TENANT_ID;
entry.sequenceNumber = 1;      // ← nullable=false
entry.entryType = LedgerEntryType.COMMAND;
entry.actorId = "test-actor";
entry.actorType = ActorType.AGENT;
entry.actorRole = "test-role";
entry.occurredAt = Instant.now();
// id is assigned by @PrePersist — do not set manually
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The method parameter is named `channelId`, naturally suggesting it matches the `channelId` column. The `MessageLedgerEntry` has both `subjectId` (inherited) and `channelId` (own column), which hold the same UUID in normal use — so the mismatch only surfaces in tests that seed only one of the two. The query itself is not exposed in the public API surface.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
subjectId = ?1 AND correlationId = ?2 AND tenancyId = ?3
channelId column not referenced in JPQL
messageType must be COMMAND or HANDOFF

entries.title: casehub-ledger LedgerProcessor build step blocks em.persist() on LedgerEntry subclasses — use LedgerEntryRepository.save()
entries.body:
casehub-ledger LedgerProcessor build step blocks em.persist() on LedgerEntry subclasses — use LedgerEntryRepository.save()

### Symptom
`IllegalStateException: LedgerEntry must be persisted through LedgerEntryRepository, which handles sequence allocation, enrichment, hashing, and signing. Direct em.persist() bypasses the entire save pipeline.`

Thrown at runtime when code calls `em.persist(entry)` on any `LedgerEntry` subclass (`CaseLedgerEntry`, `MessageLedgerEntry`, `WorkerDecisionEntry`, etc.).

### Context
A Quarkus extension using casehub-ledger, after upgrading to a SNAPSHOT that added a `LedgerProcessor` Quarkus build step. Any existing code that directly persisted `LedgerEntry` subclasses via `EntityManager.persist()` breaks with the above error.

### Root cause
`casehub-ledger` ships a `LedgerProcessor` Quarkus deployment build step (`validateDomainContentBytes`) that also adds a JPA `@PrePersist` interceptor to every `LedgerEntry` subclass. The interceptor throws `IllegalStateException` if it detects a direct persist (i.e. the entity was not saved through the `LedgerEntryRepository` save pipeline).

The intent: `LedgerEntryRepository.save()` handles sequence number allocation (via `ledger_subject_sequence` table), leaf hash computation, Merkle chain update, and agent signature — bypassing it produces invalid ledger entries.

### Fix
Replace `em.persist(entry)` + `em.flush()` with `ledgerRepo.save(entry, tenancyId)`:

```java
// ❌ Blocked since casehub-ledger SNAPSHOT (will throw at runtime):
em.persist(entry);
em.flush();

// ✅ Correct:
@Inject LedgerEntryRepository ledgerRepo;
// ...
ledgerRepo.save(entry, tenancyId);
// save() handles sequence allocation, Merkle hash, and signing; no manual flush needed.
```

Also remove `@LedgerPersistenceUnit EntityManager em` injection if it was only used for `persist()` + `flush()` and the `nextSequenceNumber()` query (the repo handles sequencing internally).

### Why this is non-obvious
The `IllegalStateException` message is clear once seen, but:
1. The validation is added at Quarkus augmentation time via a deployment build step — it does not appear in the `LedgerEntryRepository` interface Javadoc or any user-facing docs.
2. Code that was previously working (`em.persist()`) breaks silently if the SNAPSHOT is updated but the calling code is not.
3. The `@PrePersist` interceptor is injected by the Quarkus extension's deployment artifact (`casehub-ledger-deployment`) — the mechanism is invisible when reading the entity class.

### Why this fix
`LedgerEntryRepository.save()` is the only supported path because it atomically allocates the per-subject sequence number from `ledger_subject_sequence`, computes the Merkle leaf hash, and updates the Merkle frontier — operations that must be coordinated to maintain chain integrity. Any bypass produces a ledger entry with an incorrect or missing sequence number and hash.

### Caveats
- `LedgerEntryRepository.save()` triggers a full Merkle chain update — see GE-20260531-d2ed26 for concurrent-write implications.
- The `ledger_subject_sequence` table must exist in the database. In test contexts using `hibernate.database.generation=drop-and-create`, this native SQL table is not created from JPA entities — use `quarkus.hibernate-orm.<pu-name>.sql-load-script` to create it (see also GE-20260612-*).

**See also:** [GE-20260612-de141c](GE-20260612-de141c.md) — casehub-ledger LedgerProcessor build step requires domainContentBytes() on all LedgerEntry subclasses with @Column fields

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`EntityManager.persist()` on `LedgerEntry` subclasses
`LedgerEntryRepository.save()` sequence allocation
`IllegalStateException` `em.persist()` bypass

entries.title: casehub-work SNAPSHOT @RequestScoped CurrentPrincipal displaces @DefaultBean test mock — null tenancyId on Vert.x threads
entries.body:
casehub-work SNAPSHOT @RequestScoped CurrentPrincipal displaces @DefaultBean test mock — null tenancyId on Vert.x threads

## Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` investigation tests fail with `caseInstance.tenancyId=null`. Ledger saves fail with a NOT NULL constraint violation on `tenancy_id`. No exception is thrown at the principal injection site — the bean resolves, returns null silently, and the null propagates into the entity before the constraint fires.

Tests that worked against the previous SNAPSHOT begin failing without any change in the AML project itself.

## Context

casehub-work June 2026 SNAPSHOT added `TenantScopedPrincipal @RequestScoped` implementing `CurrentPrincipal`. The AML project's test module provides `MockCurrentPrincipal @DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` to supply a fixed test tenancyId.

`@DefaultBean` loses to ANY non-default bean for the same type. `TenantScopedPrincipal` is not `@DefaultBean`, so CDI selects it over `MockCurrentPrincipal` — the mock is silently displaced. On the test HTTP thread, the request context is active and `TenantScopedPrincipal` can be instantiated. On Vert.x event loop threads (where the case engine invokes workers and fires async observers), no CDI request context exists. The `@RequestScoped` proxy either returns null or throws `ContextNotActiveException` (caught internally), resulting in a null tenancyId propagating into `CaseInstance` and any ledger entries written during engine execution.

## Root Cause

`@DefaultBean` is not a "test wins" mechanism — it is a "lowest priority" marker. Any competing bean for the same type that is NOT annotated `@DefaultBean` displaces it, regardless of scope mismatch. A SNAPSHOT that introduces a `@RequestScoped` implementation of a SPI used in async/event-loop contexts silently breaks all consumers that relied on `@DefaultBean` displacement.

## Fix

Until casehub-work marks `TenantScopedPrincipal` as `@DefaultBean` (tracked as aml#59), workaround options:

**Option A — @Alternative @Priority(1) test bean** (if the project's @DefaultBean is in its own test classpath):
```java
@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped
public class TestCurrentPrincipal implements CurrentPrincipal {
    @Override public String tenancyId() { return TenancyConstants.DEFAULT_TENANT_ID; }
}
```
`@Alternative @Priority(1)` wins over ALL non-alternative beans regardless of scope.

**Option B — exclude TenantScopedPrincipal from CDI in tests:**
```properties
# src/test/resources/application.properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.principal.TenantScopedPrincipal
```
Only works if `TenantScopedPrincipal` is NOT in a Jandex-indexed JAR — see GE-20260601-848232.

**Option C — ARC bean container exclusion (if B fails):**
Add the FQN to `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` in the JAR's own `META-INF/beans.xml` (requires access to casehub-work source).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` sounds like "the default wins when nothing else provides it." The actual semantics are the opposite: any non-`@DefaultBean` bean for the same type displaces it — including a `@RequestScoped` bean that is incompatible with the async execution context where the SPI is actually called. The null tenancyId appears in a completely different part of the stack from the principal resolution, making the connection invisible. The failure manifests as a NOT NULL constraint violation on the ledger, not as a CDI resolution error.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`@QuarkusTest` tests failing with `caseInstance.tenancyId=null`
`ContextNotActiveException` on Vert.x threads
`@DefaultBean` displacement by non-default bean

entries.title: casehub-ledger LedgerEntry api/runtime split — consumer subclasses must extend JpaLedgerEntry, not LedgerEntry
entries.body:
casehub-ledger LedgerEntry api/runtime split — consumer subclasses must extend JpaLedgerEntry, not LedgerEntry

casehub-ledger LedgerEntry api/runtime split — consumer subclasses must extend JpaLedgerEntry, not LedgerEntry

### Symptom

Hibernate generates INSERT statements that include ALL parent columns (`actor_id`, `actor_role`, `actor_type`, `occurred_at`, `digest`, `subject_id`, `tenancy_id`, etc.) in the consumer's subclass table. The database returns `Column "ACTOR_DID" not found` (or whichever parent column was most recently added).

### Context

`casehub-ledger` split `LedgerEntry` into two classes:
- `io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry` — `@MappedSuperclass`, field definitions only, no JPA inheritance. Lives in `casehub-ledger-api` (no framework deps).
- `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry` — `@Entity @Inheritance(JOINED) @DiscriminatorColumn`, extends `LedgerEntry`. Lives in `casehub-ledger` runtime module.

Consumer subclass tables (e.g. `aml_case_opened_ledger_entry`) were designed for JOINED inheritance — they only contain the join column (`id` FK to `ledger_entry`) plus subclass-specific columns. Parent columns live in the `ledger_entry` base table.

### Root cause

When a consumer `@Entity` extends `LedgerEntry` (the `@MappedSuperclass`), Hibernate treats it as a standalone entity — ALL parent fields are mapped directly to the subclass table. The `@DiscriminatorValue` annotation on the subclass is silently ignored (no `@Inheritance` on the parent). Hibernate generates INSERTs with 20+ parent columns that don't exist in the subclass table.

### Fix

Change consumer subclasses from `extends LedgerEntry` to `extends JpaLedgerEntry`:

```java
// WRONG — @MappedSuperclass, duplicates all parent columns to subclass table
import io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry;
public class AmlCaseOpenedLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry { ... }

// CORRECT — @Entity @Inheritance(JOINED), subclass table only needs its own columns
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry;
public class AmlCaseOpenedLedgerEntry extends JpaLedgerEntry { ... }
```

The engine-ledger module (`CaseLedgerEntry`, `WorkerDecisionEntry`) already extends `JpaLedgerEntry` — consumer modules must follow the same pattern.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error message (`Column "ACTOR_DID" not found`) points at a missing column, suggesting a migration fix. The natural response is to add the column via Flyway — which leads to adding ALL parent columns to every subclass table, fundamentally misunderstanding the schema design. The actual fix (changing the superclass) is in the Java import, not the SQL.

### Why this fix

Adding parent columns to subclass tables "works" but creates a TABLE_PER_CLASS schema that duplicates data, breaks the shared `ledger_entry` base table design, and defeats the purpose of JOINED inheritance. Extending `JpaLedgerEntry` preserves the original schema contract.

### Alternatives considered

- **Add all parent columns to each subclass table via Flyway** — compiles and runs but creates redundant data storage, breaks FK relationships, and diverges from the engine-ledger module's pattern.
- **Add `io.casehub.ledger.api.model` to the Hibernate PU packages** — makes Hibernate see the `@MappedSuperclass` but doesn't fix the inheritance strategy; still generates wrong INSERT statements.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Hibernate insert all parent columns
JpaLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry error
Inheritance and discriminator column mapping issues

entries.title: Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails
entries.body:
Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException: column "tenancy_id" violates not-null constraint
```

Entities persisted via a static factory or utility method fail on INSERT even though the owning
parent entity has `tenancyId` set correctly.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleTree.append(digest, currentFrontier, subjectId)` is a pure static utility that
builds new `LedgerMerkleFrontier` nodes. It has no knowledge of tenancy context. The caller
in `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()` sets `tenancyId` on the `LedgerEntry` being saved
but forgot to propagate it to the frontier nodes returned by `append()`. The nodes go into
`session.persist()` with `tenancyId = null`, violating the NOT NULL constraint.

### Root cause

Static factory and utility methods that create JPA entities operate outside any tenancy context.
Multi-tenancy fields (`tenancyId`, `tenantKey`, etc.) are caller responsibilities, not factory
responsibilities. The omission is invisible until the `session.persist()` flush fires — and only
on code paths where the NOT NULL column is actually written.

### Fix

Propagate multi-tenancy fields from the parent entity onto all child entities immediately after
the factory call, before any `session.persist()`:

```java
final List<LedgerMerkleFrontier> newFrontier =
    LedgerMerkleTree.append(e.digest, currentFrontier, e.subjectId);
newFrontier.forEach(node -> node.tenancyId = e.tenancyId);  // ← propagate before persist
// ... then session.persist(node) for each
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The parent entity (`LedgerEntry`) has `tenancyId` set correctly and was used for all prior
operations. The factory method looks complete — it takes all the structural parameters it needs.
The tenancy propagation step is easy to forget because it is not part of the factory's contract
and there is no type system or annotation to enforce it.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Hibernate ConstraintViolationException tenancy_id null
Static entity factory JPA not-null insert
LedgerMerkleTree tenancyId propagation

entries.title: Hibernate named query gains a parameter in one repo — sibling repo call site silently unbound until runtime
entries.body:
Hibernate named query gains a parameter in one repo — sibling repo call site silently unbound until runtime

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.QueryParameterException: No argument for named parameter ':tenancyId'
  at ReactiveSqmQueryImpl.executeReactiveUpdate
```

All message dispatches fail with HTTP 500 when `casehub.ledger.hash-chain.enabled=true`.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleFrontier.deleteBySubjectAndLevel` is a `@NamedQuery` defined in `casehub-ledger`.
The ledger repo added a `:tenancyId` predicate to the query. `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()`
in `casehub-qhorus` (a sibling repo) calls this named query but was never updated to bind the new parameter.
The call site compiled and deployed without error — the unbound parameter only surfaces at runtime
when the query executes.

### Root cause

JPA named queries are resolved by name at runtime, not by signature at compile time. When the
query definition in one repo gains a new parameter, every call site in every sibling repo that
uses the same named query must be manually updated. There is no compile-time or build-time
enforcement — neither the Java compiler nor the Maven build reports the mismatch.

### Fix

Bind the new parameter at every call site that uses the named query:

```java
session.createNamedQuery("LedgerMerkleFrontier.deleteBySubjectAndLevel")
    .setParameter("subjectId", e.subjectId)
    .setParameter("level", node.level)
    .setParameter("tenancyId", e.tenancyId)  // ← add when query gains this param
    .executeUpdate()
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The build succeeds. The CDI wiring is correct. The error only appears on a specific code
path (`hash-chain.enabled=true`) that may not be covered by standard CI tests. The exception
message names the parameter (`':tenancyId'`) but gives no indication of which call site is
missing the binding — a classpath-wide search is required to find the stale call site.

**See also:** [GE-20260617-54b75b](GE-20260617-54b75b.md) — Hibernate Reactive Panache repo.update() converts positional ?N params to named params — unbound at runtime

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
hibernate named query parameter exception
reactive jpa repository named query
hibernate query parameter binding

entries.title: casehub-ledger: actor-scoped erasure receipt queries return empty after GDPR erase — tokenisation severs the link
entries.body:
casehub-ledger: actor-scoped erasure receipt queries return empty after GDPR erase — tokenisation severs the link

### Symptom
After calling `GdprErasureService.erase(actorId, tenancyId, reason)`, a JPQL query
scoped to the case's actors returns zero erasure receipts — even though receipts exist.

### Context
A compliance service builds per-case GDPR evidence. The natural approach is to extract
`actorId` values from the case's ledger entries, then query:
`SELECT e.id FROM ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry e WHERE e.tenancyId = :tenancyId AND e.erasedActorId IN :actorIds`

### What was tried (didn't work)
Scoping the erasure receipt query by the case's actor IDs. The query returns empty
because the actor IDs in the ledger entries are now opaque tokens, not the original
identity strings stored in `ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry.erasedActorId`.

### Root cause
`GdprErasureService.erase()` tokenises the actor's identity in all ledger entries —
replacing the original `actorId` with an opaque token and severing the token→identity
mapping. `ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry` stores the *original* `erasedActorId` (pre-tokenisation).
Post-erasure, `entry.actorId` (token) ≠ `receipt.erasedActorId` (original). The IN clause
matches nothing.

### Fix
Query erasure receipts by tenant only — not by actor:
```sql
SELECT e.id FROM ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry e WHERE e.tenancyId = :tenancyId
```
This is the only correct approach post-tokenisation. The compliance report answers
"has any GDPR erasure been performed in this tenant?" — it cannot answer "was this
specific case's actor erased?" because that link is intentionally destroyed.

### Why this is non-obvious
The actor-scoped query is the natural first instinct — it's more precise and avoids
false positives from unrelated erasures. It compiles, runs without error, and returns
an empty list. No exception, no warning. The silent empty result is only detectable
through test flakiness when test ordering varies.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
JPQL query returns zero erasure receipts
`GdprErasureService.erase` tokenisation
`erasedActorId` vs `actorId` mapping

entries.title: Ledger save pipeline re-computes Merkle hash after modifying entry fields — caller hash silently overwritten
entries.body:
Ledger save pipeline re-computes Merkle hash after modifying entry fields — caller hash silently overwritten

### Symptom
Merkle leaf hash verification fails — `LedgerMerkleTree.leafHash(entry)` computed after reading the entry from the database doesn't match `entry.digest` stored at persist time. Hash chain appears broken.

### Context
Two save implementations exist:
1. `JpaLedgerEntryRepository.save()` (ledger runtime) — tokenises `actorId`, re-allocates `sequenceNumber`, runs enricher pipeline, THEN computes `entry.digest = LedgerMerkleTree.leafHash(entry)`. The hash reflects the post-modification field values.
2. `JpaWorkItemLedgerEntryRepository.save()` (casehub-work-ledger) — does raw `em.persist(entry)` without the pipeline. Callers must compute the hash themselves.

A caller (e.g. `LedgerEventCapture`) that computes the hash before calling save via path 1 gets a mismatch — the pipeline overwrites the hash with one computed from modified fields. A caller using path 2 must set ALL fields (including `tenancyId`) before computing the hash — any field null at hash time but set at persist time produces a mismatch on re-verification.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Removing hash computation from the caller and relying on the save pipeline — breaks path 2 where the pipeline doesn't exist
- Computing hash before setting `tenancyId` — `canonicalBytes()` includes `tenancyId`, so the stored hash has the real value but the computed hash had empty string

### Root cause
`canonicalBytes()` is `final` on `LedgerEntry` and includes all fields in a deterministic canonical form. `domainContentBytes()` is `protected` and overridable by subclasses. The hash must be computed with ALL fields in their final state — any mutation between hash computation and persistence (or between persistence and re-verification) breaks the chain.

### Fix
For path 2 (raw persist without pipeline): set `entry.tenancyId` before computing the hash, not after:

```java
// Wrong — tenancyId is null during hash computation
entry.digest = LedgerMerkleTree.leafHash(entry);  // tenancyId = null → canonical uses ""
ledgerRepo.save(entry, currentPrincipal.tenancyId());  // save sets tenancyId

// Right — tenancyId set before hash
entry.tenancyId = currentPrincipal.tenancyId();
entry.digest = LedgerMerkleTree.leafHash(entry);  // tenancyId present → canonical uses real value
ledgerRepo.save(entry, entry.tenancyId);
```

For path 1 (pipeline save): do NOT compute the hash — the pipeline does it after all field modifications.

### Why this is non-obvious
Two repository implementations with the same interface but different hash responsibilities. Nothing in the type system or API signals which path you're on. The mismatch only surfaces during hash verification — at persist time, both paths appear to work correctly.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
LedgerMerkleTree leafHash mismatch
JpaLedgerEntryRepository save hash overwrite
tenancyId canonicalBytes discrepancy

entries.title: casehub-ledger SNAPSHOT split: LedgerEntry → api @MappedSuperclass + JpaLedgerEntry runtime @Entity
entries.body:
casehub-ledger SNAPSHOT split: LedgerEntry → api @MappedSuperclass + JpaLedgerEntry runtime @Entity

### Symptom

After updating casehub-ledger to the July 2026 SNAPSHOT, every file that imports `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.LedgerEntry` fails with "cannot find symbol." Every file importing `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.repository.LedgerEntryRepository` also fails. The old jar resolves from the local .m2 cache, so the build may appear green until a `mvn -U` forces a SNAPSHOT refresh — then 50+ files break simultaneously.

### Context

casehub-ledger restructured its class hierarchy. The single `LedgerEntry` class was split into two:

| Before | After |
|--------|-------|
| `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.LedgerEntry` (@Entity, JOINED inheritance) | `io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry` (@MappedSuperclass — fields, canonical bytes, supplements) |
| — | `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry` (@Entity, JOINED inheritance, JPA listeners, JPA supplements) |

Additionally:
- `LedgerEntryRepository` moved from `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.repository` to `io.casehub.ledger.api.spi`
- `ComplianceSupplement` moved from `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.supplement` to `io.casehub.ledger.api.model.supplement`
- New `JpaComplianceSupplement` in `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.supplement` — must be instantiated instead of `ComplianceSupplement` for JPA persistence
- `LedgerVerificationService` moved from `io.casehub.ledger.api.service` to `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.service`
- `LedgerErasureService` moved from `io.casehub.ledger.api.privacy` to `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.privacy`

### Root cause

The split separates the pure-Java API model (portable, no JPA runtime) from the JPA persistence layer. `LedgerEntry` as `@MappedSuperclass` can be used in non-JPA contexts; `JpaLedgerEntry` carries the `@Entity`, `@Inheritance(JOINED)`, `@DiscriminatorColumn`, listeners, and named queries.

No migration guide was shipped with the SNAPSHOT.

### Fix

Three import replacements cover the migration:

**1. Entity subclasses** (files in `*.ledger.*LedgerEntry.java`):
```java
// Before
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.LedgerEntry;
public class MyLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry { ... }

// After
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry;
public class MyLedgerEntry extends JpaLedgerEntry { ... }
```

**2. Type references** (services, resources, tests — anything that uses `LedgerEntry` as a type but doesn't extend it):
```java
// Before
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.LedgerEntry;

// After
import io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry;
```

**3. Repository and service imports:**
```java
// Before
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.repository.LedgerEntryRepository;

// After
import io.casehub.ledger.api.spi.LedgerEntryRepository;
```

**4. Supplement instantiation:**
```java
// Before
new ComplianceSupplement(...)

// After
new JpaComplianceSupplement(...)
// import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.supplement.JpaComplianceSupplement
```

casehub-clinical required 55 file changes across this migration.

### Why this is non-obvious

The old `LedgerEntry` import resolves against a stale SNAPSHOT jar in the local .m2 cache. The build stays green until the cache is refreshed. When it breaks, it breaks everywhere simultaneously with no hint about the new class hierarchy. The `JpaLedgerEntry` class name doesn't appear in any error message — you have to inspect the jar contents to discover it exists.

### Why this fix

The alternative — staying on `LedgerEntry` from the API package — compiles but fails at runtime: `@MappedSuperclass` entities are not registered in the JPA metamodel, so JOINED inheritance queries fail silently or throw opaque Hibernate errors. Consumer entity subclasses MUST extend `JpaLedgerEntry` for the discriminator column and named queries to work.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`LedgerEntry` @MappedSuperclass
`JpaLedgerEntry` @Entity
`LedgerEntryRepository` spi

entries.title: casehub-ledger JpaLedgerEntry is abstract — use PlainLedgerEntry for test entry creation
entries.body:
casehub-ledger JpaLedgerEntry is abstract — use PlainLedgerEntry for test entry creation

### Symptom

Test code attempts to instantiate `JpaLedgerEntry` directly:

```java
var entry = new JpaLedgerEntry();  // compilation error: abstract; cannot be instantiated
```

### Context

`casehub-ledger` uses a two-tier JPA inheritance model:
- `LedgerEntry` (`@MappedSuperclass`) — defines all persistent fields
- `JpaLedgerEntry` (`@Entity`, abstract) — JOINED inheritance root
- Concrete subclasses: `PlainLedgerEntry`, `KeyRotationEntry`, `ActorIdentityBindingEntry`, `ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry`

Test code that creates generic audit entries needs the concrete `PlainLedgerEntry`, not the abstract base.

### Root cause

`JpaLedgerEntry` is the JPA inheritance root marked `abstract` — it exists to carry `@Entity`, `@Inheritance(JOINED)`, `@NamedQuery`, and `@EntityListeners` annotations. Domain-specific subclasses extend it for join-table fields. `PlainLedgerEntry` is the concrete subclass for domain-agnostic event writes (introduced with `OutcomeRecorder` in V1009).

### Fix

```java
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.PlainLedgerEntry;

var entry = new PlainLedgerEntry();
entry.subjectId = UUID.randomUUID();
entry.entryType = LedgerEntryType.EVENT;
entry.actorId = "test-actor";
entry.actorType = ActorType.AGENT;
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The class hierarchy has four levels (`LedgerEntry` → `JpaLedgerEntry` → `PlainLedgerEntry`), and `JpaLedgerEntry` appears to be the "runtime" entity that tests should use. The name `PlainLedgerEntry` doesn't immediately suggest "this is what you instantiate in tests" — it sounds like a simplified variant rather than the default concrete type.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`JpaLedgerEntry abstract error`
`PlainLedgerEntry test instantiation`
`LedgerEntry inheritance model`

entries.title: Java 'cannot find symbol' names the class FQCN — not which artifact is missing it
entries.body:
Java 'cannot find symbol' names the class FQCN — not which artifact is missing it

## Symptom

CI fails with `cannot find symbol: variable tenancyId / location: variable entry of type io.casehub.ledger.model.CaseLedgerEntry`. The error names the class FQCN and the missing symbol, but not the Maven artifact that should provide them.

## Context

Any Java project where two Maven artifacts share a package namespace prefix. The compilation error is accurate but insufficient for diagnosis when multiple artifacts use the same package root.

## Root cause

`javac` reports the symbol and its declaring type, but has no awareness of which Maven artifact that type came from. When two artifacts share a namespace prefix (e.g., `io.casehub.ledger.model` from `casehub-engine-ledger` vs `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model` from standalone `casehub-ledger`), the error message leads to the wrong artifact.

In the case above: `CaseLedgerEntry` is in `casehub-engine-ledger` (package `io.casehub.ledger.model`), not in the standalone `casehub-ledger` library (package `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model`). The namespace prefix `io.casehub.ledger` is shared, so the error sends diagnostics — and cross-team communication — to the wrong place.

## Fix

When `cannot find symbol` points to a class in a shared namespace, identify the correct artifact by:

1. Checking which artifact declares that specific sub-package:
   ```bash
   find ~/.m2 -name "*.jar" | xargs -I{} jar tf {} 2>/dev/null | grep "casehub/ledger/model/CaseLedgerEntry"
   ```
2. Or grepping the source repo:
   ```bash
   find /path/to/repos -name "CaseLedgerEntry.java" 2>/dev/null
   ```
3. Then checking whether that artifact's published SNAPSHOT includes the missing symbol.

### Alternatives considered

- Reading the error message's package prefix and assuming it maps to the artifact of the same name — fails when namespaces overlap
- Checking `mvn dependency:tree` — shows artifact versions but not package-to-artifact mapping at the class level

## Why this is non-obvious

Developers assume the package prefix uniquely identifies the artifact (`io.casehub.ledger` → `casehub-ledger`). In a multi-artifact project where one standalone library and one framework-internal module share a root namespace, this assumption breaks. The error is accurate; the inference from package to artifact is wrong.

**See also:** [GE-20260516-42a11c](GE-20260516-42a11c.md) — git stash pop conflict markers cause 'cannot find symbol' for classes in the same package

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`cannot find symbol` `io.casehub.ledger.model`
`CaseLedgerEntry` `package name`
`javac` `Maven artifact`
