entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement: base class NOT NULL fails despite subclass field being set
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement: base class NOT NULL fails despite subclass field being set

### Symptom

`org.hibernate.PropertyValueException: not-null property references a null or transient value for entity CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId`

The test code explicitly sets `cle.tenancyId = "test-tenant"`. Java field access confirms the value is set. The error is impossible — except it isn't.

### Context

JPA JOINED inheritance with a base class (`LedgerEntry`) and subclass (`CaseLedgerEntry`). Both declare a `tenancyId` field with `@Column(name = "tenancy_id", nullable = false)`. In JOINED inheritance, these map to separate columns on separate tables (`ledger_entry.tenancy_id` and `case_ledger_entry.tenancy_id`).

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Setting `tenancyId` on the entity before calling `save()` — still fails
2. Using `em.persist()` directly instead of the repository's `save()` — still fails
3. Setting the base field via reflection workaround — works but is wrong
4. Clean rebuild (`mvn clean`) to rule out stale bytecode — still fails

### Root cause

Java field shadowing creates two separate fields: `LedgerEntry.tenancyId` and `CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId`. They share the same name but are different fields in the JVM.

Hibernate bytecode enhancement (active by default in Quarkus 3.x) intercepts field access on entity classes. When code does `cle.tenancyId = "value"`, the enhancement transparently routes to the subclass field. When code does `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId`, the enhancement ALSO routes to the subclass field — making the shadowing invisible to Java code.

But `em.persist()` reads field values via reflection on the actual declared fields. `LedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId")` reads the base class field — which was never set (all writes were routed to the subclass by enhancement). The `nullable = false` constraint on the base table column fires.

### Diagnostic

```java
CaseLedgerEntry cle = new CaseLedgerEntry();
cle.tenancyId = "from-subclass";

// Java access (enhanced — both route to subclass):
cle.tenancyId                           → "from-subclass"
((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId           → "from-subclass"

// Reflection (raw — reveals the actual field state):
CaseLedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId").get(cle) → "from-subclass"
LedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId").get(cle)     → null  // THE BUG
```

### Fix

Remove the shadowing field from the subclass. JPA JOINED inheritance maps the base class field to the base table automatically — the subclass does not need its own declaration.

```java
// BEFORE (broken):
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    @Column(name = "tenancy_id", nullable = false)
    public String tenancyId;  // SHADOWS LedgerEntry.tenancyId
}

// AFTER (correct):
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    // tenancyId inherited from LedgerEntry — no shadowing
}
```

Migration: drop the `tenancy_id` column from the join table (it's redundant with `ledger_entry.tenancy_id`).

### Why this is non-obvious

Hibernate's bytecode enhancement makes the shadowing completely invisible to Java code. Both `cle.tenancyId` and `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId` return the same value. The error message names the subclass entity but the actual null is on the base class — and you can't see it without reflection. The symptom appears impossible: "the field is null but I literally just set it."

### Why this fix

Removing the shadowing field is the only correct fix. Workarounds (setting the base field via reflection, using a special save method) are fragile — they couple application code to JPA internals and break when the entity hierarchy changes. The field belongs on the base class; the subclass inherits it.

### Alternatives considered

- **Reflection workaround in test helpers** — sets the base field directly. Works but couples tests to the field shadowing structure and masks the underlying design bug.
- **Setting both fields explicitly** — impossible via normal Java code because enhancement intercepts the access. Would require reflection on every write path.
- **Hibernate `@Access(AccessType.PROPERTY)` with getter/setter** — might route correctly but changes the access strategy for all fields and is a much larger change.

### Caveats

- This only triggers when bytecode enhancement is active. Without enhancement (e.g. plain Hibernate outside Quarkus), both `cle.tenancyId` and `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId` access their respective declared fields — the shadowing is visible and the developer would naturally set both.
- The fix requires a Flyway migration to drop the redundant column from the join table.

**See also:** [GE-20260609-58e5d9](GE-20260609-58e5d9.md) — JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
cle.tenancyId = "test-tenant";
em.persist(cle);

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance subclass with its own repository bypasses base-class save() invariants — invisible until a constraint surfaces it
JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping — setting child field leaves parent nullable=false column null
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping — setting child field leaves parent nullable=false column null

## Context

A JPA JOINED inheritance hierarchy where the child entity redeclares a field already declared in
the parent entity — both with `@Column(nullable = false)`. The child table gets a denormalized copy
of the column (e.g. for a local index to avoid joins). This pattern is intentional for performance
but creates a hidden trap for external writers.

Example from casehub platform:
- `LedgerEntry.tenancyId @Column(name="tenancy_id", nullable=false)` — in `ledger_entry` table
- `CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId @Column(name="tenancy_id", nullable=false, length=64)` — in `case_ledger_entry` table

## Symptom

```
org.hibernate.PropertyValueException: not-null property references a null or transient value
  for entity io.casehub.ledger.model.CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId
```

Thrown even though the code explicitly sets `entry.tenancyId = "tenant-1"` before calling
`em.persist()`. The value is visibly non-null; the error says it is null.

## Root cause

Java field access is statically resolved by the reference type at compile time. When `entry`
is declared as `CaseLedgerEntry`:

```java
entry.tenancyId = value;   // resolves to CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId (shadow field)
```

This writes to the child's own field (mapped to `case_ledger_entry.tenancy_id`). The parent's
field `LedgerEntry.tenancyId` (mapped to `ledger_entry.tenancy_id`, also `nullable=false`) is
never written. Hibernate's nullability check validates BOTH the child's property AND the parent's
property — the parent's property is null → `PropertyValueException`.

## Fix

Set both fields explicitly from any external code that touches the entity:

```java
entry.tenancyId = tenancyId;                    // CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId (case_ledger_entry)
((LedgerEntry) entry).tenancyId = tenancyId;    // LedgerEntry.tenancyId (ledger_entry)
```

The explicit cast forces the Java compiler to emit `PUTFIELD LedgerEntry.tenancyId` — a
separate bytecode instruction targeting the parent class's field declaration, distinct from
the child's shadow field.

The correct long-term fix: remove the field redeclaration from the child entity. Use a
`@SecondaryTable` or a Hibernate `@Formula` to maintain the index without the shadow field.

## Why this is non-obvious

The call site `entry.tenancyId = value` looks complete. The entity compiles and CDI-deploys
without warnings. The failure surfaces at `em.persist()` with a message naming the child entity
and property — which ARE set — not the parent entity and property — which are NOT set.

The Hibernate nullability check message `entity CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId` refers to the
property-path in the entity class hierarchy, not the Java field that is actually null. This
leads to the investigation going in the wrong direction (inspecting the child's field assignment
rather than the parent's).

Any code that uses direct field access from outside the entity (common in JPA entities without
getters/setters) is silently broken when this pattern is in play. Only tests that actually
perform a database persist — not those that simply assign and read back — will catch it.

**See also:** [GE-20260612-1f4ed8](GE-20260612-1f4ed8.md) — JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement causes NOT NULL failure

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId null property exception
LedgerEntry tenancyId shadow field
JPA JOINED inheritance nullability conflict

entries.title: Hibernate generates invalid `check ((dtype in ()))` DDL when JPA subclasses are not on test classpath
entries.body:
Hibernate generates invalid `check ((dtype in ()))` DDL when JPA subclasses are not on test classpath

## Symptom

Schema creation fails with:
```
ERROR: syntax error at or near ")"
create table ledger_entry (..., dtype varchar(31) not null check ((dtype in ())), ...)
```
Both PostgreSQL and H2 reject the empty `IN` clause. The error appears during `@QuarkusTest` startup, not at runtime.

## Context

Occurs when a JPA entity uses `@Inheritance` (JOINED or SINGLE_TABLE strategy) and not all subclasses of the hierarchy are on the test classpath. Hibernate 6.x generates a discriminator CHECK constraint that lists known subclasses — if none are found, the list is empty, producing invalid SQL.

Typical scenario: a base entity lives in an API/library module; a concrete subclass lives in a separate module that is NOT included as a test dependency of the module being tested.

## What Was Tried

- Adding `beans.xml` and Jandex to the base entity's module — no effect (subclass module still absent)
- Adding `quarkus.index-dependency` for the base module — no effect
- Disabling Flyway — no effect (schema generation is Hibernate DDL, not Flyway)

## Root Cause

Hibernate 6.x generates `check ((dtype in (...)))` by scanning indexed subclasses at augmentation time. If the concrete subclass JAR (`casehub-engine-ledger` containing `CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry`) is not on the classpath, Hibernate sees zero subclasses and generates `dtype in ()` — which is illegal SQL.

## Fix

Add the subclass module as a **test scope** dependency to every module whose tests bring the base entity onto the classpath:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.casehub</groupId>
    <artifactId>casehub-engine-ledger</artifactId>
    <version>${project.version}</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

Also ensure the subclass module has `jandex-maven-plugin` configured so Quarkus can index it.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The error message (`syntax error at or near ")"`) points to invalid SQL, not a missing dependency. The natural investigation path is SQL syntax, Hibernate config, or schema setup — not classpath completeness. The base entity module may be correctly indexed and discoverable; only the subclass is missing.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`hibernate check ((dtype in ()))` error
`JPA subclass in test classpath`
`quarkus test dependency inheritance`

entries.title: JPA InheritanceType.JOINED forces all hierarchy entities into one persistence unit
entries.body:
JPA InheritanceType.JOINED forces all hierarchy entities into one persistence unit

## Symptom

Migrating to named Hibernate persistence units fails with an error about missing entities or a persistence unit resolution error, even though the entities are correctly annotated. The issue only appears when entities from two different libraries share a `JOINED` inheritance hierarchy.

## Context

Occurs when: (1) migrating from the default Hibernate PU to a named PU, (2) entity `B extends A` with `@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.JOINED)`, and (3) `A` and `B` live in different Maven modules or libraries.

## Root Cause

JPA requires all entities in an inheritance hierarchy to share a single persistence unit. If `A` is in `io.lib.model` and `B` is in `io.other.entity`, the named PU `packages` config must include both packages — even if you only want the `io.other` entities in that PU. Specifying only `io.other` causes Hibernate to fail because it can't resolve the full hierarchy.

## Fix

Include both packages in the named PU configuration:

```properties
quarkus.hibernate-orm.mypu.packages=io.other.entity,io.lib.model
```

This forces the parent entity's library into the same persistence unit, which may have schema implications (both libraries' tables are created/migrated by the same Flyway run).

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The constraint is a JPA specification requirement, but the error message from Quarkus/Hibernate does not say "hierarchy entities must share a PU." It typically presents as a mapping exception or missing entity error that points to the child entity, not to the inheritance relationship. The fix — including an external library's package in your PU config — feels wrong and is not mentioned in Quarkus named datasource documentation.

**See also:** GE-20260422-f86f42 — dual-PU setup when a library injects @Default EntityManager

**See also:** [GE-20260512-4d6f48](GE-20260512-4d6f48.md) — Panache entities cannot be scanned by two Quarkus persistence units simultaneously

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
"JPA JOINED inheritance persistence unit error"
"Hibernate named PU missing entity"
"@InheritanceType JOINED multiple libraries"

entries.title: H2 + Hibernate 6.6 JOINED inheritance — empty discriminator CHECK kills @QuarkusTest silently
entries.body:
H2 + Hibernate 6.6 JOINED inheritance — empty discriminator CHECK kills @QuarkusTest silently

### Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` fails at startup with:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: This method is normally automatically overridden in subclasses:
did you forget to annotate your entity with @Entity?
  at io.quarkus.hibernate.orm.panache.PanacheEntityBase.listAll()
```

Only reproduces after `mvn clean`. Incremental builds pass.

### Context

A Quarkus application uses JOINED inheritance entities from external jars (e.g. `LedgerEntry` from casehub-ledger). Test config uses `quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=drop-and-create` with H2 in PostgreSQL mode. The entity packages list includes the base class package but subtypes in the external jar are not discovered.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Adding `@Entity` to the failing class — already annotated
- Switching to Hibernate `update` strategy — same error
- Adding `quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation.halt-on-error=false` — tables still not created
- Enabling Flyway instead of DDL — version collision across migration paths (`V1` in multiple locations)
- Excluding ledger entity packages from test Hibernate config — same Panache error (independent issue)

### Root cause

Hibernate 6.6 generates a CHECK constraint on JOINED inheritance discriminator columns:

```sql
dtype varchar(31) not null check ((dtype in ('SubtypeA', 'SubtypeB')))
```

When entity scanning doesn't discover subtypes from external jars, the list is empty:

```sql
dtype varchar(31) not null check ((dtype in ()))
```

H2 rejects this syntax (`expected "INTERSECTS (, NOT, EXISTS, UNIQUE, INTERSECTS"`). The DDL failure is logged as WARN — not ERROR — so Hibernate continues. Tables depending on the failed DDL are never created. When a `@Startup` observer calls `PanacheEntityBase.listAll()` on one of those tables, Panache throws `implementationInjectionMissing`.

The issue is masked by Quarkus augmentation cache — stale build artifacts from previous runs have pre-computed DDL that works. Only `mvn clean test` forces re-augmentation with the current entity set.

### Fix

None known — open issue. Workarounds:

1. **Avoid `clean` builds** — incremental builds use cached augmentation that doesn't regenerate the problematic DDL. Fragile.
2. **Exclude JOINED inheritance entities from test packages** — removes the base class so no CHECK is generated. Only works if tests don't need those entities.
3. **Use Flyway for tests** — handwritten SQL avoids the CHECK constraint entirely. Requires non-overlapping version numbers across migration paths.

### Why this is non-obvious

Three misdirections compound: (1) the error message says "@Entity annotation missing" when the entity IS annotated — the real issue is table creation failure; (2) the DDL error is a WARN log buried in hundreds of startup lines — easy to miss; (3) the Quarkus augmentation cache masks the problem entirely — the issue only appears after `mvn clean`, making it look like a flaky test environment rather than a reproducible bug.

### Why this fix

No fix exists yet. The workarounds each have significant trade-offs. The cleanest long-term fix would be Hibernate not generating CHECK constraints with empty discriminator lists, or generating them only when subtypes are actually discovered.

### Alternatives considered

- `quarkus.hibernate-orm.discriminator.ignore-explicit-for-joined=true` — not a valid Quarkus/Hibernate property
- Custom `SchemaFilterProvider` to skip CHECK constraints — would work but adds complexity for a test-only issue
- Switching to TestContainers with PostgreSQL — eliminates the H2 compatibility layer entirely but adds test infrastructure weight

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`java.lang.IllegalStateException` `@Entity`
`H2 JOINED inheritance discriminator CHECK`
`quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation`

entries.title: Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails
entries.body:
Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException: column "tenancy_id" violates not-null constraint
```

Entities persisted via a static factory or utility method fail on INSERT even though the owning
parent entity has `tenancyId` set correctly.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleTree.append(digest, currentFrontier, subjectId)` is a pure static utility that
builds new `LedgerMerkleFrontier` nodes. It has no knowledge of tenancy context. The caller
in `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()` sets `tenancyId` on the `LedgerEntry` being saved
but forgot to propagate it to the frontier nodes returned by `append()`. The nodes go into
`session.persist()` with `tenancyId = null`, violating the NOT NULL constraint.

### Root cause

Static factory and utility methods that create JPA entities operate outside any tenancy context.
Multi-tenancy fields (`tenancyId`, `tenantKey`, etc.) are caller responsibilities, not factory
responsibilities. The omission is invisible until the `session.persist()` flush fires — and only
on code paths where the NOT NULL column is actually written.

### Fix

Propagate multi-tenancy fields from the parent entity onto all child entities immediately after
the factory call, before any `session.persist()`:

```java
final List<LedgerMerkleFrontier> newFrontier =
    LedgerMerkleTree.append(e.digest, currentFrontier, e.subjectId);
newFrontier.forEach(node -> node.tenancyId = e.tenancyId);  // ← propagate before persist
// ... then session.persist(node) for each
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The parent entity (`LedgerEntry`) has `tenancyId` set correctly and was used for all prior
operations. The factory method looks complete — it takes all the structural parameters it needs.
The tenancy propagation step is easy to forget because it is not part of the factory's contract
and there is no type system or annotation to enforce it.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Hibernate ConstraintViolationException tenancy_id null
Static entity factory JPA not-null insert
LedgerMerkleTree tenancyId propagation

entries.title: Flyway NOT NULL + DEFAULT column not reflected in Hibernate drop-and-create — test fixtures must set the field explicitly
entries.body:
Flyway NOT NULL + DEFAULT column not reflected in Hibernate drop-and-create — test fixtures must set the field explicitly

## Symptom

Tests fail with `NULL not allowed for column "TENANCY_ID"` (or similar NOT NULL constraint violation) after a Flyway production migration adds a NOT NULL column with a DEFAULT value to an existing table. Production works correctly. The error message names the column but gives no indication that the missing DEFAULT is the root cause.

## Context

Quarkus test setup commonly uses:
- `quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=false` — Flyway disabled in tests
- `quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=drop-and-create` — Hibernate creates the schema from JPA annotations

When a production Flyway migration adds a NOT NULL column with a DEFAULT:
```sql
ALTER TABLE work_item_template
  ADD COLUMN tenancy_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL DEFAULT '278776f9-e1b0-46fb-9032-8bddebdcf9ce';
```

Hibernate generates the schema from the JPA entity definition. If the JPA entity has `@Column(nullable = false)` without `@ColumnDefault`, Hibernate creates:
```sql
tenancy_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
```

No DEFAULT. Any INSERT that doesn't provide a value for `tenancy_id` fails immediately.

## What was tried

Searching for `LEDGER_SUBJECT_SEQUENCE` (the symptom described in the session handover) — this was wrong. The actual failing column was `TENANCY_ID`. The misleading handover description added diagnostic time.

## Root cause

Flyway DEFAULT values exist only in the SQL migration script — they are not embedded in the JPA `@Column` annotation and are not propagated to Hibernate's schema generator. Hibernate uses JPA annotations as the sole source of truth for drop-and-create. The DEFAULT disappears when Flyway doesn't run.

## Fix

Explicitly set the field in every test fixture that creates the affected entity:

```java
// Before (fails after V35__tenancy_id.sql adds NOT NULL tenancy_id)
WorkItemTemplate t = new WorkItemTemplate();
t.name = name;
t.persist();

// After
WorkItemTemplate t = new WorkItemTemplate();
t.name = name;
t.tenancyId = "278776f9-e1b0-46fb-9032-8bddebdcf9ce";  // platform default
t.persist();
```

The test fixture must own the value. The DEFAULT only applies when Flyway runs the migration.

## Why this is non-obvious

The Flyway migration looks correct — `NOT NULL DEFAULT '...'` is standard SQL. Production is unaffected. The error message (`NULL not allowed for column "TENANCY_ID"`) points at the column with no hint that the cause is a missing DEFAULT in the Hibernate-generated schema. A developer would naturally look at the insert code, not at the Flyway/Hibernate schema gap. The problem only surfaces after adding a new NOT NULL Flyway column — existing columns were added before drop-and-create was in place.

## Alternatives considered

- **Add `@ColumnDefault` to the JPA entity** — forces the DEFAULT into the Hibernate schema. Works, but couples the JPA entity to an implementation detail of the production migration value, and requires changes to a peer repo entity.
- **Enable Flyway in tests** — conflicts with `drop-and-create`; Flyway runs before Hibernate, then Hibernate drops everything.
- **Switch to Flyway-only in tests** — removes `drop-and-create`; requires all migrations to be H2-compatible. Higher maintenance burden.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Hibernate drop-and-create NULL constraint
Flyway default value missing
tenancy_id NOT NULL default

entries.title: JPA @Column(nullable=false) NOT NULL violation fires at REQUIRES_NEW commit (flush), not at save()
entries.body:
JPA @Column(nullable=false) NOT NULL violation fires at REQUIRES_NEW commit (flush), not at save()

### Symptom
`ledgerEntryRepository.save(entry)` with `entry.notifiedAt = null` returned without error.
The test then failed at a later `assertThat(entry).isNotNull()` — appearing to suggest the
listener was propagating an exception, not that the write silently failed.

### Context
An `@ObservesAsync @Transactional(REQUIRED)` observer catches an exception and calls
a fallback method annotated `@Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW)`. Inside the fallback,
`entity.notifiedAt = null` is set and `ledgerEntryRepository.save(entity)` is called.
The entity's `@Column(name = "notified_at", nullable = false)` maps to a NOT NULL column.

### Root cause
Hibernate ORM queues inserts in an action queue — `save()` / `persist()` does not execute
the INSERT immediately. The INSERT executes during the flush, which happens at transaction
commit time. When the `REQUIRES_NEW` transaction commits, Hibernate flushes, the NOT NULL
constraint fires, Narayana throws `RollbackException` wrapped in `ArcUndeclaredThrowableException`.

An inner `catch (Exception e)` around the fallback call correctly swallowed the exception —
the outer observer did not throw. But the fallback write never persisted.

### Fix
Do not set NOT NULL columns to null. If the semantic intent is "unknown/not applicable",
use a separate nullable column as the discriminator. For example, `connectorId=null` can
distinguish "error occurred before the notifier was reached" from `connectorId` set +
`delivered=false` ("connector delivery failed") — no schema change required.

Alternatively, make the column nullable via a Flyway migration before attempting null writes.

### Why this is non-obvious
`save()` / `persist()` completes without exception in both success and failure cases.
The constraint violation is asynchronous from the application's perspective — it surfaces
only at TX commit, wrapped in JTA-specific exception types. The inner catch correctly
swallows the wrapped exception, so no exception propagates, but the write still failed.
The REQUIRES_NEW boundary gives the impression the inner TX is isolated — it is, but
the isolation includes the rollback, which is invisible to the caller.

### Why this fix
Setting null in a NOT NULL column and expecting it to persist (or to fail visibly at
save() time) is the natural assumption. The flush-at-commit model means the failure
arrives far from the call site, wrapped in JTA machinery.

**See also:** [GE-20260428-5c3e93](GE-20260428-5c3e93.md) — REQUIRES_NEW suspends outer transaction — inner JPA queries see pre-commit state

**See also:** [GE-20260609-62a1a7](GE-20260609-62a1a7.md) — H2 MERGE WHEN NOT MATCHED races under concurrent transactions | [GE-20260618-0ed34c](GE-20260618-0ed34c.md) — H2 LOCK_MODE=1 has no effect with MVStore

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
JPA @Column(nullable=false) NOT NULL constraint violation
Hibernate action queue flush timing
REQUIRES_NEW transaction commit not null exception

entries.title: Hibernate dirty-check flushes PanacheEntity field writes inside Panache.withSession() — even for in-memory test stores
entries.body:
Hibernate dirty-check flushes PanacheEntity field writes inside Panache.withSession() — even for in-memory test stores

### Symptom
A JPA UPDATE fires for a field write on a `PanacheEntity` subclass, even though:
- The CDI injection test confirms the in-memory store (`InMemoryReactiveChannelStore`) is selected, not the JPA store
- The entity was created with `new Channel()` — never explicitly `persist()`ed or loaded in the current session
- `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is correctly configured

Error:
```
org.hibernate.QueryParameterException: No argument for named parameter ':tenancyId'
```

### Context
`ReactiveMessageService.dispatch()` wraps the entire dispatch in `Panache.withSession("qhorus", () -> ...)`. Inside that session scope, the in-memory store's `updateLastActivity()` does:

```java
channel.lastActivityAt = Instant.now();
```

`Channel` is a Hibernate-enhanced `PanacheEntity`. The field write is intercepted by Hibernate's dirty tracker within the active session scope and generates a JPA UPDATE at session flush.

### Root cause
Hibernate's bytecode enhancement instruments all `PanacheEntity` subclasses with dirty tracking. Any field write on an enhanced entity within an active `Panache.withSession()` scope is detected and queued for flush — regardless of whether the entity was explicitly persisted or loaded in that session. The CDI injection test proves the right bean is injected, but it does not reveal that Hibernate's session-scoped dirty tracker is intercepting field mutations on enhanced entities.

### Fix
Make the in-memory store's `updateLastActivity()` a no-op. Do not modify enhanced entity fields in-place within a `withSession()` scope:

```java
@Override
public Uni<Void> updateLastActivity(UUID channelId, String tenancyId) {
    // No-op — modifying the Hibernate-enhanced entity in-place triggers
    // a dirty-check flush when called from within Panache.withSession().
    return Uni.createFrom().voidItem();
}
```

`lastActivityAt` is set at channel creation time via `put()`; staleness tracking is irrelevant in test contexts.

### Why this is non-obvious
The CDI direct injection test is a convincing false positive: `@Inject ReactiveChannelStore` returns `InMemoryReactiveChannelStore` ✅. This proves the right bean is injected, but it does not prove that field mutations on Hibernate-enhanced entities are safe within the dispatch session scope. The JPA UPDATE is generated by Hibernate's session-level flush mechanism, not by the in-memory store calling `repo.update()` directly.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
PanacheEntity dirty-check flush
Hibernate session scope dirty tracker
quarkus arc panache withSession

entries.title: Quarkus @Entity subclass validation needs ValidationPhaseBuildItem — JPA hierarchy not resolved at AdditionalBean phase
entries.body:
Quarkus @Entity subclass validation needs ValidationPhaseBuildItem — JPA hierarchy not resolved at AdditionalBean phase

## Quarkus @Entity subclass validation needs ValidationPhaseBuildItem

### Symptom

A `@BuildStep` that checks the JPA entity hierarchy (e.g. verifying that
`@Entity` subclasses with persistent fields override a specific method) finds
zero subclasses when producing an `AdditionalBeanBuildItem`. The entity hierarchy
appears flat — only the base class is visible.

### Context

Quarkus augmentation runs in phases. The `AdditionalBeanBuildItem` phase runs
early — before Hibernate ORM has fully resolved JPA `@Entity` inheritance
(`JOINED`, `SINGLE_TABLE`, `TABLE_PER_CLASS`). At this phase, the Jandex index
knows the classes exist, but Hibernate's entity hierarchy metadata is not yet
available.

### Root cause

JPA entity inheritance resolution happens in a later build phase. A `@BuildStep`
that produces or consumes `AdditionalBeanBuildItem` runs before entity subclass
relationships are fully materialized. The Jandex index can find annotated classes,
but determining parent-child relationships across `@Inheritance` boundaries
requires the entity hierarchy to be resolved.

### Fix

Use `ValidationPhaseBuildItem` instead. This phase runs after Hibernate ORM has
resolved the full entity hierarchy. The `@BuildStep` can then use the Jandex
index to walk `@Entity` subclasses reliably:

```java
@BuildStep
void validateEntitySubclasses(ValidationPhaseBuildItem validation,
                               CombinedIndexBuildItem index) {
    // At this phase, Jandex reliably reflects the full entity hierarchy
    ClassInfo baseClass = index.getIndex()
        .getClassByName(DotName.createSimple("com.example.LedgerEntry"));
    Collection<ClassInfo> subclasses = index.getIndex()
        .getAllKnownSubclasses(baseClass.name());
    // subclasses now includes all @Entity subclasses
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The Jandex index itself is available at all build phases — `getAllKnownSubclasses()`
returns results at any phase. The issue is that the results are incomplete during
early phases for entity classes using `@Inheritance`. A developer writing an
extension-level validation naturally reaches for the earliest phase that has
Jandex access, and gets no error — just silently incomplete results.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

`Jandex index JPA inheritance`
`ValidationPhaseBuildItem AdditionalBeanBuildItem`

entries.title: @TestTransaction swallows unique-constraint violations — Hibernate never flushes within the test body
entries.body:
@TestTransaction swallows unique-constraint violations — Hibernate never flushes within the test body

## @TestTransaction swallows unique-constraint violations — Hibernate never flushes within the test body

**ID:** GE-20260414-7ce32b
**Stack:** Quarkus 3.32.2, Hibernate ORM 6.x, Panache active record, JUnit 5
**Symptom:** `assertThrows(PersistenceException.class, () -> entity.persist())` or `assertThrows(..., () -> service.create(...))` does not throw — the assertion fails with "expected exception was not thrown". The DB unique constraint is correctly defined, and the same operation fails as expected against a committed database.
**Context:** Testing that a unique constraint (e.g. unique channel name) is enforced by writing two entities with the same key inside a `@TestTransaction`-annotated test method.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Verifying the constraint exists in the Flyway migration — it did
- Adding `Entity.flush()` inside the lambda passed to `assertThrows` — partially worked but marked the transaction rollback-only, making subsequent test code unreliable
- Using `@TestTransaction` on the class — same behaviour

### Root cause

Within a single `@TestTransaction`, Hibernate queues all pending INSERTs and only flushes them to the database at the end of the transaction (commit time). When two entities with the same unique-constrained value are created inside the test body, both INSERTs are queued. The unique constraint violation only fires when Hibernate flushes — which happens **after** `assertThrows` has already exited without catching anything.

Calling `Entity.flush()` inside the lambda forces the flush, which does trigger the exception. However, once a `PersistenceException` is thrown during a `@TestTransaction` test, Hibernate marks the persistence context invalid and the transaction rollback-only. Any code after the `assertThrows` block may see unexpected exceptions or stale state.

### Fix

Use `QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew()` so each operation runs in its own committed transaction. The first commits successfully; the second fails at commit with the constraint violation; cleanup runs in a third transaction:

```java
@Test
void duplicateNameThrowsException() {
    String name = "dup-test-" + System.nanoTime();

// First create — commits cleanly
    QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew().run(() ->
            channelService.create(name, "First", ChannelSemantic.APPEND, null));

// Second create — fails at commit with constraint violation
    assertThrows(Exception.class, () ->
            QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew().run(() ->
                    channelService.create(name, "Second", ChannelSemantic.APPEND, null)));

// Cleanup the committed first record
    QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew().run(() -> Channel.delete("name", name));
}
```

Note: no `@TestTransaction` on this test — each `requiringNew()` lambda is its own transaction.

### Why non-obvious

`@TestTransaction` is the recommended isolation mechanism for Quarkus data tests, and it works well for happy paths. The constraint-test failure looks like the constraint is missing, not like a flush-timing issue — there's no exception, just a missing one. The `QuarkusTransaction` API is not prominently featured in Quarkus testing docs; most examples use `@TestTransaction` or `@Transactional`.

**See also:** GE-20260414-99854d [@TestTransaction + Hibernate JPQL bulk update = silently stale first-level cache] | GE-20260415-e92f89 [@TestTransaction + @Transactional method call + REST assertion — data invisible]

**See also:** GE-20260414-278875 — QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew() pattern for testing DB constraints that need independent commits (the fix)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`@TestTransaction` unique constraint workaround
Hibernate flush behavior in tests
PersistenceException JUnit 5 test

entries.title: Named Hibernate ORM persistence unit requires both @PersistenceUnit qualifier AND packages config for entity discovery
entries.body:
Named Hibernate ORM persistence unit requires both @PersistenceUnit qualifier AND packages config for entity discovery

### Symptom

JPA queries return empty results or `em.find()` returns null for entities that exist in the database. No error, no warning — Hibernate simply doesn't see the entity class.

### Context

Adding a JPA entity to an application that shares a foundation module's named persistence unit (e.g. Qhorus's `qhorus` PU). The entity is in a different package than the foundation module's entities.

### Root cause

Two independent configuration points must both be set:

1. `@PersistenceUnit("qhorus")` on the EntityManager injection — without it, the default PU is used, which has no datasource configured
2. `quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages` must include the new entity's package — Hibernate only scans packages listed in this config for the named PU

Missing either one causes silent failure. The compound nature is what makes this non-obvious — setting only the annotation or only the packages config both appear correct in isolation but produce empty results.

### Fix

Both changes are required:

```java
@Inject
@PersistenceUnit("qhorus")
EntityManager em;
```

```properties
# application.properties — extend the existing packages list
quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages=io.casehub.qhorus.runtime,io.casehub.ledger.runtime,io.casehub.drafthouse
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Each configuration point has its own diagnostic blind spot:
- Missing `@PersistenceUnit`: the default PU has no datasource, so Quarkus may fail at startup with an opaque CDI error OR silently use a different (empty) schema
- Missing packages config: the entity class exists on the classpath and the PU is correct, but Hibernate's entity scan doesn't find it — no warning, just empty results
- Both missing: you get the compound failure of both above

Related entries cover individual aspects — GE-20260422-334eb8 covers the annotation import (`io.quarkus.hibernate.orm.PersistenceUnit` not `jakarta.persistence.PersistenceUnit`), GE-20260424-6b88a0 covers datasource routing. This entry covers the compound requirement.

**See also:** [GE-20260612-8e925b](GE-20260612-8e925b.md) — Quarkus quarkus.hibernate-orm.<pu-name>.sql-load-script for named PU | [GE-20260512-ea776c](GE-20260512-ea776c.md) — Quarkus named persistence units silently skip schema generation | [GE-20260521-2b82e7](GE-20260521-2b82e7.md) — Panache.withTransaction() uses the default persistence unit | [GE-20260530-da427e](GE-20260530-da427e.md) — Quarkus multi-PU sub-package matching assigns entities to wrong PU | [GE-20260423-fce720](GE-20260423-fce720.md) — quarkus-work-core FilterRule JPA entity requires datasource | [GE-20260429-21e6cf](GE-20260429-21e6cf.md) — JPA entity in dependency forces datasource config on all downstream consumers

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
@PersistenceUnit("qhorus") EntityManager
quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages

entries.title: quarkus-rest does not include Bean Validation — @NotBlank/@Valid silently ignored without quarkus-hibernate-validator
entries.body:
quarkus-rest does not include Bean Validation — @NotBlank/@Valid silently ignored without quarkus-hibernate-validator

## Symptom

`@Valid` on a JAX-RS method parameter and `@NotBlank`/`@NotNull`/`@Positive` on request body record fields compile, CDI wires, and the app starts — but validation never fires. A missing required field returns 200 instead of 400. A null enum field causes a 500 on persist instead of a 400 at the REST layer.

## Context

Quarkus REST application using `quarkus-rest` and `quarkus-rest-jackson`. Bean Validation annotations are on record component fields. `@Valid` is on the JAX-RS method parameter.

## Root Cause

`quarkus-rest` does not transitively include `quarkus-hibernate-validator`. The Jakarta Validation API is on the classpath (from another transitive dep), so annotations resolve at compile time, but the validation provider that actually enforces constraints is absent. Quarkus silently skips validation rather than throwing a startup error.

## Fix

Add `quarkus-hibernate-validator` explicitly to `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
    <artifactId>quarkus-hibernate-validator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Once added, `@Valid` triggers constraint evaluation and returns 400 with a constraint violation body on failure.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Quarkus RESTEasy Classic included validation transitively. Developers migrating to `quarkus-rest` (the new reactive REST layer) expect the same behaviour. The silent failure — annotations present, app starts, but constraints don't fire — gives no diagnostic signal. The only way to discover it is a failing test showing 200 where 400 was expected.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

quarkus-hibernate-validator missing
"@Valid" not triggering quarkus

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance: filtering by subclass column vs inherited column for same UUID — only inherited uses the index
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance: filtering by subclass column vs inherited column for same UUID — only inherited uses the index

## JPA JOINED inheritance: filtering by subclass column vs inherited column for same UUID — only inherited uses the index

### Symptom

A JPQL query using `WHERE e.caseId = :id` runs full scans on the subclass join despite an index existing for the same logical filter. Switching to `WHERE e.subjectId = :id` — where `subjectId` is set to the same UUID — makes the query use the index.

### Context

In JPA `JOINED` inheritance, the entity hierarchy maps to multiple tables joined on `id`. Consider:

```java
@Entity @Table(name = "ledger_entry")
public abstract class LedgerEntry {
    @Column(name = "subject_id") public UUID subjectId;  // indexed
    @Column(name = "sequence_number") public int sequenceNumber;
}

@Entity @Table(name = "case_ledger_entry")
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    @Column(name = "case_id") public UUID caseId;  // same value, NOT indexed
}
```

DB index: `CREATE INDEX idx ON ledger_entry (subject_id, sequence_number)` — on the **parent** table only.

At runtime, `caseId` and `subjectId` are always set to the same UUID. But the JPQL predicate determines which table column the WHERE clause targets:

```sql
-- WHERE e.caseId = :id → filters on case_ledger_entry.case_id (no index)
SELECT ... FROM ledger_entry l JOIN case_ledger_entry c ON l.id = c.id WHERE c.case_id = ?

-- WHERE e.subjectId = :id → filters on ledger_entry.subject_id (indexed)
SELECT ... FROM ledger_entry l JOIN case_ledger_entry c ON l.id = c.id WHERE l.subject_id = ?
```

### Fix

When the same UUID is stored in both the subclass and inherited columns, always query via the inherited field to use the index:

```java
// Correct — uses idx_ledger_entry_subject_seq:
em.createQuery(
    "SELECT e FROM CaseLedgerEntry e WHERE e.subjectId = :id ORDER BY e.sequenceNumber DESC",
    CaseLedgerEntry.class)
  .setParameter("id", caseId)
  .setMaxResults(1)
  .getResultStream().findFirst();

// Avoid — same result, no index benefit:
em.createQuery(
    "SELECT e FROM CaseLedgerEntry e WHERE e.caseId = :id ORDER BY e.sequenceNumber DESC",
    CaseLedgerEntry.class)
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Hibernate makes both fields appear semantically equivalent in the Java model — same type, same runtime value, same query results. There is no warning from Hibernate's query plan, no IDE hint, and no mention of this in the JPA or Hibernate ORM documentation for JOINED inheritance. The only way to discover it is to inspect the schema DDL and trace which table each mapped column lives on.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`e.subjectId = :id`
`JPQL filtering by UUID`
`JOINED inheritance index usage`

entries.title: casehub-ledger LedgerEntry api/runtime split — consumer subclasses must extend JpaLedgerEntry, not LedgerEntry
entries.body:
casehub-ledger LedgerEntry api/runtime split — consumer subclasses must extend JpaLedgerEntry, not LedgerEntry

casehub-ledger LedgerEntry api/runtime split — consumer subclasses must extend JpaLedgerEntry, not LedgerEntry

### Symptom

Hibernate generates INSERT statements that include ALL parent columns (`actor_id`, `actor_role`, `actor_type`, `occurred_at`, `digest`, `subject_id`, `tenancy_id`, etc.) in the consumer's subclass table. The database returns `Column "ACTOR_DID" not found` (or whichever parent column was most recently added).

### Context

`casehub-ledger` split `LedgerEntry` into two classes:
- `io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry` — `@MappedSuperclass`, field definitions only, no JPA inheritance. Lives in `casehub-ledger-api` (no framework deps).
- `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry` — `@Entity @Inheritance(JOINED) @DiscriminatorColumn`, extends `LedgerEntry`. Lives in `casehub-ledger` runtime module.

Consumer subclass tables (e.g. `aml_case_opened_ledger_entry`) were designed for JOINED inheritance — they only contain the join column (`id` FK to `ledger_entry`) plus subclass-specific columns. Parent columns live in the `ledger_entry` base table.

### Root cause

When a consumer `@Entity` extends `LedgerEntry` (the `@MappedSuperclass`), Hibernate treats it as a standalone entity — ALL parent fields are mapped directly to the subclass table. The `@DiscriminatorValue` annotation on the subclass is silently ignored (no `@Inheritance` on the parent). Hibernate generates INSERTs with 20+ parent columns that don't exist in the subclass table.

### Fix

Change consumer subclasses from `extends LedgerEntry` to `extends JpaLedgerEntry`:

```java
// WRONG — @MappedSuperclass, duplicates all parent columns to subclass table
import io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry;
public class AmlCaseOpenedLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry { ... }

// CORRECT — @Entity @Inheritance(JOINED), subclass table only needs its own columns
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry;
public class AmlCaseOpenedLedgerEntry extends JpaLedgerEntry { ... }
```

The engine-ledger module (`CaseLedgerEntry`, `WorkerDecisionEntry`) already extends `JpaLedgerEntry` — consumer modules must follow the same pattern.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error message (`Column "ACTOR_DID" not found`) points at a missing column, suggesting a migration fix. The natural response is to add the column via Flyway — which leads to adding ALL parent columns to every subclass table, fundamentally misunderstanding the schema design. The actual fix (changing the superclass) is in the Java import, not the SQL.

### Why this fix

Adding parent columns to subclass tables "works" but creates a TABLE_PER_CLASS schema that duplicates data, breaks the shared `ledger_entry` base table design, and defeats the purpose of JOINED inheritance. Extending `JpaLedgerEntry` preserves the original schema contract.

### Alternatives considered

- **Add all parent columns to each subclass table via Flyway** — compiles and runs but creates redundant data storage, breaks FK relationships, and diverges from the engine-ledger module's pattern.
- **Add `io.casehub.ledger.api.model` to the Hibernate PU packages** — makes Hibernate see the `@MappedSuperclass` but doesn't fix the inheritance strategy; still generates wrong INSERT statements.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Hibernate insert all parent columns
JpaLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry error
Inheritance and discriminator column mapping issues

entries.body:
Await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain via Uni.createFrom().completionStage()

## Await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain

### Context

A Quarkus @ConsumeEvent handler returns Uni<Void>. Inside the chain, lifecycleEvents.fireAsync(event)
is called inside .invoke(). The CompletionStage is discarded. @ObservesAsync observers may run AFTER
the handler's Uni completes.

### The technique

Split the terminal .invoke() into two steps:

```java
// Before — CompletionStage discarded
.invoke(() -> {
    eventBus.publish(addr, payload);
    lifecycleEvents.fireAsync(event); // discarded
});

// After — CDI delivery awaited in .chain()
.invoke(() -> {
    eventBus.publish(addr, payload); // still fire-and-forget
})
.chain(() ->
    Uni.createFrom()
        .completionStage(() -> lifecycleEvents.fireAsync(event))
        .onFailure()
        .recoverWithItem(t -> { LOG.warnf(t, "observer failed"); return null; })
        .replaceWithVoid())
```

The handler's Uni does not complete until all @ObservesAsync observers have run.
onFailure().recoverWithItem() prevents observer exceptions from breaking the handler.

### Why this is non-obvious

.invoke() reads as a side-effect callback but is fire-and-forget for CompletionStage —
Mutiny does not chain off it. Moving to .chain() with completionStage() makes CDI
delivery part of the reactive pipeline.

Use the Supplier form completionStage(() -> fireAsync(...)) — lazy, ensures fireAsync()
is called at subscription time (correct thread context), not at chain construction time.

**See also:** [GE-20260517-f31786](GE-20260517-f31786.md) — fireAsync() returns CompletionStage<Event<T>> not CompletionStage<Void> — Mutiny bridge needs .replaceWith() | [GE-20260512-0fe012](GE-20260512-0fe012.md) — CDI fireAsync() inside @Transactional dispatches immediately

**See also:** [GE-20260518-a61d1b](GE-20260518-a61d1b.md) — @ConsumeEvent(blocking=true) and @Transactional on the same method work correctly

**See also:** [GE-20260616-6f1743](GE-20260616-6f1743.md) — AtomicReference to capture values across Mutiny Uni chain when chain switches threads

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: `event.fireAsync()` returns `CompletionStage<Event<T>>` not `CompletionStage<Void>` — Mutiny bridge needs `.replaceWith()`
entries.body:
`event.fireAsync()` returns `CompletionStage<Event<T>>` not `CompletionStage<Void>` — Mutiny bridge needs `.replaceWith()`

### Symptom

Type mismatch when bridging `Event.fireAsync()` to a Mutiny `Uni` pipeline:

```java
// Fails — CompletionStage<Event<MyEvent>>, not CompletionStage<VerificationResult>
return Uni.createFrom().completionStage(
    () -> suspectEvent.fireAsync(new MyEvent(...)))
    // compiler error: cannot convert Uni<Event<MyEvent>> to Uni<VerificationResult>
```

### Context

Quarkus reactive service using CDI `Event<T>` needs to fire an async event and return a `Uni<SomeType>` from the same pipeline.

### Root cause

`Event.fireAsync()` is declared in the CDI spec as returning `CompletionStage<Event<T>>` — it returns the event object itself wrapped in a completion stage, not `CompletionStage<Void>`. Most usage examples ignore the return value entirely, hiding the actual type.

### Fix

Use `.replaceWith()` to discard the `Event<T>` wrapper and substitute the intended result:

```java
return Uni.createFrom().completionStage(
    () -> suspectEvent.fireAsync(new MyEvent(entryId, actorId, keyRef)))
    .replaceWith(VerificationResult.SUSPECT);
```

### Why this is non-obvious

CDI spec says "returns a CompletionStage" without emphasising the `<Event<T>>` type parameter. Developers writing async event firing naturally assume `CompletionStage<Void>` because they're triggering a side effect and discarding the event payload. The full generic type is only visible in the CDI API Javadoc — not in any tutorials or common usage examples.

**See also:** [GE-20260423-daef97](GE-20260423-daef97.md) — CDI event.fire() does not deliver to @ObservesAsync observers — fireAsync() required

**See also:** [GE-20260529-e43076](GE-20260529-e43076.md) — await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain

entries.body:
Place fireAsync() before internal dispatch to decouple delivery paths in @Transactional methods

## Place fireAsync() before internal dispatch to decouple delivery paths in @Transactional methods

### Symptom

A `@Transactional` method fires a CDI event and also calls an internal dispatch (channel write, database write, queue push). When the internal dispatch throws — rate-limit rejection, policy violation, missing resource — the CDI event silently never fires. The external delivery path is dead with no error.

### Context

Any method that must make two independent deliveries inside a `@Transactional` boundary:
one via CDI `fireAsync()` (external observers, notification systems) and one via an internal
service call. The pattern appears in watchdog alerting, domain event publishing, and audit
side-channels.

### Root cause

Ordering. If `fireAsync()` is placed *after* the internal dispatch and dispatch throws, the
stack unwinds before `fireAsync()` is reached. The two paths are not independent — external
delivery is silently contingent on internal dispatch succeeding.

### Fix

Place `fireAsync()` as the first statement inside the method, before the internal dispatch:

```java
private void fireAlert(Watchdog w, String summary, AlertContext context, Instant now) {
    // External delivery FIRST — not contingent on internal channel success.
    // A rate-limited, paused, or policy-rejected dispatch must not suppress this.
    alertEvents.fireAsync(new WatchdogAlertEvent(
            w.id, w.targetName, w.notificationChannel, summary, now, context));

// Internal dispatch SECOND — failure does not suppress the event already fired.
    Optional<Channel> ch = channelService.findByName(w.notificationChannel);
    if (ch.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }
    messageService.dispatch(MessageDispatch.builder()
            .channelId(ch.get().id)
            .sender("system:watchdog")
            .type(MessageType.STATUS)
            .content(summary)
            .build());
}
```

The CDI event fires unconditionally (after the guard checks). The internal dispatch is the
conditional secondary path.

### Accepted trade-off

If the outer `@Transactional` rolls back after `fireAsync()` dispatches, the observer runs
for a state change that never committed — a ghost notification. The window is narrow in
practice (only a post-dispatch interceptor or infrastructure failure causes an outer rollback).
For alerting systems: accepted — false-positive alert is better than missed alert. For audit
or ledger systems: not acceptable — use a transactional outbox pattern instead.

### Why this is non-obvious

CDI events feel like side effects. By convention, developers put them at the *end* of a method,
after "the main work" is done. When the event IS the primary delivery path — not a side effect
— this ordering must invert. The distinction only surfaces when the two paths need to be
genuinely independent rather than sequential. Without this insight, a failing internal dispatch
silently kills external delivery with no error or log entry.

**See also:** [GE-20260512-0fe012](GE-20260512-0fe012.md) — fireAsync() dispatches immediately inside @Transactional (the timing gotcha this technique builds on)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
fireAsync() after internal dispatch
@Transactional event suppression
rate-limit rejection CDI event

@ObservesAsync CDI handlers run without the caller's OTel span — traceId silently null on async thread
entries.body:
@ObservesAsync CDI handlers run without the caller's OTel span — traceId silently null on async thread

## Symptom

`@ObservesAsync` handler runs, JPA `@PrePersist` fires, but a field populated from
`Span.current().getSpanContext().getTraceId()` is null — even though an active HTTP request
span existed when the CDI event was fired.

No error is thrown. The persist succeeds. The `traceId` column is silently null.

## Context

Any Quarkus CDI `@ObservesAsync` handler that runs code which reads the active OTel span
(directly or via a JPA entity listener like `LedgerTraceListener`).

## Root Cause

`@ObservesAsync` dispatches to a Quarkus managed thread pool. OTel span context is stored in
a thread-local (`io.opentelemetry.context.Context`). It does **not** automatically transfer to
the async thread.

When the managed thread calls `Span.current()`, it finds an invalid/no-op span — not the span
that was active on the original Vert.x handler thread. Any field that reads the trace ID from
the current span receives null.

The existing Quarkus OTel extension propagates context for Vert.x handlers and Mutiny pipelines,
but NOT for raw CDI `@ObservesAsync` dispatch.

## Proof

The JPA entity listener itself confirms this with its own test:
`LedgerTraceListenerIT.traceId_nullWhenNoActiveSpan()` explicitly asserts `traceId` is null
when no span is active — the async handler always hits this code path.

## Fix

### Solution 1 — Capture context before the async boundary

On the originating (synchronous) thread, capture `Context.current()` and set the field
explicitly before the async handoff:

```java
// On the synchronous Vert.x handler thread (BEFORE fireAsync):
String capturedTraceId = Span.current().getSpanContext().getTraceId();
// Then in the @ObservesAsync handler, set it directly:
entry.traceId = capturedTraceId.isBlank() ? null : capturedTraceId;
```

### Solution 2 — Wrap async executor with OTel context

Use the OTel context propagation API to wrap the executor used by the CDI event:

```java
Context otelCtx = Context.current(); // captured on calling thread
event.fireAsync(payload, NotificationOptions.builder()
    .setExecutor(otelCtx.wrap(managedExecutor))
    .build());
```

This propagates the span to the async thread transparently.

Solution 1 is simpler and lower risk for isolated write paths. Solution 2 is better when the
async handler does multiple things that each need the span.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The Quarkus OTel extension documentation states it propagates trace context automatically.
It does — for Vert.x and Mutiny pipelines. CDI `@ObservesAsync` uses a different thread
pool that is not instrumented the same way. The documentation does not call this out.

A developer seeing null `traceId` in production would first suspect the entity listener
configuration, then the JPA lifecycle, before looking at thread-local context propagation.

**See also:** [GE-20260422-70b817](GE-20260422-70b817.md) — Span.wrap(SpanContext).makeCurrent() creates OTel trace context in tests without SDK

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

Quarkus OTel context propagation for `@ObservesAsync`

PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY @QuarkusTest: subscribe to unfiltered stream to confirm channel active before asserting on filtered results
entries.body:
PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY @QuarkusTest: subscribe to unfiltered stream to confirm channel active before asserting on filtered results

## Symptom

A `@QuarkusTest` integration test for a PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY broadcaster
fails intermittently with `ConditionTimeoutException` — the awaitility condition
times out even though the test logic is correct and passing in most CI runs. The
same commit SHA shows both pass and fail on successive runs.

## Context

`PostgresWorkItemEventBroadcaster.startListening()` is annotated `@PostConstruct`.
It issues a `LISTEN <channel>` command via the Vert.x reactive PG client — an async
call that returns immediately; the LISTEN is established on the Vert.x event loop
after control returns to the caller. Quarkus marks the application ready after all
`@PostConstruct` calls return, but does not wait for their async work to complete.

Tests that subscribe to a filtered stream and immediately fire events may do so
before the LISTEN is registered with PostgreSQL. Events published via `pg_notify`
reach the subscriber connection only after LISTEN is active — events fired before
that are silently dropped.

## What was tried (didn't work)

Increasing the awaitility timeout from 5 seconds to 10 seconds: reduced flake
frequency but did not eliminate it (the root cause is the LISTEN not being active,
not the notify→receive path being slow).

## Fix — Warm-up probe

Before subscribing to the filtered stream, subscribe to the **unfiltered** stream and
wait for a known event to arrive. This confirms the LISTEN channel is established and
the full async path (pg_notify → subscriber connection → BroadcastProcessor) is working:

```java
// 1. Subscribe to unfiltered stream BEFORE creating any items
final List<WorkItemLifecycleEvent> warmup = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
broadcaster.stream(null, null).subscribe().with(warmup::add);

// 2. Create the target item and wait for its CREATED event to arrive
final WorkItem target = createWorkItem("Target item");
Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .until(() -> warmup.stream().anyMatch(e -> target.id.equals(e.workItemId())));

// 3. LISTEN channel confirmed active — now subscribe to the filtered stream
final List<WorkItemLifecycleEvent> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
broadcaster.stream(target.id, null).subscribe().with(received::add);

// 4. Proceed with the test (noise items, claims, assertions)
```

The `BroadcastProcessor` is a hot stream — events emitted before subscription are
lost. Subscribing before creating any items ensures the warm-up probe captures the
CREATED event and the subsequent filtered subscription captures all later events.

## Why this is non-obvious

The application appears fully ready (HTTP is serving, CDI is wired) when the tests
start. The `@PostConstruct` has returned. There is no visible gap — but the LISTEN
command is in flight on the Vert.x event loop and may not have been acknowledged by
PostgreSQL yet. The failure only appears when the first `pg_notify` fires before that
acknowledgement arrives, which depends on container startup speed and event loop
scheduling in CI.

Bumping the awaitility timeout is the instinctive fix but addresses the wrong problem.
The test doesn't need more time to wait for the result — it needs to confirm the
infrastructure is ready before generating the result.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
LISTEN NOTIFY ConditionTimeoutException QuarkusTest
pg_notify subscriber connection
unfiltered stream verify

entries.body:
Quarkus Flow `listen` task does not receive from SmallRye in-memory channels

## Quarkus Flow `listen` task does not receive from SmallRye in-memory channels

**ID:** GE-0070
**Stack:** `io.quarkiverse.flow:quarkus-flow:0.7.1`, Quarkus 3.34.2, SmallRye Reactive Messaging
**Symptom:** A `Flow` subclass with `listen("tick", toOne("org.acme.example.tick"))` in its `descriptor()` never fires when a `MutinyEmitter<MyType>` emits on a SmallRye in-memory channel. No error is thrown. The workflow is silently idle.
**Context:** Attempting to wire a SmallRye `@Channel("my-channel") MutinyEmitter<MyType>` to a Quarkus Flow workflow using the FuncDSL `listen` task.

### Root cause

The `listen` task in Quarkus Flow (CNCF Serverless Workflow spec) subscribes to CloudEvents, not to SmallRye Reactive Messaging channels. The `toOne("org.acme.example.tick")` string is a CloudEvent type, not a channel name. SmallRye in-memory channels carry plain Java objects — they are not CloudEvents and cannot be received by the `listen` task without additional CloudEvent wrapping infrastructure.

### Fix

Bridge SmallRye to the Flow engine using `@Incoming` + `startInstance()` directly on the `Flow` subclass. See GE-0071.

```java
// BROKEN — listen() doesn't receive from SmallRye in-memory @Channel
@Override
public Workflow descriptor() {
    return workflow("my-flow")
        .tasks(
            listen("tick", toOne("org.acme.example.tick")),  // never fires
            ...
        ).build();
}
```

### Why non-obvious

The quarkus-flow documentation and FuncDSL skill show `listen` as a standard reactive task. Nothing indicates it requires CloudEvent format specifically. The failure is silent — no error, no log, the flow just never starts. Developers naturally try the `listen` task first when integrating with SmallRye messaging.

*Score: 13/15 · Included because: silent failure, non-obvious CloudEvent requirement, affects the primary integration pattern developers will attempt · Reservation: only verified on 0.7.1 with in-memory connector*

**See also:** GE-20260414-5b3897 — quarkus-flow uses the CNCF Serverless Workflow SDK directly — not Kogito

entries.title: @ObservesAsync CDI events are silently not delivered in @QuarkusTest — call observer directly
entries.body:
@ObservesAsync CDI events are silently not delivered in @QuarkusTest — call observer directly

## @ObservesAsync CDI events are silently not delivered in @QuarkusTest — call observer directly

### Symptom

`@ObservesAsync` observer methods are never invoked during `@QuarkusTest` runs. No exception, no warning — `Event.fireAsync(event)` completes normally but the observer body never executes.

### Context

Any `@QuarkusTest` class that relies on CDI async event delivery to exercise listener logic. The pattern often surfaces when testing event-driven workflows where a terminal event (e.g. case lifecycle, job completion) is supposed to trigger a listener that updates state.

### Root cause — timing (primary)

The async event delivery in Quarkus test context relies on a managed executor whose completion is not awaited within the synchronous test flow. `fireAsync()` returns a `CompletionStage` that the caller discards — the observer may execute after the test has already asserted and exited, or may not execute within the test JVM's lifecycle at all. There is no error because CDI considers delivery complete when the `CompletionStage` is returned, regardless of whether the observer ran.

### Root cause — build-time registration (inner-class test beans)

A second, independent root cause applies specifically to `@ObservesAsync` methods on `@ApplicationScoped` **inner-class** beans declared inside a `@QuarkusTest` with `@TestProfile`. Quarkus ArC processes CDI observer registrations **at build time**. Inner-class beans in `@TestProfile` test classes are added to the CDI container (injection works — `@Inject LifecycleCapture capture` succeeds), but their observer methods may not be in ArC's build-time observer registry. `Event.fireAsync()` then completes immediately with zero observers dispatched — no error, no warning.

Distinguishing symptoms:
- **Timing root cause**: the event fires into real observers that execute asynchronously (logging inside the observer confirms this, if waited long enough)
- **Registration root cause**: `fireAsync()` returns immediately regardless of timeout; the observer body never executes even with 60-second `Awaitility` waits; no "observer failed" log appears

The registration issue cannot be worked around by awaiting the `CompletionStage` — the stage completes immediately because there are no registered observers to await.

### Fix

Inject the observer bean directly and call the observer method synchronously:

```java
// ❌ relies on CDI async delivery — silently does nothing in @QuarkusTest
event.fireAsync(myEvent);

// ✅ inject and invoke directly
@Inject MyListener listener;

// in the test body:
listener.onEvent(myEvent); // synchronous — guaranteed to run before assertions
```

Document the workaround in the test comment:

```java
// CDI @ObservesAsync delivery is unreliable in @QuarkusTest context.
// Invoke the listener directly to test the observer logic synchronously.
listener.onCaseLifecycle(completedEvent);
```

For tests that cannot call the observer directly (e.g. testing a full async chain), move the observer bean to main sources so ArC registers it at build time. Observers in main sources are always registered regardless of test profile.

### Why this is non-obvious

The symptom is total silence — no exception, no skipped assertion. The obvious debugging path (add logging to `fireAsync()`) confirms the event was fired. Only adding logging inside the observer itself reveals it never ran. The test passes or fails based on pre-observer state, giving false confidence.

The registration root cause is especially misleading because `@Inject MyCapture capture` succeeds — the bean IS in the CDI container. Only the observer method is absent from the registry.

**See also:** [GE-20260517-712fe5](GE-20260517-712fe5.md) — @ApplicationScoped capture bean technique | [GE-20260501-9de50b](../quarkus/GE-20260501-9de50b.md) — @ObservesAsync events leak between tests

**See also:** [GE-20260519-dcdac5](GE-20260519-dcdac5.md) — @Transactional dropped when @ObservesAsync observer calls this.method()

**See also:** [GE-20260525-f04530](GE-20260525-f04530.md) — inject Event<T> in @QuarkusTest as synchronous test driver for @Observes handlers

**See also:** [GE-20260531-e1ce47](GE-20260531-e1ce47.md) — CDI @Observes and @ObservesAsync are separate delivery channels

**See also:** [GE-20260602-9ae24a](GE-20260602-9ae24a.md) — @ObservesAsync REQUIRES_NEW write causes intermittent test failure

**See also:** [GE-20260609-d93a6d](GE-20260609-d93a6d.md) — @ObservesAsync is a PARAMETER annotation — method-level placement silently has no effect

EndpointCapability.RECEIVE is wrong for poll streams — use QUERY
entries.body:
EndpointCapability.RECEIVE is wrong for poll streams — use QUERY

## Symptom

`EndpointRegistry.discover()` filtered by `EndpointCapability.RECEIVE` returns poll target endpoints alongside Kafka topics and webhook receivers. Filtering by `EndpointProtocol.HTTP` alone does not distinguish poll targets from webhook inbound receivers. The wrong module picks up endpoints it should not handle.

## Context

When registering stream endpoint descriptors — Kafka topics, AMQP queues, webhooks, poll targets — all feel like "receiving data." The natural choice for all five is `EndpointCapability.RECEIVE`. But poll uses a different access pattern from the others.

## Root cause

`EndpointCapability.RECEIVE` means "Endpoint can push data to the caller (webhook delivery, Kafka consume, SSE)." This is correct for:
- Kafka — the broker pushes messages to our consumer
- AMQP — same push semantics
- Webhook — external system POSTs to our endpoint
- Camel — route delivers to CDI observer

But **poll** (platform-streams-poll) initiates an HTTP GET — we pull from the endpoint. That is `QUERY`: "Caller can issue a read request and receive a synchronous response (HTTP GET, MCP query)."

Both poll and webhook use `EndpointProtocol.HTTP`. Without the correct capability, there is no way to distinguish them in `EndpointRegistry.discover()` queries.

## Fix

Use `EndpointCapability.QUERY` for poll targets:

```java
// WRONG — poll target registered as RECEIVE
EndpointDescriptor wrong = new EndpointDescriptor(
    path, tenancyId, EndpointType.SYSTEM, EndpointProtocol.HTTP,
    Map.of(...), null,
    Set.of(EndpointCapability.RECEIVE));  // incorrect for pull/GET

// CORRECT — poll target registered as QUERY
EndpointDescriptor correct = new EndpointDescriptor(
    path, tenancyId, EndpointType.SYSTEM, EndpointProtocol.HTTP,
    Map.of(...), null,
    Set.of(EndpointCapability.QUERY));   // HTTP GET initiated by us
```

The poll module discovers endpoints with `EndpointCapability.QUERY`; webhook registers with `EndpointCapability.RECEIVE`. Both use `HTTP` protocol — capability is the only discriminator.

## Why this is non-obvious

"Receiving data" semantically covers both patterns. The distinction ("who initiates?") only surfaces when you read the Javadoc carefully: RECEIVE = endpoint pushes to caller; QUERY = caller issues a read request. The failure mode is silent — wrong module discovery, no error, no warning.

**See also:** [GE-20260615-d008ea](GE-20260615-d008ea.md) — EndpointPropertyKeys.URL does not apply to KAFKA — only HTTP, GRPC, MCP, CAMEL, QHORUS

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
EndpointCapability.RECEIVE vs. QUERY
`EndpointRegistry.discover` filtering by `EndpointCapability.RECEIVE`
`EndpointDescriptor` with `EndpointCapability.RECEIVE` for poll targets

Place fireAsync() before internal dispatch to decouple delivery paths in @Transactional methods
entries.body:
Place fireAsync() before internal dispatch to decouple delivery paths in @Transactional methods

## Place fireAsync() before internal dispatch to decouple delivery paths in @Transactional methods

### Symptom

A `@Transactional` method fires a CDI event and also calls an internal dispatch (channel write, database write, queue push). When the internal dispatch throws — rate-limit rejection, policy violation, missing resource — the CDI event silently never fires. The external delivery path is dead with no error.

### Context

Any method that must make two independent deliveries inside a `@Transactional` boundary:
one via CDI `fireAsync()` (external observers, notification systems) and one via an internal
service call. The pattern appears in watchdog alerting, domain event publishing, and audit
side-channels.

### Root cause

Ordering. If `fireAsync()` is placed *after* the internal dispatch and dispatch throws, the
stack unwinds before `fireAsync()` is reached. The two paths are not independent — external
delivery is silently contingent on internal dispatch succeeding.

### Fix

Place `fireAsync()` as the first statement inside the method, before the internal dispatch:

```java
private void fireAlert(Watchdog w, String summary, AlertContext context, Instant now) {
    // External delivery FIRST — not contingent on internal channel success.
    // A rate-limited, paused, or policy-rejected dispatch must not suppress this.
    alertEvents.fireAsync(new WatchdogAlertEvent(
            w.id, w.targetName, w.notificationChannel, summary, now, context));

// Internal dispatch SECOND — failure does not suppress the event already fired.
    Optional<Channel> ch = channelService.findByName(w.notificationChannel);
    if (ch.isEmpty()) {
        return;
    }
    messageService.dispatch(MessageDispatch.builder()
            .channelId(ch.get().id)
            .sender("system:watchdog")
            .type(MessageType.STATUS)
            .content(summary)
            .build());
}
```

The CDI event fires unconditionally (after the guard checks). The internal dispatch is the
conditional secondary path.

### Accepted trade-off

If the outer `@Transactional` rolls back after `fireAsync()` dispatches, the observer runs
for a state change that never committed — a ghost notification. The window is narrow in
practice (only a post-dispatch interceptor or infrastructure failure causes an outer rollback).
For alerting systems: accepted — false-positive alert is better than missed alert. For audit
or ledger systems: not acceptable — use a transactional outbox pattern instead.

### Why this is non-obvious

CDI events feel like side effects. By convention, developers put them at the *end* of a method,
after "the main work" is done. When the event IS the primary delivery path — not a side effect
— this ordering must invert. The distinction only surfaces when the two paths need to be
genuinely independent rather than sequential. Without this insight, a failing internal dispatch
silently kills external delivery with no error or log entry.

**See also:** [GE-20260512-0fe012](GE-20260512-0fe012.md) — fireAsync() dispatches immediately inside @Transactional (the timing gotcha this technique builds on)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

@Transactional event suppression

entries.title: Await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain via Uni.createFrom().completionStage()
entries.body:
Await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain via Uni.createFrom().completionStage()

## Await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain

### Context

A Quarkus @ConsumeEvent handler returns Uni<Void>. Inside the chain, lifecycleEvents.fireAsync(event)
is called inside .invoke(). The CompletionStage is discarded. @ObservesAsync observers may run AFTER
the handler's Uni completes.

### The technique

Split the terminal .invoke() into two steps:

```java
// Before — CompletionStage discarded
.invoke(() -> {
    eventBus.publish(addr, payload);
    lifecycleEvents.fireAsync(event); // discarded
});

// After — CDI delivery awaited in .chain()
.invoke(() -> {
    eventBus.publish(addr, payload); // still fire-and-forget
})
.chain(() ->
    Uni.createFrom()
        .completionStage(() -> lifecycleEvents.fireAsync(event))
        .onFailure()
        .recoverWithItem(t -> { LOG.warnf(t, "observer failed"); return null; })
        .replaceWithVoid())
```

The handler's Uni does not complete until all @ObservesAsync observers have run.
onFailure().recoverWithItem() prevents observer exceptions from breaking the handler.

### Why this is non-obvious

.invoke() reads as a side-effect callback but is fire-and-forget for CompletionStage —
Mutiny does not chain off it. Moving to .chain() with completionStage() makes CDI
delivery part of the reactive pipeline.

Use the Supplier form completionStage(() -> fireAsync(...)) — lazy, ensures fireAsync()
is called at subscription time (correct thread context), not at chain construction time.

**See also:** [GE-20260517-f31786](GE-20260517-f31786.md) — fireAsync() returns CompletionStage<Event<T>> not CompletionStage<Void> — Mutiny bridge needs .replaceWith() | [GE-20260512-0fe012](GE-20260512-0fe012.md) — CDI fireAsync() inside @Transactional dispatches immediately

**See also:** [GE-20260518-a61d1b](GE-20260518-a61d1b.md) — @ConsumeEvent(blocking=true) and @Transactional on the same method work correctly

**See also:** [GE-20260616-6f1743](GE-20260616-6f1743.md) — AtomicReference to capture values across Mutiny Uni chain when chain switches threads
