entries.title: CDI event observers in @QuarkusTest test classpath do not reliably receive synchronous Event.fire() from production code — use Mockito unit tests instead
entries.body:
CDI event observers in @QuarkusTest test classpath do not reliably receive synchronous Event.fire() from production code — use Mockito unit tests instead

## Symptom

A `@ApplicationScoped` CDI bean defined in the test classpath observes `ChannelInitialisedEvent` with `@Observes`. Production code calls `Event<ChannelInitialisedEvent>.fire()` synchronously inside a `@TestTransaction` test. The observer's list of captured events remains empty — `onMessage()` is never called.

Two variants tried:

1. **Static inner class** inside the `@QuarkusTest` class — annotated `@ApplicationScoped`, injected into the test. Observer method never fires.
2. **Separate top-level class** in the test package — same result.

No error or warning. The observer bean is injected successfully (non-null), but events fired by production code do not reach it.

## Root Cause

Quarkus CDI's augmentation-time bean discovery may not activate `@ApplicationScoped` observer beans defined in the test classpath without explicit configuration, even when they appear to be discovered (injection succeeds). The `Event.fire()` call dispatches to observers known to the CDI container at augmentation time; test-classpath beans without `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` configuration are in a grey zone.

The CDI injection point (`@Inject BindingUpdateObserver observer`) resolves via a proxy that may be a valid CDI bean but whose observer method registration is incomplete.

## Fix

Use a **Mockito unit test** (no CDI, no `@QuarkusTest`) to verify that `Event<T>.fire()` is called with the correct payload:

```java
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
Event<ChannelInitialisedEvent> events = mock(Event.class);
// wire the service under test manually
service.channelInitialisedEvents = events;

service.updateConnectorBinding(channelId, "new-connector", "new-dest");

verify(events).fire(new ChannelInitialisedEvent(channelId, "my-channel", false));
```

Use `@QuarkusTest` integration tests to verify the state outcome (binding fields updated in store), not the event firing mechanics. Keep event-firing verification in pure unit tests where the `Event<T>` is a mock you fully control.

## Why this is non-obvious

- The observer bean IS injectable — `@Inject BindingUpdateObserver` does not throw `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`. The proxy resolves. But events don't reach it.
- Synchronous `Event.fire()` "should" always reach all active observers in the same CDI container. The gap between compile-time bean activation and runtime observer registration is not visible from application code.
- No warning is emitted when a `@Observes` method is registered on an observer that won't receive events in a `@QuarkusTest` context.

**See also:** [GE-20260517-712fe5](GE-20260517-712fe5.md) — @ApplicationScoped capture bean with CountDownLatch for @ObservesAsync (alternative approach)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

`QuarkusTest event observer`

entries.body:
`event.fireAsync()` returns `CompletionStage<Event<T>>` not `CompletionStage<Void>` — Mutiny bridge needs `.replaceWith()`

### Symptom

Type mismatch when bridging `Event.fireAsync()` to a Mutiny `Uni` pipeline:

```java
// Fails — CompletionStage<Event<MyEvent>>, not CompletionStage<VerificationResult>
return Uni.createFrom().completionStage(
    () -> suspectEvent.fireAsync(new MyEvent(...)))
    // compiler error: cannot convert Uni<Event<MyEvent>> to Uni<VerificationResult>
```

### Context

Quarkus reactive service using CDI `Event<T>` needs to fire an async event and return a `Uni<SomeType>` from the same pipeline.

### Root cause

`Event.fireAsync()` is declared in the CDI spec as returning `CompletionStage<Event<T>>` — it returns the event object itself wrapped in a completion stage, not `CompletionStage<Void>`. Most usage examples ignore the return value entirely, hiding the actual type.

### Fix

Use `.replaceWith()` to discard the `Event<T>` wrapper and substitute the intended result:

```java
return Uni.createFrom().completionStage(
    () -> suspectEvent.fireAsync(new MyEvent(entryId, actorId, keyRef)))
    .replaceWith(VerificationResult.SUSPECT);
```

### Why this is non-obvious

CDI spec says "returns a CompletionStage" without emphasising the `<Event<T>>` type parameter. Developers writing async event firing naturally assume `CompletionStage<Void>` because they're triggering a side effect and discarding the event payload. The full generic type is only visible in the CDI API Javadoc — not in any tutorials or common usage examples.

**See also:** [GE-20260423-daef97](GE-20260423-daef97.md) — CDI event.fire() does not deliver to @ObservesAsync observers — fireAsync() required

**See also:** [GE-20260529-e43076](GE-20260529-e43076.md) — await CDI fireAsync() delivery in @ConsumeEvent reactive chain

@ObservesAsync methods in indexed external jars silently not dispatched by Quarkus CDI in complex deployments

## Symptom

`WorkItemLifecycleAdapter.onWorkItemLifecycle(@ObservesAsync WorkItemLifecycleEvent)` in `casehub-engine-work-adapter` is never invoked when events are fired from a devtown application, even though:
- The bean IS discoverable — it can be `@Inject`ed and its methods called directly
- `@ObservesAsync` works for test-scope beans in the same application module
- The Jandex index in the work-adapter jar contains both `ObservesAsync` and `onWorkItemLifecycle`
- `DefaultAsyncObserverExceptionHandler` never logs an error (method is not called at all)

The engine's own work-adapter test suite (`WorkItemLifecycleAdapterTest` in `io.casehub.workadapter`) successfully dispatches to the same method.

## Context

Complex Quarkus application (`casehub-devtown-app`) with: `quarkus-rest`, `quarkus-rest-jackson`, multiple datasources (qhorus H2 + work H2), many event-bus subscribers, and `casehub-engine-work-adapter` declared as a `quarkus.index-dependency` external jar.

## Root Cause (working theory)

Quarkus CDI augmentation may not fully register `@ObservesAsync` observer methods from `quarkus.index-dependency` jars in the same way it does for beans in the application's own source tree. The engine test works because the test class is in the same module as `WorkItemLifecycleAdapter` (same package `io.casehub.workadapter`), giving Quarkus the full augmentation context it needs.

## Fix

Invoke the observer method directly from the application where CDI dispatch cannot be relied on:

```java
// After WorkItemService.completeFromSystem(), get the completed WorkItems and call adapter directly
completedWorkItems.forEach(wi -> lifecycleAdapter.onWorkItemLifecycle(
    WorkItemLifecycleEvent.of("COMPLETED", wi, "system", wi.resolution)));
```

Verify CDI async delivery separately using a test-scope `@ApplicationScoped` bean in the application module:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
class WorkItemCompletionCapture {
    @ObservesAsync WorkItemLifecycleEvent event fires correctly
    // because the bean is in the app module, not an external jar
}
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The bean IS injected by CDI (`@Inject WorkItemLifecycleAdapter adapter` works). The Jandex index IS present. `DefaultAsyncObserverExceptionHandler` never fires — the method is not called at all, not called and throwing. In the engine module's own tests, the same observer works perfectly. There is no startup error or warning. The only indication is the absence of observable side effects (context not updated).

entries.body:
Call @ConsumeEvent/@ObservesAsync handlers directly via injected CDI proxy — preserves @Transactional, eliminates async waiting in tests

## Call @ConsumeEvent/@ObservesAsync handlers directly via injected CDI proxy — preserves @Transactional, eliminates async waiting in tests

### Stack
Quarkus 3.32.2, JUnit 5, Vert.x Event Bus

### Symptom
Tests for `@ConsumeEvent` (Vert.x) or `@ObservesAsync` (CDI async) handlers require
`Awaitility.await()` or `Thread.sleep()` to wait for async delivery before asserting.
Negative-path tests ("nothing happened") are especially brittle — the sleep must be long
enough that the handler *would* have run, but there's no signal to know it did.

### Context
`eventBus.publish()` is fire-and-forget; the handler runs asynchronously on a worker
thread. Any test calling `publish()` must bridge the async gap. With `@ObservesAsync`,
delivery is additionally unreliable in `@QuarkusTest` contexts (observer methods
silently never invoked in some Quarkus versions).

### Fix

Inject the handler bean directly and call the `@ConsumeEvent`/`@ObservesAsync` method
synchronously. The injected bean is a CDI proxy, so all interceptors — including
`@Transactional` — apply exactly as in production:

```java
@QuarkusTest
class MyHandlerTest {

@Inject MyHandler handler;   // CDI proxy — @Transactional applies

@Test
    void handler_creates_record_on_event() {
        // Direct call — synchronous, no await/sleep needed
        handler.onMyEvent(new MyEvent(caseId, ...));

// Assert immediately — handler has returned, transaction committed
        assertThat(repository.findByCaseId(caseId)).isPresent();
    }
}
```

Keep one wiring test that uses `eventBus.publish()` + `await()` to confirm the
`@ConsumeEvent` route is actually registered:

```java
@Test
void eventBus_routes_event_to_handler() {
    eventBus.publish(MY_ADDRESS, new MyEvent(...));
    await().atMost(5, SECONDS).untilAsserted(() ->
        assertThat(someObservableEffect()).isTrue());
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Developers assume that calling a `@ConsumeEvent` or `@ObservesAsync` method directly
bypasses framework behaviour (e.g. transactions, interceptors). It does not — the injected
bean is a CDI proxy, and the interceptor chain fires on every method call through that
proxy, regardless of how the call originates. The method is `public`, the proxy is
injectable, and `@Transactional` commits on the same thread that called the method.

The `@ConsumeEvent(blocking = true)` annotation only controls Vert.x thread dispatch —
it has no effect when the method is called directly. The transaction behaviour is
entirely determined by the `@Transactional` CDI interceptor, which is unaffected.

### Why this fix
Eliminates all timing machinery from the test suite: no `Awaitility`, no `Thread.sleep`,
no `CountDownLatch` (except in one wiring test). Negative-path tests become deterministic
assertions rather than "wait long enough and hope". The wiring test retains integration
coverage of the event bus route without imposing async overhead on every test.

**See also:** GE-20260519-12efe9 — QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() for per-class CDI scoping

**See also:** [GE-20260513-b15933](GE-20260513-b15933.md) — @ObservesAsync events silently not delivered — explains why direct invocation is needed

**See also:** [GE-20260530-5a9f02](GE-20260530-5a9f02.md) — @ObservesAsync + @Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW) decouples audit persistence (production use of @ObservesAsync)

**See also:** [GE-20260522-831b53](GE-20260522-831b53.md) — unit test @Observes StartupEvent via package-private method

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Inject CDI proxy for @ConsumeEvent/@ObservesAsync handlers
@Transactional proxy for async handlers QuarkusTest
CDI proxy workaround for silent observer methods

entries.title: langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types
entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
DeclarativeUtil chatSupplierParameterResolvers
@ChatModelSupplier CDI resolver hook
CdiBean workaround limitations

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus ambiguous resolution ChatModel @Default
quarkus @DefaultBean conflicts with @Default SYNTHETIC
Ollama extension ChatModel registration error

AgentProviderChatModel uses langchain4j close-timeout (PT30S), not agent.claude.default-timeout — silent truncation
entries.body:
AgentProviderChatModel uses langchain4j close-timeout (PT30S), not agent.claude.default-timeout — silent truncation

## AgentProviderChatModel uses langchain4j close-timeout (PT30S), not agent.claude.default-timeout — silent truncation

### Symptom
Claude CLI subprocess appears to time out silently — the `QueryExpandingCaseRetriever` decorator catches a `TimeoutException` and falls back to the original query. Benchmark results are identical to baseline despite the decorator being active in the CDI graph. No error logged by `AgentProviderChatModel` — only the decorator's catch block emits a WARNING.

### Context
The call chain is: `LlmQueryExpander` → `ChatModel.chat()` → `AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` → `agentProvider.invoke()` → `ClaudeAgentProvider` → Claude CLI subprocess. Two separate timeout configurations exist:
- `casehub.platform.agent.claude.default-timeout` (default PT5M) — used by `ClaudeAgentClient` for the subprocess wall-clock timeout
- `casehub.platform.agent.langchain4j.close-timeout` (default PT30S) — used by `AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` when awaiting the Mutiny stream

### What was tried (didn't work)
Setting `casehub.platform.agent.claude.default-timeout=PT3M` — queries still timed out at exactly 30 seconds. The Claude agent timeout was never the bottleneck.

### Root cause
`AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` calls `.await().atMost(properties.closeTimeout())` where `properties` is `AgentLangchain4jProperties`, not `ClaudeAgentProperties`. The LangChain4j bridge has its own timeout that fires before the Claude agent timeout. The two config prefixes are different packages with no cross-reference in documentation or logging.

### Fix
Set the correct timeout:
```properties
casehub.platform.agent.langchain4j.close-timeout=PT3M
```

Or bypass the ChatModel bridge entirely by using `AgentProvider.openSession()` directly — the session approach avoids both timeouts and provides prompt caching benefits.

### Why this is non-obvious
Two timeout configs (`agent.claude.default-timeout` and `agent.langchain4j.close-timeout`) control the same call chain at different layers. Setting the wrong one has zero effect — no error, no warning, no log indicating which timeout fired. The `TimeoutException` stack trace shows Mutiny internals, not which config governed the timeout.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
langchain4j close-timeout PT30S
AgentProviderChatModel doChat timeout
Claude CLI subprocess timeout

entries.title: LangChain4j 1.x: implementing both ChatModel and StreamingChatModel requires explicit overrides for all four shared default methods
entries.body:
LangChain4j 1.x: implementing both ChatModel and StreamingChatModel requires explicit overrides for all four shared default methods

### Symptom
Java compile error when a class implements both `ChatModel` and `StreamingChatModel`:
the compiler reports ambiguous default methods.

### Context
When building a LangChain4j adapter that needs to satisfy both `ChatModel` (blocking)
and `StreamingChatModel` (streaming) injection points in a single CDI bean.

### What was tried
Implementing both interfaces and overriding only the extension-point methods —
`doChat(ChatRequest) → ChatResponse` and `doChat(ChatRequest, StreamingChatResponseHandler)`.
These compile fine in isolation.

### Root cause
Both `ChatModel` and `StreamingChatModel` declare four identical default method signatures:
- `listeners()` → `List<ChatModelListener>`
- `defaultRequestParameters()` → `ChatRequestParameters`
- `provider()` → `ModelProvider`
- `supportedCapabilities()` → `Set<Capability>`

Java's diamond rule requires a class implementing both interfaces to explicitly override
every method where both declare a default. All four must be overridden — not just the
extension points.

### Fix
Override all four in the implementing class:

```java
@Override public ModelProvider provider() { return ModelProvider.ANTHROPIC; }

@Override public Set<Capability> supportedCapabilities() { return Set.of(); }

@Override public ChatRequestParameters defaultRequestParameters() {
    return DefaultChatRequestParameters.EMPTY;
}

@Override public List<ChatModelListener> listeners() {
    return List.of();  // or return injected CDI listeners
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
`ChatModel` and `StreamingChatModel` are designed as complementary interfaces —
implementing both in one class is a natural choice when building a single adapter for
both injection points. The shared default methods aren't mentioned in LangChain4j
documentation. The compiler error only appears when implementing both simultaneously;
either interface alone compiles cleanly with only the `doChat()` extension point overridden.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`ChatModel` `StreamingChatModel` default method override ambiguity
`Java diamond rule` `override default methods`
`CDI bean` `ChatRequestParameters`

entries.title: LangChain4J 1.14.1 AiMessage and ChatResponse cannot be Mockito-mocked — use real constructors/builders
entries.body:
LangChain4J 1.14.1 AiMessage and ChatResponse cannot be Mockito-mocked — use real constructors/builders

## Symptom

```java
AiMessage msg = mock(AiMessage.class);
when(msg.text()).thenReturn("{...json...}");  // → UnfinishedStubbingException
```

`mock(AiMessage.class)` appears to succeed, but `when(msg.text())...` throws `UnfinishedStubbingException`. Mockito correctly detects that the stubbing started but could not complete — the exception message references the `stubResponse()` call site, not the `when()` line, which further obscures the cause.

## Root Cause

`AiMessage` has final methods in LangChain4J 1.14.1. Mockito's standard `mock()` cannot intercept final methods (requires the Mockito `mockito-extensions/org.mockito.plugins.MockMaker` with `mock-maker-inline` configured). The mock is created but the `when()` call cannot set up the stub because the method call in the `when()` argument executes the real final method, which doesn't register with Mockito as expected.

## Fix

Use the real constructors and builders directly — they are simple and public:

```java
// AiMessage — string constructor
AiMessage msg = new AiMessage("{...json...}");

// ChatResponse — builder
ChatResponse resp = ChatResponse.builder()
    .aiMessage(new AiMessage("{...json...}"))
    .build();
```

For use in test stubs:

```java
private static ChatResponse stubResponse(final String json) {
    return ChatResponse.builder()
            .aiMessage(new AiMessage(json))
            .build();
}
```

`ChatModel` itself IS an interface and CAN be Mockito-mocked. Only the value types it returns (`AiMessage`, `ChatResponse`) are non-mockable.

## Why this is non-obvious

The `UnfinishedStubbingException` message cites the `mock(AiMessage.class)` call site as the problem — not the `when()` call. This leads developers to inspect the mock creation rather than the stub setup. The root cause (final method) is only discoverable by checking the LangChain4J source code.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Mockito UnfinishedStubbingException AiMessage
AiMessage final method Mockito
ChatResponse builder constructor

entries.title: Ollama format=json enforces structurally valid JSON at sampling level — bypasses small model instruction-following failures
entries.body:
Ollama format=json enforces structurally valid JSON at sampling level — bypasses small model instruction-following failures

## Technique

Set `quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json` (or pass `format: "json"` in the Ollama API request) to force structurally valid JSON output at the token-sampling level, bypassing the model's instruction-following behaviour entirely.

```properties
quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json
```

This is distinct from prompt engineering. A model instruction saying "Return ONLY raw JSON" is a soft directive — small models (3B, 4B) routinely ignore it and produce preamble ("Here is the JSON:", "Here's my evaluation:") or natural language responses with no `{` at all. `format=json` is a hard constraint: the Ollama runtime biases token selection to produce valid JSON structure regardless of the model's tendency to ignore the instruction.

## Context

Useful in any eval harness or structured extraction pipeline using Ollama. The constraint is applied by Ollama's inference engine, not by the model itself — it works even when the model has no explicit training for JSON output. All four models tested (llama3.2:3b, gemma3:4b, llama3.1:8b, qwen3.6:35b) produced parseable JSON with `format=json`; without it, the 3B model failed on roughly 30–50% of calls with non-JSON preamble.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The obvious approach is to improve the instruction — "Return ONLY raw JSON, no preamble, no markdown". This works reliably with large instruction-tuned models (7B+) but fails unpredictably with smaller models. Developers typically iterate on prompt wording rather than recognising that the constraint needs to operate at the sampling layer. The `format=json` parameter is documented in Ollama's API reference but not prominently surfaced in the Quarkus extension docs.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json
format: "json" ollama

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs

## What it is

The Quarkus LangChain4j Ollama extension sets a **10-second default REST client timeout**
for all chat requests. This is undocumented. For local LLMs (8B+ parameter models on CPU
or M-series Neural Engine), a single JSON-structured chat request typically takes 15–120
seconds, so the default silently causes every judge call to fail.

## Context

Appears when running eval harness tests with Ollama models as the judge. The `PromptJudge`
call fails with:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Judge LLM call failed — check judge model configuration
Caused by: javax.ws.rs.ProcessingException: The timeout period of 10000ms has been exceeded
  while executing POST /api/chat for server localhost:11434
```

The timeout fires before the model finishes generating the structured JSON response.

## Fix

Pass the timeout override via system property:

```bash
"-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

The property is not documented in the Quarkus LangChain4j extension docs or the
quarkus.io reference (as of 2026-06-14). It's discoverable only by reading the
extension's `OllamaConfig` source.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("check judge model configuration") points to configuration rather
than networking/timeout, leading to checks of model name, format=json flag, and CDI
wiring — none of which are the problem. The 10-second timeout is plausible for
hosted APIs but is impractical for any local model above 3B parameters.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus langchain4j timeout error
Ollama REST client timeout default value
judge llm call failed java IllegalStateException

entries.title: LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
JSON response format without schema
Anthropic UnsupportedFeatureException
JSON schema requirement

SPLADE (MS MARCO) has zero Java domain vocabulary — expands ChatModel to hotel/beauty/renovation
entries.body:
SPLADE (MS MARCO) has zero Java domain vocabulary — expands ChatModel to hotel/beauty/renovation

### Symptom
Adding SPLADE sparse embeddings to dense retrieval (RRF fusion) churns result sets without improving quality for Java/CDI domain queries. All 28 queries changed, 3 highly relevant entries were displaced while 40 noise entries were removed — net effect ambiguous.

### Context
Hortora engine hybrid search benchmark (#28). SPLADE (`Splade_PP_en_v1`) added as sparse embedding alongside nomic-embed-text dense vectors. RRF fusion (k=60, denseTopK=40, sparseTopK=40). Tested across 14 real-world scenarios covering Java class names, CDI annotations, JPA patterns, and Quarkus framework terms.

SPLADE vocabulary analysis decoded the activated tokens for each query:

| Query | Top SPLADE Expansions | Expected (Java domain) |
|-------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `DefaultBean\|AmbiguousResolutionException` | ambiguity, groups, unclear | cdi, qualifier, alternative, inject |
| `ChatModel\|AgentSession\|LangChain4j` | agent, talk, beauty, renovation, genre | model, inference, provider, adapter |
| `Priority(100)\|CDI priority` | priorities, cds (music), urgency, precedence | qualifier, scope, alternative, bean |

Zero Tier 1 domain term activations across all 14 KW queries. Not one activation of `panache`, `jandex`, `qualifier`, `interceptor`, `singleton`, `persist`, or any unambiguous Java/CDI term.

### Root cause
Two compounding failures:

1. **BERT WordPiece tokenizer** fragments Java class names into meaningless subwords: `AmbiguousResolutionException` → `["am", "##bi", "##guous", "##reso", "##lution", "##exception"]`. The semantic content is destroyed before SPLADE runs.

2. **MS MARCO training data** contains no Java ecosystem content. SPLADE's learned vocabulary expansion maps "chat" to web-domain associations (hotels, beauty, renovation) — not to software engineering concepts.

This is expected behaviour for this model architecture, not a defect. The same limitation applies to nomic-embed-text (see GE-20260627-4712de) — the difference is that SPLADE actively ADDS noise through irrelevant expansions, whereas nomic-embed-text merely fails to discriminate.

### Fix
Do not use general-purpose (MS MARCO-trained) SPLADE models for Java/CDI domain retrieval. Three alternatives:

1. **BM25 keyword matching** (casehubio/neural-text#47/#48) — exact token matching via Qdrant full-text index. Directly addresses the vocabulary gap.
2. **Code-domain SPLADE model** (casehubio/neural-text#49) — if one exists with Java training data.
3. **Code-domain dense embedding model** (casehubio/neural-text#49) — models like CodeBERT, UniXcoder trained on source code.

### Why this is non-obvious
SPLADE is presented as a vocabulary expansion technique that recovers keyword precision lost by dense embeddings. The expectation is that it bridges the gap between semantic search and keyword matching. For general-domain web queries, this is true. For Java class names, it actively makes things worse by introducing irrelevant web-domain associations into the sparse vector.

### Why this fix
BM25 is the highest-leverage fix because it directly solves the failure mode (exact token matching for Java identifiers) without requiring model training or fine-tuning. Code-domain models are the long-term architectural fix but have higher uncertainty and longer timeline.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`AmbiguousResolutionException` Java CDI
`ChatModel\|AgentSession\|LangChain4j` vocabulary
`Priority(100)\|CDI priority` term activations

quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache

## Symptom

After adding `quarkus-langchain4j-ollama` as a test-scope dependency inside a Maven profile
(`-Peval-ollama`), the Ollama `ChatModel` bean is not registered. Config keys are logged as
`Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"`, and the
test fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for `ChatModel`.

## Context

The module was previously built without the Ollama extension. Maven resolves the Ollama JAR
when the profile is active, but Quarkus reuses its disk-based augmentation cache from the
prior build — before the Ollama extension was on the classpath. The Ollama extension is
silently absent from augmentation: no beans registered, no config processors active.

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Running `mvn test -Peval,eval-ollama` after the JAR appeared in `~/.m2` — stale augmentation
  cache persisted, config keys still unrecognized.
- Adding `-Dquarkus.test.profile=eval` explicitly — no effect on cache.

## Root cause

Quarkus augmentation is disk-cached in `target/quarkus-app/`. When classpath changes occur
(new extension added via Maven profile), the cache invalidation heuristic does not always
detect the change, especially when the Ollama JAR was already present in `~/.m2` from a
prior `mvn dependency:resolve` call (updating file timestamps). The cache is reused, and
the Ollama extension's CDI beans are never registered.

## Fix

Run `mvn clean` before the first test run with the new profile:

```bash
JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 26) mvn clean test -pl eval -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dtest=PromptEvalTest#evaluateRealWorldScenarios \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name=qwen3:8b" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

Subsequent runs without `clean` work correctly — the Ollama-aware augmentation is now cached.

## Why this is non-obvious

The "unrecognized configuration key" warning does not hint at augmentation caching — it reads
as though the extension was not added at all, not that a stale build artifact is in play.
The Ollama JAR is visible in `mvn dependency:resolve` output, making the missing registration
doubly confusing. The standard fix for missing CDI beans (`check your imports, check your
annotations`) leads nowhere.

**See also:** [GE-20260530-0178fd](GE-20260530-0178fd.md) — Quarkus @QuarkusTest augmentation requires extension deployment JARs in ~/.m2 | [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension @Default ChatModel clashes with @DefaultBean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.body:
Standalone agentic agent invocation skips RAG pipeline — ContentRetriever.retrieve() never called outside agentic system

### Symptom
`ContentRetriever.retrieve()` is never called after invoking a standalone agentic
agent, even though the retriever is correctly wired to the `AgentBuilder` via
`builder.contentRetriever(bean)`. The `AtomicBoolean called` flag on a recording
retriever stays `false`.

### Context
Occurs when testing CDI auto-wiring of `ContentRetriever` into agents. The agent
is invoked directly (`agent.ask("hello")`) rather than as a sub-agent inside a
`@SequenceAgent`, `@SupervisorAgent`, or other workflow composition. langchain4j
logs: "Improper invocation of a standalone agent outside of an agentic system,
consider using AiServices instead."

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. Verified the CDI bean was resolved (`assertThat(retriever).isNotNull()`) — passed
2. Verified the injection point existed (app booted without `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`) — passed
3. Added `assertThat(retriever.called.get()).isTrue()` after `agent.ask()` — failed
4. Checked `isResolvable()` on the `Instance<ContentRetriever>` — returned `true`
5. Confirmed `agentBuilder.contentRetriever(bean)` was called in the consumer — it was

### Root cause
langchain4j-agentic's `AgentInvocationHandler` only executes the full agent
lifecycle (including RAG augmentation via `RetrievalAugmentor`/`ContentRetriever`)
when the agent is invoked within an agentic system scope. Standalone invocation
bypasses the RAG pipeline — the `ContentRetriever` is wired to the builder but
never consulted during the invocation.

### Fix
Test CDI auto-wiring by verifying the injection point resolves (app boots) and the
agent is invocable, rather than asserting that `retrieve()` was called. To test
actual RAG invocation, wrap the agent in a `@SequenceAgent` or `@SupervisorAgent`
workflow.

### Why this is non-obvious
The `AgentBuilder.contentRetriever()` API suggests the retriever will be used on
every invocation. The wiring IS correct — the retriever IS set on the builder. The
disconnect is that the invocation handler skips RAG for standalone agents. There is
no error, no warning about the skipped retrieval — only the logged "improper
invocation" message hints at the limitation.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
ContentRetriever retrieve() not called in standalone agentic invocation
AgentBuilder contentRetriever injection fails
langchain4j agent invocation RAG pipeline bypass

### Symptom

Config override for `@SupervisorAgent(maxAgentsInvocations=10)` does not work even though `AgenticServices.setWorkflowAgentsBuilder()` is correctly set with a config-aware wrapper.

### Context

`WorkflowAgentsBuilder` covers loop, sequence, parallel, conditional, and parallelMapper builders. But `SupervisorAgentService` is NOT created through it.

### Root cause

`buildSupervisorAgent()` in `AgenticServices` creates the builder directly:
```java
var builder = new SupervisorAgentServiceImpl<>(agentServiceClass, agentMethod, chatModel)
    .maxAgentsInvocations(supervisorAgent.maxAgentsInvocations())
```

This bypasses the `WorkflowAgentsBuilder` SPI entirely. There is no interception point.

### Fix

None available in current upstream. Config for `maxAgentsInvocations` can be declared in the config interface but cannot be wired until upstream provides either a supervisor builder SPI or the workflow-level `AgentConfigurator` (langchain4j/langchain4j#5399).

### Why this is non-obvious

All other workflow builders (loop, sequence, parallel, conditional) go through `WorkflowAgentsBuilder`. The supervisor is the exception — and there's no documentation or API design hint that it's different.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
SupervisorAgentService builder bypass SPI
WorkflowAgentsBuilder agent config override

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus ambiguous resolution ChatModel @Default
quarkus @DefaultBean conflicts with @Default SYNTHETIC
Ollama extension ChatModel registration error

entries.title: AgentProviderChatModel uses langchain4j close-timeout (PT30S), not agent.claude.default-timeout — silent truncation
entries.body:
AgentProviderChatModel uses langchain4j close-timeout (PT30S), not agent.claude.default-timeout — silent truncation

## AgentProviderChatModel uses langchain4j close-timeout (PT30S), not agent.claude.default-timeout — silent truncation

### Symptom
Claude CLI subprocess appears to time out silently — the `QueryExpandingCaseRetriever` decorator catches a `TimeoutException` and falls back to the original query. Benchmark results are identical to baseline despite the decorator being active in the CDI graph. No error logged by `AgentProviderChatModel` — only the decorator's catch block emits a WARNING.

### Context
The call chain is: `LlmQueryExpander` → `ChatModel.chat()` → `AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` → `agentProvider.invoke()` → `ClaudeAgentProvider` → Claude CLI subprocess. Two separate timeout configurations exist:
- `casehub.platform.agent.claude.default-timeout` (default PT5M) — used by `ClaudeAgentClient` for the subprocess wall-clock timeout
- `casehub.platform.agent.langchain4j.close-timeout` (default PT30S) — used by `AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` when awaiting the Mutiny stream

### What was tried (didn't work)
Setting `casehub.platform.agent.claude.default-timeout=PT3M` — queries still timed out at exactly 30 seconds. The Claude agent timeout was never the bottleneck.

### Root cause
`AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` calls `.await().atMost(properties.closeTimeout())` where `properties` is `AgentLangchain4jProperties`, not `ClaudeAgentProperties`. The LangChain4j bridge has its own timeout that fires before the Claude agent timeout. The two config prefixes are different packages with no cross-reference in documentation or logging.

### Fix
Set the correct timeout:
```properties
casehub.platform.agent.langchain4j.close-timeout=PT3M
```

Or bypass the ChatModel bridge entirely by using `AgentProvider.openSession()` directly — the session approach avoids both timeouts and provides prompt caching benefits.

### Why this is non-obvious
Two timeout configs (`agent.claude.default-timeout` and `agent.langchain4j.close-timeout`) control the same call chain at different layers. Setting the wrong one has zero effect — no error, no warning, no log indicating which timeout fired. The `TimeoutException` stack trace shows Mutiny internals, not which config governed the timeout.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
langchain4j close-timeout PT30S
AgentProviderChatModel doChat timeout
Claude CLI subprocess timeout

LangChain4j 1.x: implementing both ChatModel and StreamingChatModel requires explicit overrides for all four shared default methods
entries.body:
LangChain4j 1.x: implementing both ChatModel and StreamingChatModel requires explicit overrides for all four shared default methods

### Symptom
Java compile error when a class implements both `ChatModel` and `StreamingChatModel`:
the compiler reports ambiguous default methods.

### Context
When building a LangChain4j adapter that needs to satisfy both `ChatModel` (blocking)
and `StreamingChatModel` (streaming) injection points in a single CDI bean.

### What was tried
Implementing both interfaces and overriding only the extension-point methods —
`doChat(ChatRequest) → ChatResponse` and `doChat(ChatRequest, StreamingChatResponseHandler)`.
These compile fine in isolation.

### Root cause
Both `ChatModel` and `StreamingChatModel` declare four identical default method signatures:
- `listeners()` → `List<ChatModelListener>`
- `defaultRequestParameters()` → `ChatRequestParameters`
- `provider()` → `ModelProvider`
- `supportedCapabilities()` → `Set<Capability>`

Java's diamond rule requires a class implementing both interfaces to explicitly override
every method where both declare a default. All four must be overridden — not just the
extension points.

### Fix
Override all four in the implementing class:

```java
@Override public ModelProvider provider() { return ModelProvider.ANTHROPIC; }

@Override public Set<Capability> supportedCapabilities() { return Set.of(); }

@Override public ChatRequestParameters defaultRequestParameters() {
    return DefaultChatRequestParameters.EMPTY;
}

@Override public List<ChatModelListener> listeners() {
    return List.of();  // or return injected CDI listeners
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
`ChatModel` and `StreamingChatModel` are designed as complementary interfaces —
implementing both in one class is a natural choice when building a single adapter for
both injection points. The shared default methods aren't mentioned in LangChain4j
documentation. The compiler error only appears when implementing both simultaneously;
either interface alone compiles cleanly with only the `doChat()` extension point overridden.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`ChatModel` `StreamingChatModel` default method override ambiguity
`Java diamond rule` `override default methods`
`CDI bean` `ChatRequestParameters`

langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types
entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
DeclarativeUtil chatSupplierParameterResolvers
@ChatModelSupplier CDI resolver hook
CdiBean workaround limitations

entries.title: LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
JSON response format without schema
Anthropic UnsupportedFeatureException
JSON schema requirement

entries.body:
OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

## OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

**ID:** GE-20260614-328420
**Stack:** OpenClaw v2026.6.x

### Symptom

Calling OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint with a provider model
name returns HTTP 400:

```json
{"error":{"message":"Invalid `model`. Use `openclaw` or `openclaw/<agentId>`.",
 "type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

### Context

When `gateway.http.endpoints.chatCompletions.enabled: true` is set in `openclaw.json`,
OpenClaw exposes `POST /v1/chat/completions`. The natural assumption is to use the
configured upstream model ID (e.g. `"mock-llm/mock-model"`, `"anthropic/claude-opus-4-6"`).

### Root cause / Undocumented behaviour

The `model` field in the request does not name the upstream LLM. It names the OpenClaw
agent. OpenClaw IS the model from the caller's perspective — it receives the request,
routes it through its agent pipeline, and calls the configured upstream provider
internally. The upstream provider model is determined by the agent's config, not the
request.

Valid model values:
- `"openclaw"` — uses the default agent
- `"openclaw/<agentId>"` — routes to a specific named agent

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:18789/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"openclaw","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'
```

OpenClaw then calls its configured upstream provider (e.g. `mock-llm/mock-model` via
WireMock, or `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`) transparently.

### Why this is non-obvious

The OpenClaw docs describe the chatCompletions endpoint as OpenAI-compatible, which
implies `model` should identify the LLM. The error message does clarify the correct
values, but the architectural reason (OpenClaw = the model, upstream = internal) is
not explained anywhere in the docs. The distinction only becomes clear after reading
the error response.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`OpenClaw model error 400`
`openclaw model agentId`
`chatCompletions model invalid`

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-core Quarkus extension stalls @QuarkusTest augmentation when no model provider is configured
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-core Quarkus extension stalls @QuarkusTest augmentation when no model provider is configured

## Symptom

`mvn test` hangs indefinitely during Quarkus augmentation when `quarkus-langchain4j-core` is a compile-scope dependency of a non-extension library module and no AI model provider is configured. No error message, no timeout — the build just blocks.

## Context

Occurs when a library module (Jandex-indexed, not a full Quarkus extension) adds `io.quarkiverse.langchain4j:quarkus-langchain4j-core` as a compile dependency to use the `EmbeddingModel` interface. During `@QuarkusTest` augmentation, the Quarkus extension activates and waits for a model provider that never arrives.

## What was tried

Adding `quarkus-langchain4j-core` as a `provided` scope — still stalls because the extension's deployment artifact is resolved transitively during augmentation.

## Root cause

`quarkus-langchain4j-core` is a Quarkus extension (has both runtime and deployment jars). When it appears on the augmentation classpath, Quarkus activates it and expects at least one model provider (OpenAI, Ollama, etc.) to be configured. Without one, augmentation stalls waiting for the CDI bean to resolve.

## Fix

Use `dev.langchain4j:langchain4j-core` (the plain Java library, **not** the Quarkus extension) as the compile dependency. This provides the `EmbeddingModel` interface for compilation without triggering Quarkus extension activation:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>langchain4j-core</artifactId>
  <version>1.13.0</version>
</dependency>
```

For CDI injection, use `Instance<EmbeddingModel>` instead of `@Inject EmbeddingModel`:

```java
@Inject
public MyBean(final Instance<EmbeddingModel> modelInstance) {
    this.model = modelInstance.isResolvable() ? modelInstance.get() : null;
}
```

When no provider is configured, `instance.isResolvable()` returns `false` gracefully. The consuming app brings `quarkus-langchain4j-openai` (or any other provider extension), which satisfies the CDI bean at their own augmentation time.

## Why this is non-obvious

The symptom is a hang with no error — not a compilation failure or a clear exception. The natural instinct is to add the Quarkus extension for its CDI integration, but the correct separation is: library module uses the plain Java API, consuming application brings the Quarkus extension.

### Why this fix

The plain Java `langchain4j-core` provides the same `EmbeddingModel` interface without triggering extension activation. `Instance<EmbeddingModel>` makes the dependency optional at CDI resolution time, so the library works both with and without a configured provider.

**See also:** GE-20260422-3242bf — Use Instance<T> for optional CDI injection — resolves gracefully when no bean exists

### Alternatives considered

- `provided` scope: still triggers augmentation because the extension's deployment artifact is resolved transitively
- Mocking `EmbeddingModel` via `@InjectMock` in every `@QuarkusTest`: works but requires all existing tests to be updated

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus langchain4j core augmentation stalls without model provider
quarkus test augmentation stalls compile scope langchain4j
embeddingmodel instance isresolvable false error

entries.title: LangChain4j EmbeddingModel does not implement TokenCountEstimator — use character-based DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int)
entries.body:
LangChain4j EmbeddingModel does not implement TokenCountEstimator — use character-based DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int)

`DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int, TokenCountEstimator)` requires a `TokenCountEstimator` as the third argument for token-based segment sizing. `EmbeddingModel` does NOT implement `TokenCountEstimator` — they are separate interface hierarchies with no inheritance relationship.

### Symptom

Design spec or implementation assumes `EmbeddingModel` can be passed as the `TokenCountEstimator` argument to `DocumentSplitters.recursive()`. Compilation fails with "incompatible types."

### Context

When building a RAG chunking pipeline, the natural assumption is: "I already have an `EmbeddingModel` that handles tokenization for embeddings — it should work as a `TokenCountEstimator` for splitting too." The naming and domain proximity reinforce this assumption.

### Root cause

`EmbeddingModel` and `TokenCountEstimator` are independent interfaces in LangChain4j. `EmbeddingModel` knows how to embed text into vectors. `TokenCountEstimator` knows how to count tokens in text. Some LLM provider implementations (e.g. `OpenAiEmbeddingModel`) implement both, but the base `EmbeddingModel` interface does not extend `TokenCountEstimator`. ONNX-based models (`OnnxEmbeddingModel`) implement only `EmbeddingModel`.

### Fix

Use the character-based 2-arg overload:

```java
DocumentSplitter splitter = DocumentSplitters.recursive(1000, 200);
```

This splits by character count (paragraph → line → sentence → word fallback chain). Character counts are approximate by nature — the imprecision vs token counts is negligible for RAG chunk sizing.

### Why this is non-obvious

The `EmbeddingModel` interface handles tokenization internally (it must tokenize text before embedding it). A developer reasonably infers it exposes this capability via `TokenCountEstimator`. The class names reinforce the assumption: "Embedding" + "Model" + "Token" + "Count" — all in the same domain. The actual type hierarchy has no inheritance link between them.

### Alternatives considered

- Implementing a custom `TokenCountEstimator` that delegates to the embedding model's internal tokenizer — rejected because ONNX embedding models don't expose their tokenizer publicly
- Using HuggingFace Tokenizers JNI directly as a `TokenCountEstimator` — possible but adds JNI complexity for marginal accuracy improvement over character-based splitting

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
LangChain4j TokenCountEstimator incompatibility
EmbeddingModel recursive DocumentSplitters
OpenAiEmbeddingModel token count estimation

entries.title: SPLADE (MS MARCO) has zero Java domain vocabulary — expands ChatModel to hotel/beauty/renovation
entries.body:
SPLADE (MS MARCO) has zero Java domain vocabulary — expands ChatModel to hotel/beauty/renovation

### Symptom
Adding SPLADE sparse embeddings to dense retrieval (RRF fusion) churns result sets without improving quality for Java/CDI domain queries. All 28 queries changed, 3 highly relevant entries were displaced while 40 noise entries were removed — net effect ambiguous.

### Context
Hortora engine hybrid search benchmark (#28). SPLADE (`Splade_PP_en_v1`) added as sparse embedding alongside nomic-embed-text dense vectors. RRF fusion (k=60, denseTopK=40, sparseTopK=40). Tested across 14 real-world scenarios covering Java class names, CDI annotations, JPA patterns, and Quarkus framework terms.

SPLADE vocabulary analysis decoded the activated tokens for each query:

| Query | Top SPLADE Expansions | Expected (Java domain) |
|-------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `DefaultBean\|AmbiguousResolutionException` | ambiguity, groups, unclear | cdi, qualifier, alternative, inject |
| `ChatModel\|AgentSession\|LangChain4j` | agent, talk, beauty, renovation, genre | model, inference, provider, adapter |
| `Priority(100)\|CDI priority` | priorities, cds (music), urgency, precedence | qualifier, scope, alternative, bean |

Zero Tier 1 domain term activations across all 14 KW queries. Not one activation of `panache`, `jandex`, `qualifier`, `interceptor`, `singleton`, `persist`, or any unambiguous Java/CDI term.

### Root cause
Two compounding failures:

1. **BERT WordPiece tokenizer** fragments Java class names into meaningless subwords: `AmbiguousResolutionException` → `["am", "##bi", "##guous", "##reso", "##lution", "##exception"]`. The semantic content is destroyed before SPLADE runs.

2. **MS MARCO training data** contains no Java ecosystem content. SPLADE's learned vocabulary expansion maps "chat" to web-domain associations (hotels, beauty, renovation) — not to software engineering concepts.

This is expected behaviour for this model architecture, not a defect. The same limitation applies to nomic-embed-text (see GE-20260627-4712de) — the difference is that SPLADE actively ADDS noise through irrelevant expansions, whereas nomic-embed-text merely fails to discriminate.

### Fix
Do not use general-purpose (MS MARCO-trained) SPLADE models for Java/CDI domain retrieval. Three alternatives:

1. **BM25 keyword matching** (casehubio/neural-text#47/#48) — exact token matching via Qdrant full-text index. Directly addresses the vocabulary gap.
2. **Code-domain SPLADE model** (casehubio/neural-text#49) — if one exists with Java training data.
3. **Code-domain dense embedding model** (casehubio/neural-text#49) — models like CodeBERT, UniXcoder trained on source code.

### Why this is non-obvious
SPLADE is presented as a vocabulary expansion technique that recovers keyword precision lost by dense embeddings. The expectation is that it bridges the gap between semantic search and keyword matching. For general-domain web queries, this is true. For Java class names, it actively makes things worse by introducing irrelevant web-domain associations into the sparse vector.

### Why this fix
BM25 is the highest-leverage fix because it directly solves the failure mode (exact token matching for Java identifiers) without requiring model training or fine-tuning. Code-domain models are the long-term architectural fix but have higher uncertainty and longer timeline.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`AmbiguousResolutionException` Java CDI
`ChatModel\|AgentSession\|LangChain4j` vocabulary
`Priority(100)\|CDI priority` term activations

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs

## What it is

The Quarkus LangChain4j Ollama extension sets a **10-second default REST client timeout**
for all chat requests. This is undocumented. For local LLMs (8B+ parameter models on CPU
or M-series Neural Engine), a single JSON-structured chat request typically takes 15–120
seconds, so the default silently causes every judge call to fail.

## Context

Appears when running eval harness tests with Ollama models as the judge. The `PromptJudge`
call fails with:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Judge LLM call failed — check judge model configuration
Caused by: javax.ws.rs.ProcessingException: The timeout period of 10000ms has been exceeded
  while executing POST /api/chat for server localhost:11434
```

The timeout fires before the model finishes generating the structured JSON response.

## Fix

Pass the timeout override via system property:

```bash
"-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

The property is not documented in the Quarkus LangChain4j extension docs or the
quarkus.io reference (as of 2026-06-14). It's discoverable only by reading the
extension's `OllamaConfig` source.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("check judge model configuration") points to configuration rather
than networking/timeout, leading to checks of model name, format=json flag, and CDI
wiring — none of which are the problem. The 10-second timeout is plausible for
hosted APIs but is impractical for any local model above 3B parameters.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus langchain4j timeout error
Ollama REST client timeout default value
judge llm call failed java IllegalStateException

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache

## Symptom

After adding `quarkus-langchain4j-ollama` as a test-scope dependency inside a Maven profile
(`-Peval-ollama`), the Ollama `ChatModel` bean is not registered. Config keys are logged as
`Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"`, and the
test fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for `ChatModel`.

## Context

The module was previously built without the Ollama extension. Maven resolves the Ollama JAR
when the profile is active, but Quarkus reuses its disk-based augmentation cache from the
prior build — before the Ollama extension was on the classpath. The Ollama extension is
silently absent from augmentation: no beans registered, no config processors active.

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Running `mvn test -Peval,eval-ollama` after the JAR appeared in `~/.m2` — stale augmentation
  cache persisted, config keys still unrecognized.
- Adding `-Dquarkus.test.profile=eval` explicitly — no effect on cache.

## Root cause

Quarkus augmentation is disk-cached in `target/quarkus-app/`. When classpath changes occur
(new extension added via Maven profile), the cache invalidation heuristic does not always
detect the change, especially when the Ollama JAR was already present in `~/.m2` from a
prior `mvn dependency:resolve` call (updating file timestamps). The cache is reused, and
the Ollama extension's CDI beans are never registered.

## Fix

Run `mvn clean` before the first test run with the new profile:

```bash
JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 26) mvn clean test -pl eval -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dtest=PromptEvalTest#evaluateRealWorldScenarios \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name=qwen3:8b" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

Subsequent runs without `clean` work correctly — the Ollama-aware augmentation is now cached.

## Why this is non-obvious

The "unrecognized configuration key" warning does not hint at augmentation caching — it reads
as though the extension was not added at all, not that a stale build artifact is in play.
The Ollama JAR is visible in `mvn dependency:resolve` output, making the missing registration
doubly confusing. The standard fix for missing CDI beans (`check your imports, check your
annotations`) leads nowhere.

**See also:** [GE-20260530-0178fd](GE-20260530-0178fd.md) — Quarkus @QuarkusTest augmentation requires extension deployment JARs in ~/.m2 | [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension @Default ChatModel clashes with @DefaultBean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"
Augmentation cache stale test-scope Ollama ChatModel

entries.title: GraalVM tracing agent as sole discovery path for ONNX Runtime + DJL native-image config
entries.body:
GraalVM tracing agent as sole discovery path for ONNX Runtime + DJL native-image config

### The technique
When building GraalVM native images with JNI libraries that have no upstream reachability metadata, the tracing agent in JVM mode is the only viable discovery path for the complete config. No manual inspection of source code or documentation can reliably produce the full set of JNI, reflection, and resource entries.

### How to apply

Run the application in JVM mode with the tracing agent:

```bash
java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=target/agent-config \
  -jar target/quarkus-app/quarkus-run.jar \
  <application-args>
```

Exercise all code paths that use JNI. The agent generates `reachability-metadata.json` capturing every reflection, JNI, and resource access. Copy the output to `src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/<group>/<artifact>/`.

### Why this is non-obvious
The intuitive approach is to inspect library source for `native` method declarations, `System.loadLibrary()` calls, and reflection usage — then manually register each one. This fails because:

1. **Rust→Java JNI callbacks are invisible** — DJL's tokenizer has Rust code that calls `JNIEnv::NewObject` to create Java objects. These callbacks don't appear in Java source at all.
2. **JNA bridge classes are implicit** — DJL uses JNA, which has its own JNI surface (`com.sun.jna.*`) that must be registered. Dozens of JNA classes need JNI access.
3. **Transitive resource dependencies** — ONNX Runtime bundles multiple `.dylib` files (core, JNI bridge, providers, WebGPU) that all need resource registration.
4. **No upstream metadata exists** — as of June 2026, ONNX Runtime, DJL, LangChain4j, quarkiverse/quarkus-langchain4j, and the GraalVM reachability metadata repo all lack native-image config for these libraries.

### What developers would normally do instead
Manually inspect source, write JNI/reflection config by hand, and iterate on build failures. This works for simple libraries but misses Rust→Java callbacks and implicit JNA requirements, leading to hours of debugging opaque runtime failures (Rust panics, UnsatisfiedLinkError) with no clear diagnostic.

**See also:** [GE-20260606-025601](GE-20260606-025601.md) — ONNX Runtime --initialize-at-run-time must be package-level (the specific gotcha this technique addresses) | [GE-20260606-aab62a](GE-20260606-aab62a.md) — DJL 0.36.0 ships partial native-image metadata | [GE-20260606-7bf5dd](GE-20260606-7bf5dd.md) — DJL CharSpan JNI callback causes Rust panic in GraalVM native image

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
GraalVM native-image JNI discovery agent
Tracing agent for ONNX Runtime DJL native-image
Reachability metadata JSON native image config

entries.title: Ollama format=json enforces structurally valid JSON at sampling level — bypasses small model instruction-following failures
entries.body:
Ollama format=json enforces structurally valid JSON at sampling level — bypasses small model instruction-following failures

## Technique

Set `quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json` (or pass `format: "json"` in the Ollama API request) to force structurally valid JSON output at the token-sampling level, bypassing the model's instruction-following behaviour entirely.

```properties
quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json
```

This is distinct from prompt engineering. A model instruction saying "Return ONLY raw JSON" is a soft directive — small models (3B, 4B) routinely ignore it and produce preamble ("Here is the JSON:", "Here's my evaluation:") or natural language responses with no `{` at all. `format=json` is a hard constraint: the Ollama runtime biases token selection to produce valid JSON structure regardless of the model's tendency to ignore the instruction.

## Context

Useful in any eval harness or structured extraction pipeline using Ollama. The constraint is applied by Ollama's inference engine, not by the model itself — it works even when the model has no explicit training for JSON output. All four models tested (llama3.2:3b, gemma3:4b, llama3.1:8b, qwen3.6:35b) produced parseable JSON with `format=json`; without it, the 3B model failed on roughly 30–50% of calls with non-JSON preamble.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The obvious approach is to improve the instruction — "Return ONLY raw JSON, no preamble, no markdown". This works reliably with large instruction-tuned models (7B+) but fails unpredictably with smaller models. Developers typically iterate on prompt wording rather than recognising that the constraint needs to operate at the sampling layer. The `format=json` parameter is documented in Ollama's API reference but not prominently surfaced in the Quarkus extension docs.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json
format: "json" ollama
json format ollama error message
