entries.title: @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index

## Context

Building a `casehub-testing` module to provide `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory repository implementations that downstream `@QuarkusTest` classes can consume by just adding the module as a test dependency — no `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` config needed.

## Symptom

```
jakarta.enterprise.inject.UnsatisfiedResolutionException: Unsatisfied dependency
  for type io.casehub.engine.spi.CaseInstanceRepository and qualifiers [@Default]
```

Downstream `@QuarkusTest` fails to start even though `casehub-testing` is on the classpath and its `TestCaseInstanceRepository` carries `@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped`.

## Root Cause

Quarkus CDI bean discovery requires a Jandex index to scan beans from classpath JARs. If the testing helper JAR does not build a Jandex index (i.e., the `jandex-maven-plugin` or equivalent is not configured), Quarkus cannot see any of its beans — including `@Alternative @Priority(1)` classes. The annotation is present in the bytecode but the JAR is effectively invisible to CDI.

The `casehub-testing` pom.xml had no Jandex configuration, so its beans were never indexed.

## Fix

**Option A (recommended for reusable testing jars):** Add Jandex indexing to the helper module's pom.xml:

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>io.smallrye</groupId>
    <artifactId>jandex-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>make-index</id>
            <goals><goal>jandex</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

**Option B (proven fallback):** Keep in-memory implementations in `casehub-persistence-memory` without `@Priority`, and activate them via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryEventLogRepository
```

Option B is what every other module in the project already uses and is the safe, proven path.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The `@Alternative @Priority(1)` pattern is supposed to be self-activating — you expect it to "just work" when the JAR is on the classpath. The failure message says "unsatisfied dependency" which points to a missing implementation, not to a missing index. Nothing in the error or Quarkus startup log mentions Jandex.

**See also:** [GE-20260423-a01832](GE-20260423-a01832.md) — @Alternative beans in third-party test jars not scanned without explicit index config | [GE-20260421-03fa72](GE-20260421-03fa72.md) — optional module jar missing Jandex index | [GE-20260417-c59817](GE-20260417-c59817.md) — quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives activates @Alternative beans | [GE-20260427-62d3ab](GE-20260427-62d3ab.md) — @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans as test spies | [GE-20260424-59906a](GE-20260424-59906a.md) — CDI does not scan @ApplicationScoped beans in plain JAR module | [GE-0133](GE-0133.md) — CDI silently ignores beans in jars without Jandex index

**See also:** GE-20260422-ebb91d — CDI AmbiguousResolutionException when multiple @ApplicationScoped beans implement the same SPI interface
**See also:** [GE-20260415-884e48 — @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException](GE-20260415-884e48.md)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: @IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs
entries.body:
@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs

### Symptom

Adding a dev-profile-only CDI bean (e.g., a `CurrentPrincipal` for dev mode) via `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` causes startup failures — all beans from the non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` list disappear.

### Context

Quarkus profile-specific properties (`%dev.`, `%test.`, `%prod.`) completely **replace** their non-profiled counterparts. If the base `application.properties` has:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  com.example.JpaRepo,\
  com.example.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  com.example.JpaSubCaseGroupRepo
```

Adding `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` drops all three JPA alternatives in dev mode — CDI startup fails with unsatisfied dependency errors for every bean that was in the original list.

### Root cause

Profile-specific properties in Quarkus are full replacements, not merges. This is by design (SmallRye Config behaviour), but the failure mode is silent — no warning that the non-profiled value was dropped.

### Fix

Use bean-level annotations instead of `selected-alternatives`:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(150)  // beats OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)
@IfBuildProfile("dev")
public class DemoCurrentPrincipal implements CurrentPrincipal {
    @Override public String tenancyId() { return "demo-tenant"; }
    @Override public String actorId()   { return "demo-user"; }
}
```

**Requirements:**
1. The bean must live in a **Jandex-indexed JAR** (e.g., the application's own `runtime/` module). ArC discovers it automatically — no `selected-alternatives` entry needed.
2. `@IfBuildProfile("dev")` excludes the bean entirely from non-dev builds — no ambiguity in production.
3. `@Priority(150)` resolves over competing `@Alternative` beans (e.g., `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)`) via standard ArC priority resolution.

This is the same mechanism by which `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Alternative @Priority(100)` beats `MockCurrentPrincipal @DefaultBean` in production — without being listed in `selected-alternatives`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural instinct is `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MyDevBean` — it looks like the standard profile-override pattern. The replacement behaviour is documented for SmallRye Config but not prominently flagged in the Quarkus CDI guide. The failure (dropped JPA alternatives) manifests as unrelated `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors that don't mention `selected-alternatives` at all.

### Why this fix

`@IfBuildProfile + @Priority` solves the problem at the bean level — no configuration property needed. The alternative (duplicating the full `selected-alternatives` list in every profile override) is fragile and drifts as new alternatives are added.

### Alternatives considered

- **Duplicate the full list in `%dev.`** — works but fragile; every new `@Alternative` bean must be added to every profile-specific override. Drifts silently.
- **Use `@UnlessBuildProfile("prod")` instead of `@IfBuildProfile("dev")`** — activates in both dev and test profiles, which may not be desired. Test profile has its own `FixedCurrentPrincipal @Priority(200)`.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus arc selected-alternatives error
cdi startup failure dev profile
@IfBuildProfile alternative priority resolution

entries.body:
Quarkus test application.properties replaces selected-alternatives entirely — reactive in-memory repos need explicit activation

Quarkus test application.properties replaces selected-alternatives entirely — reactive in-memory repos need explicit activation

### Symptom

`quarkus:build` (production CDI validation) fails with `Unsatisfied dependency for type ReactiveCaseInstanceRepository` and similar for `ReactiveEventLogRepository`, `ReactiveSubCaseGroupRepository`. Tests pass because `engine-testing` provides `@Priority(1)` wrappers. The build step validates against main `application.properties` only.

### Context

A dual-stack engine (blocking + reactive SPIs) uses in-memory `@Alternative` implementations for both. Main `application.properties` lists only the blocking repos in `selected-alternatives`. Test `application.properties` lists different alternatives (ledger JPA repos, platform memory stores). `@Priority(1)` Test* wrappers from engine-testing auto-activate in test mode but don't exist on the production classpath.

### Root cause

Quarkus MicroProfile Config resolves `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` as a single string property. When test `application.properties` declares the same key, it **replaces** the main value entirely — it does not merge or append. The main properties' blocking repos are no longer activated in test mode, but that's fine because Test* wrappers cover them.

However, `quarkus:build` (invoked by `mvn verify`) validates CDI against the **main** `application.properties`. If the main properties only activate blocking repos, the reactive SPIs are unsatisfied. The reactive in-memory repos (`InMemoryReactiveCaseInstanceRepository`, `InMemoryReactiveEventLogRepository`, etc.) are `@Alternative` without `@Priority` — they need explicit `selected-alternatives` activation.

### Fix

Add all reactive in-memory repo alternatives to the **main** `application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryReactivePlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveCaseInstanceRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryEventLogRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveEventLogRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveCaseMetaModelRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemorySubCaseGroupRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveSubCaseGroupRepository
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Tests pass — the `@Priority(1)` Test* wrappers handle everything in test mode. The failure only appears during `quarkus:build`, which runs CDI validation against the main properties. The error messages name reactive SPI interfaces that the developer never directly uses, making it unclear which concrete beans to activate.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.body:
'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths

### What is undocumented

A service class annotated `@Alternative` and named with "Reactive" may internally use a `blockingService` field (injected blocking CDI service) for write operations and `Entity.find()` (a Panache static) for read operations. CDI `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory stores only intercept at CDI injection points — Panache statics go directly to the underlying database regardless of what alternatives are selected.

### Context

In Quarkus Qhorus (casehubio/qhorus), `ReactiveQhorusMcpTools`:
- `sendMessage()` delegates internally to `blockingMessageService` → `MessageService.send()` → `messageStore.put()` (uses the `MessageStore` CDI alternative, i.e. `InMemoryMessageStore` in tests)
- `getChannelTimeline()` delegates to `blockingGetChannelTimeline()` → `Message.<Message>find(...)` (Panache static — queries H2 directly, bypasses `MessageStore` entirely)

Result: messages written by `sendMessage()` land in `InMemoryMessageStore` (in-memory). Messages read by `getChannelTimeline()` come from H2 (empty in tests). The two paths never share data.

### Discovery

Only visible by reading the service implementation source. The class name and method signatures suggest a uniform reactive abstraction. Not mentioned in any documentation.

### Impact on tests

Tests that call `sendMessage()` then verify the timeline via `getChannelTimeline()` always see an empty timeline in test setups using `@Alternative` in-memory stores, even though the message was "successfully" posted.

### Fix / Workaround

Identify the actual data path for each operation you need to test:
1. Check which CDI service field the MCP tool method delegates to
2. Check whether that service uses CDI store injection or Panache statics
3. For end-to-end write→read tests: use the real H2 database (don't rely on in-memory stores for both sides)

Alternatively, file an upstream issue to make the read path use the same abstraction as the write path.

**See also:** [GE-20260512-66d997](GE-20260512-66d997.md) — Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores

How do Panache statics bypass CDI @Alternative in-memory stores?

entries.title: ConcurrentHashMap.compute() serializes per-key access — inner collection needs no concurrency control
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.compute() serializes per-key access — inner collection needs no concurrency control

### Context
When a `ConcurrentHashMap<K, V>` holds a mutable collection as its value (e.g.
`ConcurrentHashMap<Key, List<Item>>`), the instinct is to use a thread-safe inner
collection like `CopyOnWriteArrayList` or `Collections.synchronizedList()`.

### The technique
`ConcurrentHashMap.compute()` (and `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`) already serializes
access per key — the lambda runs under the key's bin lock. Inside the lambda, the
inner collection is accessed by exactly one thread at a time. A plain `ArrayList`
is both correct and more efficient.

```java
// Wasteful — CopyOnWriteArrayList copies the entire array on every add/remove
map.compute(key, (k, entry) -> {
    var list = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<Item>();  // O(n) copy per mutation
    list.add(item);
    return new Entry(list, Instant.now());
});

// Correct and efficient — ArrayList inside compute() is single-threaded
map.compute(key, (k, entry) -> {
    var list = new ArrayList<Item>();  // O(1) amortized add
    list.add(item);
    return new Entry(list, Instant.now());
});
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The reflex to use thread-safe collections inside concurrent data structures is deeply
ingrained. `CopyOnWriteArrayList` "looks right" because the outer map is concurrent.
But `compute()` already provides the synchronization — the inner thread-safe collection
adds O(n) overhead per mutation (full array copy) for zero benefit. The performance
difference is stark for eviction patterns: removing element 0 from a 500-element
`CopyOnWriteArrayList` copies 499 elements; from an `ArrayList` it shifts 499 references
in-place (still O(n) but without allocation).

### Caveat
This only applies inside `compute()`/`computeIfAbsent()`/`merge()` lambdas. If the value
is also accessed via `get()` outside these methods, the inner collection IS accessed
concurrently and DOES need its own synchronization. The pattern is safe when all mutations
go through `compute()` and reads go through `drain()` (which removes the entry atomically).

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`ConcurrentHashMap compute serialization`
`compute ArrayList thread safety`
`CopyOnWriteArrayList compute overhead`

entries.title: ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add() provides atomic idempotent registration without explicit locks
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add() provides atomic idempotent registration without explicit locks

### Context

You need to register a resource (e.g. a backend in a registry, a channel in a gateway, a listener on a topic) exactly once per key, even under concurrent access from multiple threads. You want to avoid explicit locks, `synchronized` blocks, and the awkward semantics of `computeIfAbsent` when the computation has side effects.

### Technique

```java
private final Set<UUID> registeredKeys = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

public void ensureRegistered(UUID key) {
    if (registeredKeys.add(key)) {   // atomic: exactly one thread returns true
        doRegistration(key);          // called exactly once per key
    }
}

public void deregister(UUID key) {
    registeredKeys.remove(key);      // subsequent ensureRegistered() will re-register
}
```

`ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()` returns a `Set<K>` backed by a ConcurrentHashMap. `Set.add()` returns `true` if the element was actually added (was absent) and `false` if it was already present. Under concurrent access, exactly one thread gets `true` — all others get `false` and skip the side effect. No explicit locking required.

### Why this is non-obvious

Most developers reach for `synchronized(this)` or `computeIfAbsent`. The `newKeySet().add()` pattern:
- Is 2 lines vs 5-10 for a `synchronized` block
- Returns the boolean signal the caller needs directly from `add()`
- Has guaranteed CAS semantics from the ConcurrentHashMap backing
- Clearly expresses intent: "register this key once, skip if already registered"

`computeIfAbsent` also works but its Javadoc warns that the computation must not modify the map — using it to trigger side effects (registration) is semantically awkward and potentially unsafe if the side effect is not pure. The `Set.add()` pattern has no such restriction.

### Constraints

The side effect in `doRegistration()` must be safe to call after `add()` returns but before other threads observe the registration in the set. If `doRegistration()` itself must be atomic with the `add()` (e.g. the registration step reads back the key), this pattern is insufficient — use a dedicated lock or a more explicit state machine.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

Set add boolean return

entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.put() happens-before only covers future get() calls — not code that obtained the value reference before the put()

## Symptom

Code uses `ConcurrentHashMap` as a thread-safe cache. One thread does `cache.put(id, obj)` then later mutates `obj.field`. A second thread calls `cache.get(id)` — which is defined to happen-after the `put()` — then reads `obj.field` and sees a stale value. Less obviously: a third thread that obtained the reference via an earlier `cache.get()` (or via any other path before the `put()`) also sees a stale `obj.field` even though the `put()` semantically "published" the object.

In this session: `CaseInstance.state` changes were invisible to threads that had obtained a reference to the `CaseInstance` before the state update was published via `cache.put()`.

## Root Cause

The JMM happens-before guarantee from `ConcurrentHashMap.put(k, v)` is: "the state seen by the mapping function or the put() call is visible to any thread that subsequently calls `get(k)` and observes the new value." This guarantee is established at the moment `get()` returns the post-put value.

It covers:
- The value `v` itself (reference visibility)
- Fields written to `v` **before** the `put()` call (publication via the put's write barrier)

It does NOT cover:
- Fields written to `v` **after** the `put()` call
- Any code path that obtained the reference to `v` before this particular `put()` — those threads have no synchronisation barrier between their earlier `get()` and the subsequent field mutation

If a thread modifies `obj.field` after `cache.put()`, that write is only guaranteed visible to threads that call `cache.get()` in a future operation. Threads that already hold a reference — whether from before the put, or from the put itself — see whatever their CPU cache contains.

## Fix

**Option A — Publish immutable state:** Use an immutable value type. Replace `obj.field = newValue` with `cache.put(id, new Obj(newValue))`. Every reader calls `get()` to see current state, establishing the happens-before at each read.

**Option B — `volatile` field:** Declare `volatile State field` on the mutable object. `volatile` writes are visible to all subsequent reads regardless of how the reference was obtained.

**Option C — Use the cache as the memory barrier:** Force all readers to call `cache.get()` for every field read — never hold the reference across mutations. Practical only if the cache is small and reads are infrequent.

In the session: `CaseInstance.state` was made `volatile` so changes published via the engine's own state machine were visible to the `CaseInstanceCache.get()` completion check without requiring a re-put.

## Why this is non-obvious

"ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe" is true but misleadingly coarse. The thread-safety guarantee is for the map structure (no corruption, consistent iteration). The happens-before guarantee is specifically for `get()` observing a `put()` — it does not extend to field-level visibility on the value object after it has been placed in the map. Developers who know that `volatile` is needed for shared fields often miss that a ConcurrentHashMap lookup alone does not establish a barrier for code holding a pre-obtained reference.

**See also:** [GE-20260616-57201e](GE-20260616-57201e.md) — ConcurrentHashMap.put() happens-before get() in the same map

entries.body:
Double-CAS pattern for lock-free coordinated state transitions across two AtomicRefs

### Symptom
Two related pieces of state must transition atomically — e.g., a lifecycle phase
index and a graph reference — but they live in different concurrent data structures
(`ConcurrentHashMap` and `AtomicReference`). Locking both kills throughput in a
hot path (reconciliation loop).

### Context
A lifecycle manager tracks phase state in a `ConcurrentHashMap<String, TenantLifecycle>`
(immutable records, replaced atomically). The reconciliation loop holds the current graph
in an `AtomicReference<DesiredStateGraph>`. A phase transition must update both: advance
the phase index AND swap the graph. A concurrent replan (from a different thread) may
modify either at any time.

### Fix
**Double-CAS with rollback:** CAS the lifecycle map first (cheap, local), then CAS the
graph ref (shared, contended). If the second CAS fails, roll back the first.

```java
// 1. CAS lifecycle state (ConcurrentHashMap.replace)
TenantLifecycle next = new TenantLifecycle(current.phases(), nextIndex);
if (!lifecycles.replace(tenancyId, current, next)) {
    return; // concurrent modification — skip, re-evaluate next cycle
}

// 2. CAS graph ref
if (!loop.compareAndSetDesired(tenancyId, expectedGraph, nextPhase.graph())) {
    // Rollback lifecycle state — graph was changed concurrently
    lifecycles.replace(tenancyId, next, current);
    return; // re-evaluate next cycle
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The naive approach is to lock both structures. The insight is that both structures
are re-evaluated on every cycle — so a failed CAS just means "skip this transition
and try again next time." The rollback on the second CAS failure is safe because
`replace(key, next, current)` only succeeds if `next` is still the current value —
if a concurrent replan already replaced the lifecycle entry, the rollback harmlessly
fails and the replan's state wins.

The ordering matters: lifecycle state first (local concern, less contended), graph ref
second (shared with the reconciliation loop, more contended). Failing on the second CAS
is the common concurrent case — rolling back a `ConcurrentHashMap.replace` is cheaper
than rolling back an `AtomicReference.compareAndSet`.

### Alternatives considered
- Synchronized block covering both mutations (correct but serialises all phase transitions
  and replans — unacceptable in a hot reconciliation loop)
- Single atomic state object combining both (forces the reconciliation loop to know about
  lifecycle phases — violates separation of concerns)
- Eventual consistency (update both independently, accept temporary mismatch) — risks
  a cycle executing against the wrong graph for the current phase

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`AtomicReference` `compareAndSetDesired` failure
`ConcurrentHashMap` `replace` conflict
lifecycle state rollback graph

entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent() + .add() is not atomic with concurrent remove() — futures can be permanently lost

## Symptom

`CompletableFuture` registered in a `ConcurrentHashMap<String, List<CompletableFuture<T>>>`
is never completed, even though `complete()` was called with the correct key.
No exception is thrown. The caller blocks indefinitely.

## Context

Pattern: a registry maps correlation keys to lists of futures. Two threads:
1. `register(key)` — calls `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(future)`
2. `complete(key, result)` — calls `pending.remove(key)` then completes all futures in the removed list

## Root cause

`computeIfAbsent()` is atomic at the map level (inserts the list if absent), but
`.add(future)` on the returned list happens **outside** the atomic window. A concurrent
`complete()` calling `pending.remove(key)` between these two steps removes the list
from the map before the future is added to it. The future is added to a list that no
longer belongs to the map and will never be seen by subsequent `complete()` calls.

```
Thread A: list = computeIfAbsent("key")  ← list inserted in map
Thread B: pending.remove("key")          ← list removed from map
Thread A: list.add(future)               ← future added to orphaned list; never completed
```

## Fix

Synchronize both `register()` and `complete()` on the map, completing futures
**outside** the lock to avoid deadlock from completion callbacks:

```java
public CompletableFuture<T> register(String key) {
    CompletableFuture<T> future = new CompletableFuture<>();
    synchronized (pending) {
        pending.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(future);
    }
    return future;
}

public void complete(String key, T result) {
    List<CompletableFuture<T>> futures;
    synchronized (pending) {
        futures = pending.remove(key);   // atomic remove under lock
    }
    if (futures == null) return;
    for (CompletableFuture<T> f : futures) {
        f.complete(result);              // complete OUTSIDE lock — callbacks may re-register
    }
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

`ConcurrentHashMap` makes individual operations atomic, so developers assume
`computeIfAbsent(...).add(...)` is safe. The atomicity guarantee covers the lookup
and insert, not the subsequent method call on the returned value. The bug is
invisible under low load (register and complete rarely interleave) but emerges under
concurrency — exactly the condition ConcurrentHashMap is meant to handle.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
ConcurrentHashMap complete future lost
computeIfAbsent add atomic remove
futures never completed

entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfPresent returning null atomically removes the map entry — eliminates TOCTOU in prune-if-empty patterns

### What

`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfPresent(key, fn)` removes the map entry atomically when the function returns `null`. The function executes under the map's internal per-bucket lock, so the condition check and the entry removal are a single atomic operation — no separate lock or CAS loop required.

### Context

Replacing the two-step "remove item from collection value, then remove map entry if empty" pattern that has a TOCTOU race window (see GE-20260522-98b286 for the gotcha this technique resolves):

```java
// WRONG — TOCTOU between isEmpty() and remove()
list.remove(item);
if (list.isEmpty()) map.remove(key, list);
```

### Technique

```java
// CORRECT — atomic collapse of remove + prune under map segment lock
map.computeIfPresent(key, (k, list) -> {
    list.remove(item);
    return list.isEmpty() ? null : list;
});
```

The lambda:
1. Runs exclusively (per-bucket lock held for the duration)
2. Mutates the list value
3. Returns `null` → entry is atomically removed
4. Returns the list → entry is atomically kept

No window exists between the empty-check and the removal for a concurrent thread to add to the list.

### Why This Is Non-Obvious

The Javadoc for `computeIfPresent` focuses on the update-in-place use case. The `null`-return semantic — that it atomically removes the entry — is documented but easy to miss. Most developers encountering the TOCTOU race would reach for a `synchronized` block on the map or a per-key `ReentrantLock`, which adds significantly more complexity and contention surface. The `computeIfPresent`/`null` pattern is zero-overhead (same cost as the existing remove path), requires no auxiliary lock, and expresses the intent clearly in four lines.

### Why This Fix

`synchronized(map)` would work but serialises all operations on all keys globally. A `ConcurrentHashMap<K, ReentrantLock>` of per-key locks works but adds allocation and lookup overhead. `computeIfPresent` already holds the per-bucket lock — returning `null` is the natural way to express "conditionally remove" within that lock without widening the critical section.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
computeIfPresent returns null atomically
map.computeIfPresent removes entry atomically
TOCTOU race window eliminate with computeIfPresent

entries.body:
H2 2.x MVStore MERGE INTO is not concurrent-safe for first-inserts

### Context

`MERGE INTO table USING (...) WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` is used as an
atomic upsert — e.g. for sequence allocation tables that need "insert if absent,
update if present."

### Symptom

Under concurrent writes from multiple threads targeting the same new primary key,
one or more transactions throw:

```
Unique index or primary key violation: "PUBLIC.PK_<table> INDEX ..."
SQL statement: MERGE INTO <table> AS t USING ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...
```

The failure only occurs on first-insert for a new key. Subsequent writes (where
the row already exists) hit `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE` and succeed. Serial tests
pass; concurrent tests fail.

### Root Cause

H2 2.0 (July 2021) switched the default storage engine from **page-store**
(table-level locking) to **MVStore** (MVCC / row-level). Under MVStore, `MERGE INTO`
evaluates `WHEN NOT MATCHED` non-atomically:

1. Transaction A reads — row absent → plans INSERT
2. Transaction B reads — row absent → plans INSERT
3. Transaction A inserts → succeeds
4. Transaction B inserts → unique constraint violation (row now exists)

The conflict is not suppressed — it propagates as a `ConstraintViolationException`,
poisoning Transaction B's `EntityManager` and requiring a full transaction rollback.

Documentation and Javadoc written for H2 1.x stated "H2 uses table-level locking."
This was true for page-store. It is false for MVStore.

### Fix

Replace the single-statement `MERGE INTO` with two statements:

```java
// INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — concurrent first-inserts are safe.
// H2 2.2+ in MODE=PostgreSQL supports the no-column-target form only:
// ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (not ON CONFLICT (col1, col2) DO NOTHING).
em.createNativeQuery(
    "INSERT INTO sequence_table (subject_id, tenancy_id, next_seq) " +
    "VALUES (CAST(?1 AS UUID), ?2, 1) " +
    "ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING")
    .setParameter(1, subjectId).setParameter(2, tenancyId).executeUpdate();

em.createNativeQuery(
    "UPDATE sequence_table SET next_seq = next_seq + 1 " +
    "WHERE subject_id = CAST(?1 AS UUID) AND tenancy_id = ?2")
    .setParameter(1, subjectId).setParameter(2, tenancyId).executeUpdate();
```

Both PostgreSQL and H2 2.2+ (in `MODE=PostgreSQL`) accept this SQL. The `UPDATE`
acquires a row lock held for the transaction duration, serialising concurrent writes.

### Why this is non-obvious

H2 2.0 silently changed the default storage engine — existing `MERGE INTO` code
that worked correctly for years under H2 1.x breaks only under concurrent load.
Serial unit tests always pass. The failure surfaces only in integration test suites
that exercise concurrent writes (e.g. Quartz workers, concurrent HTTP handlers).

The Javadoc claiming "H2 uses table-level locking" remained in the codebase long
after H2 2.x shipped, reinforcing the incorrect assumption.

### Why this fix

`MERGE INTO` evaluated in a single statement appears atomic but is not under MVCC.
The two-statement approach makes the sequence explicit: one statement that safely
handles concurrent first-inserts (DO NOTHING on conflict), and one that serialises
via row lock. This is identical to PostgreSQL's `INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING +
UPDATE` pattern and can be unified across both dialects with the same SQL.

### Alternatives considered

- **`LOCK_MODE=1` on H2 URL** — does not restore table-level locking for MVStore tables;
  the flag only affects the discontinued page-store engine.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` inner transaction for first-insert** — adds a class and transaction
  boundary just for the initial-insert edge case; rejected as unnecessary complexity.
- **`SELECT FOR UPDATE` / pessimistic lock** — cannot lock a row that doesn't exist yet;
  fails silently on first-insert (same race condition).

**See also:** [GE-20260605-b734b3](GE-20260605-b734b3.md) — SQL-standard MERGE INTO USING WHEN MATCHED/NOT MATCHED for portable H2 + PostgreSQL atomic upsert (the technique that addresses this H2 limitation)

**See also:** [GE-20260618-0ed34c](GE-20260618-0ed34c.md) — H2 LOCK_MODE=1 has no effect with MVStore (failed workaround for this problem) | [GE-20260618-73a023](GE-20260618-73a023.md) — H2 JDBC getMetaData().getURL() drops connection properties

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`MERGE INTO` concurrent insert violation
`Unique index or primary key violation` H2 MVStore
`EntityManager ConstraintViolationException` MERGE INTO

entries.title: Double-CAS pattern for lock-free coordinated state transitions across two AtomicRefs
entries.body:
Double-CAS pattern for lock-free coordinated state transitions across two AtomicRefs

### Symptom
Two related pieces of state must transition atomically — e.g., a lifecycle phase
index and a graph reference — but they live in different concurrent data structures
(`ConcurrentHashMap` and `AtomicReference`). Locking both kills throughput in a
hot path (reconciliation loop).

### Context
A lifecycle manager tracks phase state in a `ConcurrentHashMap<String, TenantLifecycle>`
(immutable records, replaced atomically). The reconciliation loop holds the current graph
in an `AtomicReference<DesiredStateGraph>`. A phase transition must update both: advance
the phase index AND swap the graph. A concurrent replan (from a different thread) may
modify either at any time.

### Fix
**Double-CAS with rollback:** CAS the lifecycle map first (cheap, local), then CAS the
graph ref (shared, contended). If the second CAS fails, roll back the first.

```java
// 1. CAS lifecycle state (ConcurrentHashMap.replace)
TenantLifecycle next = new TenantLifecycle(current.phases(), nextIndex);
if (!lifecycles.replace(tenancyId, current, next)) {
    return; // concurrent modification — skip, re-evaluate next cycle
}

// 2. CAS graph ref
if (!loop.compareAndSetDesired(tenancyId, expectedGraph, nextPhase.graph())) {
    // Rollback lifecycle state — graph was changed concurrently
    lifecycles.replace(tenancyId, next, current);
    return; // re-evaluate next cycle
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The naive approach is to lock both structures. The insight is that both structures
are re-evaluated on every cycle — so a failed CAS just means "skip this transition
and try again next time." The rollback on the second CAS failure is safe because
`replace(key, next, current)` only succeeds if `next` is still the current value —
if a concurrent replan already replaced the lifecycle entry, the rollback harmlessly
fails and the replan's state wins.

The ordering matters: lifecycle state first (local concern, less contended), graph ref
second (shared with the reconciliation loop, more contended). Failing on the second CAS
is the common concurrent case — rolling back a `ConcurrentHashMap.replace` is cheaper
than rolling back an `AtomicReference.compareAndSet`.

### Alternatives considered
- Synchronized block covering both mutations (correct but serialises all phase transitions
  and replans — unacceptable in a hot reconciliation loop)
- Single atomic state object combining both (forces the reconciliation loop to know about
  lifecycle phases — violates separation of concerns)
- Eventual consistency (update both independently, accept temporary mismatch) — risks
  a cycle executing against the wrong graph for the current phase

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`AtomicReference` `compareAndSetDesired` failure
`ConcurrentHashMap` `replace` conflict
lifecycle state rollback graph

entries.title: JPQL atomic increment (UPDATE SET count = count + 1) is simpler than @Version OCC for single-counter atomicity
entries.body:
JPQL atomic increment (UPDATE SET count = count + 1) is simpler than @Version OCC for single-counter atomicity

### The technique

When a JPA entity needs a concurrency-safe integer counter increment, replace the read-modify-write pattern (`entity.count++`) with an atomic JPQL UPDATE followed by a re-read:

```java
// Instead of: read → mutate → Hibernate dirty write (data race under READ COMMITTED)
e.completedCount++;
return Uni.createFrom().item(toDomain(e));

// Use: single atomic SQL statement + re-read
SubCaseGroupEntity.update(
    "completedCount = completedCount + 1 WHERE parentCaseId = ?1 AND groupId = ?2",
    parentCaseId, groupId)
.chain(count -> {
    if (count == 0)
        return Uni.createFrom().failure(new IllegalStateException("Group not found"));
    return SubCaseGroupEntity
        .<SubCaseGroupEntity>find("parentCaseId = ?1 AND groupId = ?2", parentCaseId, groupId)
        .firstResult()
        .onItem().ifNotNull().transform(this::toDomain)
        .onItem().ifNull().failWith(() -> new IllegalStateException("Group vanished after increment"));
});
```

In Hibernate Reactive Panache, wrap in `Panache.withTransaction()`. The `UPDATE` and `SELECT` are in the same transaction — the `SELECT` always sees the committed result of the `UPDATE`.

### When to use this

Use when:
- Only one or a few integer fields need concurrent increment/decrement
- Contention is possible but lock acquisition cost is undesirable
- You don't need retry-on-conflict behavior — atomic SQL avoids the conflict entirely

### Why this is non-obvious

The obvious approach for concurrent writes is `@Version` optimistic locking with an `OptimisticLockException` retry loop. `@Version` is correct but adds: a version column, exception handling in the caller, retry logic, and exponential backoff in high-contention scenarios.

For a single counter field, `UPDATE SET count = count + 1 WHERE ...` is a single SQL statement that the database serializes at the row level — no version column, no retry. PostgreSQL (and most RDBMS) guarantee that two concurrent executions of this UPDATE on the same row serialize without conflict: one gets `count=1, next=0`, one gets `count=1, next=1` — each sees the other's write.

The re-read returns the DB-committed value at SELECT time, which may reflect concurrent increments that committed between the UPDATE and SELECT. This is intentional: callers that compare count vs threshold see the current total, which is exactly what's needed for M-of-N coordination.

### Caveats

- The returned `SubCaseGroup` reflects DB state at SELECT time — it may include increments from other concurrent transactions. If the caller needs "my increment only" semantics, this doesn't work.
- In Hibernate Reactive, the UPDATE and re-read must be in the same `withTransaction()` block to guarantee the SELECT sees the UPDATE's result.
- "Group vanished after increment" failure path is theoretical (someone deleted the row between UPDATE and SELECT) but worth guarding against in production code.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`JPQL atomic increment error message`
`@Version OCC concurrency`
`SubCaseGroupEntity update`

H2 LOCK_MODE=1 has no effect with MVStore — concurrent MERGE races persist
entries.body:
H2 LOCK_MODE=1 has no effect with MVStore — concurrent MERGE races persist

## Symptom

Adding `LOCK_MODE=1` to the H2 JDBC URL to prevent concurrent first-insert races on a
shared table appears to succeed — no error, the application starts — but the concurrent
race condition continues unaffected. Two threads racing to INSERT the same primary key
still produce `JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException`.

```
JDBC URL:
jdbc:h2:mem:testdb;MODE=PostgreSQL;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1;LOCK_MODE=1
```

```
Error (still observed with LOCK_MODE=1):
Unique index or primary key violation: "PUBLIC.PK_LEDGER_SUBJECT_SEQUENCE
INDEX ... VALUES ( /* key:1 */ UUID '...')"; SQL statement:
MERGE INTO ledger_subject_sequence AS t USING (...) AS s ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (subject_id, tenancy_id, next_seq) VALUES (...)
```

## Context

Triggered by concurrent `MERGE INTO` on a new row that both threads see as absent (MVCC
read-committed isolation). Common in `@QuarkusTest` suites where multiple Quartz workers
or CDI async observers write to the same H2 table simultaneously for the first time.

LOCK_MODE is a documented H2 parameter. The documentation does not clearly state that it
only applies to the discontinued page-store engine and is silently ignored in MVStore mode.

## What was tried

- `LOCK_MODE=1` in JDBC URL — no effect; race persists.
- `LOCK_MODE=2` — same; still silently ignored.
- Neither URL parameter nor `SET LOCK_MODE` SQL triggers an error; the setting is accepted
  but MVStore's MVCC engine does not honour it.

## Root cause

H2 2.0 switched the default storage engine from page-store to MVStore. MVStore uses MVCC
(multi-version concurrency control) with row-level locking, not table-level locking. The
`LOCK_MODE` URL parameter only controlled the page-store engine's locking behaviour.
In H2 2.x, MVStore always uses MVCC regardless of `LOCK_MODE`. The parameter is accepted
without error for backward compatibility but has no observable effect.

## Fix

Replace `MERGE INTO` with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` + `UPDATE`. H2 2.2+
(released July 2023) added `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` support for `INSERT` statements,
including in `MODE=PostgreSQL`. The `ON CONFLICT` path is race-safe: if two transactions
simultaneously attempt the first insert, exactly one succeeds and the other silently does
nothing; both then proceed to the `UPDATE`, which serialises via the MVStore row lock.

```sql
-- Instead of:
MERGE INTO t USING (...) AS s ON t.key = s.key
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.val = t.val + 1
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (key, val) VALUES (s.key, 2)

-- Use:
INSERT INTO t (key, val) VALUES (CAST(? AS UUID), 1) ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;
UPDATE t SET val = val + 1 WHERE key = CAST(? AS UUID);
```

This is the same SQL as the PostgreSQL path — both H2 2.2+ and PostgreSQL support it, so
a single implementation works for both databases.

## Why this is non-obvious

`LOCK_MODE=1` is documented as enabling "table-level locking", which is exactly what is
needed to serialise concurrent MERGE statements. The parameter is silently accepted with no
error or warning when it has no effect. There is no runtime indication that the setting is
being ignored. The fix requires knowing that (a) H2 2.0 removed page-store, (b) MVStore is
MVStore is immune to LOCK_MODE, and (c) H2 2.2+ added ON CONFLICT support — none of these
are prominently documented together.

### Why this fix

`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` + `UPDATE` produces identical SQL for both H2 and PostgreSQL,
eliminating the dialect split that caused the original bug. The `MERGE INTO` approach
assumed H2 would serialize via table locking — an assumption that was silently wrong for
five major releases.

**See also:** [GE-20260617-6b01c4](GE-20260617-6b01c4.md) — H2 2.x MVStore MERGE INTO is not concurrent-safe for first-inserts (the root problem LOCK_MODE=1 was meant to fix) | [GE-20260618-73a023](GE-20260618-73a023.md) — H2 JDBC getMetaData().getURL() drops connection properties | [GE-20260605-b734b3](GE-20260605-b734b3.md) — SQL-standard MERGE INTO for portable H2 + PostgreSQL

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
H2 LOCK_MODE=1 MVStore race
"JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException" MERGE
MVStore MVCC row-level locking

entries.title: quarkus.datasource.active=false is runtime-only — Hibernate build step still demands a configured datasource
entries.body:
quarkus.datasource.active=false is runtime-only — Hibernate build step still demands a configured datasource

### Symptom
`io.quarkus.runtime.configuration.ConfigurationException: Datasource '<default>' is not configured` at Quarkus augmentation time, despite setting `quarkus.datasource.active=false` and `quarkus.hibernate-orm.active=false` in `application.properties`.

### Context
You have `@Entity` classes on the classpath (from a Quarkus extension runtime module) and want to boot without any real datasource — e.g. using `@Alternative @Priority(100)` in-memory stores that beat the JPA stores. Setting `datasource.active=false` seems like the right approach.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. `quarkus.datasource.active=false` + `quarkus.hibernate-orm.active=false` — both are runtime properties; the `HibernateOrmProcessor#configurationDescriptorBuilding` build step runs before runtime and demands a datasource when it sees entities.
2. `quarkus.hibernate-orm.enabled=false` — disables entity scanning at build time, but JPA store beans still inject `EntityManager`. With no `EntityManager` bean produced, you get `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`.
3. Excluding JPA stores via `quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.example.repository.jpa.*` — cascades into `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for any bean that injects the excluded stores (e.g. a `CrossTenantProducer` that injects `CrossTenantWorkItemStore`). The dependency chain is deeper than the direct excludes.

### Root cause
`quarkus.datasource.active` and `quarkus.hibernate-orm.active` are **runtime** properties — they deactivate beans at runtime but do not affect Quarkus augmentation (build-time). The `HibernateOrmProcessor` build step scans for `@Entity` annotations and validates that a matching datasource exists. This happens before any runtime property is evaluated.

### Fix
Provide a dummy H2 datasource that satisfies build-time validation. Disable Flyway so no migrations run. Let Hibernate generate schema from annotations (never used for actual data):

```properties
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:dummy;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=drop-and-create
quarkus.flyway.enabled=false
```

The `@Alternative @Priority(100)` in-memory stores handle all actual persistence. The H2 datasource exists but carries no data.

### Why this is non-obvious
The property name `quarkus.datasource.active=false` strongly implies "don't use a datasource." A developer would reasonably expect it to work at build time. The distinction between build-time augmentation and runtime configuration is not surfaced in the error message — the exception says "Datasource not configured" without mentioning that `active=false` was set and ignored.

### Why this fix
The dummy datasource approach is the only one that avoids cascading CDI failures. Both `hibernate-orm.enabled=false` and `arc.exclude-types` break the CDI wiring graph in ways that require excluding progressively more beans. The dummy datasource keeps the entire CDI graph valid while letting the alternative stores win at runtime.

### Alternatives considered
- **`hibernate-orm.enabled=false`** — rejected because JPA store beans still inject `EntityManager`, which is absent when Hibernate is disabled. Would require all JPA stores to use `@IfBuildProperty` or similar conditional registration.
- **`arc.exclude-types` on JPA packages** — rejected because the dependency chain cascades. Any service bean that injects a store interface (where the only implementation was the excluded JPA store) fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`.
- **No datasource at all** — not possible while `@Entity` classes are on the classpath and the Hibernate extension is present.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus hibernate datasource runtime property
hibernate orm processor configuration exception
datasource active false build step

entries.body:
quarkus.datasource.reactive=false suppresses Hibernate Reactive boot when extension is on classpath but no reactive pool exists

## quarkus.datasource.reactive=false suppresses Hibernate Reactive boot when extension is on classpath but no reactive pool exists

**ID:** GE-20260420-45d53b
**Stack:** Quarkus 3.32.2

**What it does:** Setting `quarkus.datasource.reactive=false` in `application.properties` prevents Hibernate Reactive from attempting to acquire a reactive (Vert.x) connection pool at startup, even when `quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache` is on the classpath and has registered reactive persistence units at build time.

**Where it works:** Test `application.properties`, per-profile properties, and main `application.properties`.

```properties
# Prevents FastBootHibernateReactivePersistenceProvider from failing
# when no reactive datasource is configured
quarkus.datasource.reactive=false
```

### Why non-obvious
Nothing in the Quarkus extension developer docs mentions this property as a reactive-boot suppressor. The reactive extension activates at build time based on classpath scanning; suppressing it at runtime via a datasource flag is counter-intuitive. The natural search path (Hibernate Reactive docs, `@Alternative`, `quarkus.hibernate-reactive.*` properties) doesn't lead here. Found by trial and error.

**See also:** GE-20260420-33b95f (specific H2+test scenario), GE-20260420-daf5dc (optional dep activation gotcha), GE-20260420-dcec35 (extension forces HR boot even with @Alternative)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache in an extension forces Hibernate Reactive to boot for all consumers — @Alternative does not prevent it
entries.body:
quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache in an extension forces Hibernate Reactive to boot for all consumers — @Alternative does not prevent it

## quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache in an extension forces Hibernate Reactive to boot for all consumers — @Alternative does not prevent it

**ID:** GE-20260420-dcec35
**Stack:** Quarkus 3.32.2, quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache

**Symptom:** Adding `quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache` to a Quarkus extension's runtime `pom.xml` causes `FastBootHibernateReactivePersistenceProvider` to try to initialise on every consumer app startup — even those with no reactive datasource configured. Error: `Unable to find datasource '<default>' for persistence unit '<default>': No pool has been defined`.

Three test classes fail that previously passed: the two using `@TestProfile` (which restart Quarkus) and the one with `@TestTransaction` that triggers JTA coordination with all registered persistence units.

### Root cause
The Hibernate Reactive Panache extension scans for `PanacheRepositoryBase` implementations at **build time** (AOT). Any class implementing the interface — even an `@Alternative` bean — causes the extension to register a reactive persistence unit for the associated entity. `@Alternative` suppresses CDI bean activation but does NOT suppress the build-step registration. At runtime, Hibernate Reactive tries to find a reactive (Vert.x) pool for the registered persistence unit and fails if none is configured.

### Fix
Add to the consumer's test `application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.datasource.reactive=false
```

This prevents Hibernate Reactive from claiming a reactive pool at runtime, even though the persistence unit was registered at build time.

### Why non-obvious
The error message points to a missing datasource pool — suggesting the fix is to configure a datasource, not to disable reactive. Marking the `PanacheRepositoryBase` bean as `@Alternative` is the obvious CDI workaround and feels correct, but `@Alternative` only controls CDI injection — it has no effect on Quarkus build steps. The fix (`quarkus.datasource.reactive=false`) suppresses the runtime pool lookup entirely, not via CDI.

### Alternatives considered
- `@Alternative` on reactive beans — does not prevent build-step registration; persistence unit still created
- `quarkus.hibernate-reactive.active=false` — property not recognised in Quarkus 3.32.2
- Testcontainers + PostgreSQL — works but adds heavy test infrastructure; unnecessary when H2 suffices

**See also:** GE-20260420-45d53b (fix: quarkus.datasource.reactive=false), GE-20260420-daf5dc (optional dep variant of same issue)

entries.title: Quarkus: JPA entity in a dependency artifact forces datasource config on ALL downstream consumers
entries.body:
Quarkus: JPA entity in a dependency artifact forces datasource config on ALL downstream consumers

## Symptom

After adding a module that contains JPA `@Entity` classes as a compile dependency, `@QuarkusTest` classes in downstream modules fail at startup with:

```
ConfigurationException: Datasource '<default>' is not configured.
To solve this, configure datasource '<default>'.
```

This happens even if the downstream module uses only in-memory repository implementations and never interacts with the new dependency's entities.

## Context

Triggered when a module (e.g. `quarkus-ledger`) bundles JPA entity classes in its main artifact. Any module that takes this as a compile dependency — even just to use a utility class like `LedgerTraceIdProvider` — inherits all entity classes on its test classpath. Hibernate ORM's Quarkus extension scans ALL entity classes on the classpath and registers them in the default persistence unit. If no datasource is configured, startup fails.

## What was tried

- Setting `quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=false` in test `application.properties` — has no effect because `migrate-at-start` is a build-time fixed property baked into the jar's `META-INF/microprofile-config.properties`.
- Setting `quarkus.hibernate-orm.enabled=false` — disables Hibernate ORM entirely, which breaks test discovery for `@QuarkusTest` classes that depend on any ORM-scoped CDI beans.
- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` to exclude the problematic beans — does not work for extension-registered beans (registered at augmentation time, not CDI discovery time).

## Root Cause

Quarkus scans the full classpath for `@Entity`-annotated classes at build/augmentation time. Any entity class on the classpath — regardless of which module it came from — is registered in the default persistence unit. There is no built-in scoping mechanism to limit entity discovery to a specific module or jar.

The architectural violation is bundling JPA entity classes alongside domain model/SPI code in a single artifact. The correct pattern: keep domain model (plain POJOs) and JPA entities in separate modules.

## Fix

**Short-term (per affected test module):** Add an H2 datasource configuration to the test `application.properties` so Hibernate can start, plus a `NoOpLedgerEntryRepository` stub (or equivalent) as `@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped` to satisfy CDI:

```properties
# application.properties (test)
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb;MODE=PostgreSQL;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
quarkus.datasource.username=sa
quarkus.datasource.password=
quarkus.hibernate-orm.schema-management.strategy=drop-and-create
quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=false
```

```java
@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped
class NoOpLedgerEntryRepository implements LedgerEntryRepository {
  // no-op implementations of all methods
}
```

**Long-term (architectural fix):** Split the offending artifact into:
- `<name>-api` — domain POJOs + SPI interfaces only, zero JPA dependency
- `<name>` or `<name>-hibernate` — JPA entity classes + Flyway migrations

Downstream consumers take `<name>-api` only. The `quarkus-work-api` module is the canonical correct example of this split.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error message says "configure datasource" but the root cause is a transitive dependency bundling entity classes. The module you added was specifically chosen for a non-persistence feature (e.g. a trace ID provider). The natural expectation is that only the entities YOU define affect your persistence unit. There is no warning at dependency declaration time that adding a module will force datasource configuration in your tests.

**See also:** GE-20260423-fce720 "quarkus-work-core FilterRule JPA entity requires a datasource — modules using in-memory persistence fail startup"

**See also:** [GE-20260512-a3838e](GE-20260512-a3838e.md) — transitive hibernate-reactive-panache causes H2 test startup failure

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus datasource configuration error
"@Entity" class classpath scanning
hibernate orm extension registration

entries.title: Quarkus dual-PU setup with a library dependency that injects @Default EntityManager requires a dummy default datasource + minimal packages config
entries.body:
Quarkus dual-PU setup with a library dependency that injects @Default EntityManager requires a dummy default datasource + minimal packages config

## What exists but isn't documented

When migrating a Quarkus project to a **named persistence unit** (e.g. `quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.*`) while depending on a library whose CDI beans inject `@Default EntityManager` (e.g. `quarkus-ledger`), the default persistence unit must **remain active** even though no application entities use it.

If you only configure `quarkus.datasource.qhorus.*` and leave the default datasource unconfigured, Quarkus boots but the library's `@Default EntityManager` injection fails at runtime with:

```
Unsatisfied dependency for type EntityManager and qualifiers [@Default]
```

## Required setup

**Test `application.properties`** — both datasources must exist:

```properties
# Default datasource — for library beans that inject @Default EntityManager
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:test;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
quarkus.datasource.username=sa
quarkus.datasource.password=

# Named 'qhorus' datasource — for application entities
quarkus.datasource.qhorus.db-kind=h2
quarkus.datasource.qhorus.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:test;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
quarkus.datasource.qhorus.username=sa
quarkus.datasource.qhorus.password=

# Default PU needs a packages config to avoid scanning all entities
# Point it at a config-only package with no @Entity classes
quarkus.hibernate-orm.packages=io.your.project.config

# Both PUs need schema generation in tests
quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=drop-and-create
quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.database.generation=drop-and-create
```

The key insight: `quarkus.hibernate-orm.packages=<config-only-package>` assigns the default PU a package that contains no `@Entity` classes. This satisfies Quarkus's requirement that every active PU declares at least one package, without accidentally routing application entities to the default PU.

## Context

Triggered by any Quarkus library (e.g. `quarkus-ledger`) that ships CDI beans with `@Inject EntityManager em` using the default qualifier. These beans cannot be updated (library code). The consuming application must keep the default PU alive to satisfy the injection point.

## Why non-obvious

Quarkus's named datasource documentation assumes the consuming app controls all its persistence. When a library dependency has `@Default EntityManager` injection, it creates a hidden constraint: the default PU must remain even after migrating all app entities to a named PU. There is no warning, error, or documentation covering this scenario. Discovery only possible by reading the library's source or hitting the boot failure.

**See also:** GE-20260422-334eb8 — named PU EntityManager injection qualifier | GE-20260423-4aa1e0 — JPA JOINED inheritance forces all hierarchy entities into same PU

**See also:** [GE-20260424-6b88a0](GE-20260424-6b88a0.md) — quarkus.ledger.datasource config property that routes to named PU

entries.title: Quarkus QuarkusTestProfile.getConfigProfile() REPLACES %test profile — production application.properties becomes active, Dev Services cannot inject URLs
entries.body:
Quarkus QuarkusTestProfile.getConfigProfile() REPLACES %test profile — production application.properties becomes active, Dev Services cannot inject URLs

## Symptom

A `@QuarkusTest` annotated with `@TestProfile` (whose `getConfigProfile()` returns a custom name,
e.g. `"reactive-pg"`) starts the application but either:
- The datasource bean is deactivated: *"Bean is not active: AgroalDataSource — URL is not set"*
- Or the wrong datasource URL is used (e.g., the production H2 file URL rather than the test
  in-memory URL), causing Flyway or Hibernate to fail with a driver mismatch

## Context

Production `application.properties` contains a datasource URL without a profile prefix:

```properties
quarkus.datasource.qhorus.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:file:~/.app/qhorus
```

The test uses `QuarkusTestProfile.getConfigProfile()` returning `"reactive-pg"` to activate
PostgreSQL-specific config. Quarkus Dev Services is expected to provide the PostgreSQL URL.

## What was tried (didn't work)

**Attempt 1** — Set `%reactive-pg.quarkus.datasource.qhorus.jdbc.url=` (empty string) to clear
the H2 URL so Dev Services can activate:

Dev Services does start the container. But Quarkus **deactivates the Agroal datasource bean
at augmentation time** because `jdbc.url` resolves to an empty string. The bean is marked
inactive before Dev Services can inject a replacement at runtime. Error: *"Datasource 'qhorus'
was deactivated automatically because its URL is not set."*

**Attempt 2** — Set `devservices.enabled=true` explicitly without any URL override:

Dev Services starts the container. But the production H2 URL (`jdbc:h2:file:...`) is still
active — Dev Services does **not** override a configured URL even when `devservices.enabled=true`
is set explicitly. Flyway connects to the H2 URL with the PostgreSQL driver → driver mismatch
failure.

## Root cause

`QuarkusTestProfile.getConfigProfile()` **replaces** the `%test` profile entirely — it does
NOT add to it. When `getConfigProfile()` returns `"reactive-pg"`:

- Active config: production `application.properties` (no profile prefix) + `%reactive-pg.*` properties
- **NOT active**: `%test.*` properties (the `%test` profile is replaced, not extended)

This means the production datasource URL (`quarkus.datasource.qhorus.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:file:...`)
is visible, while the test profile's H2 in-memory URL (`%test.quarkus.datasource.qhorus.jdbc.url`)
is not.

**Dev Services config injection priority is lower than profile config.** Dev Services injects
URLs as a late-binding runtime config source. Any explicitly configured URL — whether from
production config, profile config, or `getConfigOverrides()` — takes precedence and blocks
Dev Services injection.

**Empty-string is not "absent".** Setting `jdbc.url=` explicitly tells Quarkus the URL is
configured (to empty). Quarkus deactivates the Agroal bean because the configured URL is
empty. This happens at augmentation time; Dev Services cannot reverse it at runtime.

## Fix

Use `QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager.start()` to provide the real JDBC+reactive URLs.
Its return value is applied at the **highest config priority** — above system properties,
profile config, and production config. It is available before Quarkus augmentation.

```java
public class PostgresTestResource implements QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager {
    private PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres;

@Override
    public Map<String, String> start() {
        postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine")
                .withDatabaseName("mydb").withUsername("user").withPassword("pass");
        postgres.start();
        String reactiveUrl = "vertx-reactive:postgresql://" + postgres.getHost()
                + ":" + postgres.getMappedPort(5432) + "/" + postgres.getDatabaseName();
        return Map.of(
                "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.jdbc.url",     postgres.getJdbcUrl(),
                "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.reactive.url", reactiveUrl,
                "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.username",     postgres.getUsername(),
                "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.password",     postgres.getPassword(),
                "quarkus.flyway.qhorus.migrate-at-start", "true");
    }

@Override
    public void stop() { if (postgres != null) postgres.stop(); }
}
```

Annotate the IT class with `@QuarkusTestResource(value = PostgresTestResource.class, restrictToAnnotatedClass = true)`.

Dependencies needed: `org.testcontainers:testcontainers-postgresql` (version managed by
Quarkus BOM). For reactive calls inside tests, also add `io.quarkus:quarkus-test-vertx`
and use `@RunOnVertxContext + UniAsserter` (Panache.withTransaction() requires a Vert.x
context the JUnit thread does not have).

## Why this is non-obvious

The Quarkus documentation states that test `application.properties` is read for
`@QuarkusTest`. It does not prominently document that `getConfigProfile()` replaces (not
extends) the test profile, making production config active. The natural assumption is that
the test profile properties always apply; they don't when a custom config profile is set.

Dev Services appears to work (the container starts and logs success) but still fails to
inject the URL — the failure is silent until Hibernate/Flyway fails with a confusing
driver mismatch or empty-URL error.

**See also:** GE-20260422-13f53b — `@TestProfile` restarts not inheriting test datasource
config (broader treatment via `getConfigOverrides()`). GE-20260516-e137f6 — `getConfigOverrides()`
replaces `%test.*`-prefixed config for that profile.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus test profile datasource url
quarkus test profile override
quarkus test profile inactive bean

entries.title: quarkus-maven-plugin build goal in extension runtime pom breaks mvn install with datasource error
entries.body:
quarkus-maven-plugin build goal in extension runtime pom breaks mvn install with datasource error

## Symptom

`mvn install` on a Quarkus extension runtime module fails with:

```
Build failure: Build failed due to errors
[error]: Build step HibernateOrmProcessor#configurationDescriptorBuilding threw an exception:
  ConfigurationException: Persistence unit '<default>' defines entities [...] but its datasource
  '<default>' cannot be found: Datasource '<default>' is not configured.
```

No datasource is configured because the runtime module is an extension — not a Quarkus application.

## Context

A `quarkus-maven-plugin` block with `<goal>build</goal>` was added to the extension runtime module's `pom.xml` (typically to enable `@QuarkusTest` support). Extension modules do not build Quarkus applications — they provide build-time and runtime code that other applications consume.

## What was tried (didn't work)

Adding `quarkus.hibernate-orm.enabled=false` to test properties — doesn't help because the `build` goal runs outside the test lifecycle.

## Root cause

The `quarkus-maven-plugin:build` goal triggers a full Quarkus application build, which includes bootstrapping the full extension processor chain including Hibernate ORM. Extension runtime modules have JPA entities (for the extension's own model classes) but no datasource — they rely on the consuming application to provide one. The build goal sees the entities, tries to configure a persistence unit, and fails.

## Fix

Remove the `quarkus-maven-plugin` `<build>` execution block from the extension runtime module's `pom.xml`. The `@QuarkusTest` infrastructure works without it — Quarkus's test framework bootstraps the application through the test lifecycle, not through the `build` goal.

```xml
<!-- Remove this entire block from extension runtime pom.xml -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>${quarkus.version}</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals>
        <goal>build</goal>  <!-- WRONG in an extension module -->
      </goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

Keep the `quarkus-extension-maven-plugin` (which generates extension descriptors) — only remove the `quarkus-maven-plugin` with the `build` goal.

## Why this is non-obvious

The `quarkus-maven-plugin` with `build` goal is standard in Quarkus *application* poms. An AI assistant or junior developer adding `@QuarkusTest` support to an extension module may cargo-cult this pattern from application examples. The error message points to a missing datasource, not to the plugin configuration — misdirecting debugging.

## Variant — Library modules (no extension descriptor)

The same failure mode occurs in plain library modules (not Quarkus extensions) that have `quarkus-maven-plugin:build` in their pom — for example, modules that define domain objects or SPIs but have no SPI implementations of their own. The error in this case is a CDI validation failure at build time:

```
[ERROR] Build step io.quarkus.arc.deployment.ArcProcessor#validate threw an exception:
  jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.DeploymentException: No bean found for required type [...]
```

The module has CDI injection points (from domain classes or interfaces) but no beans to satisfy them — because the implementations live in other modules. CDI validation fires during the `build` goal's full application bootstrap and fails.

**Fix:** Same as above — remove `quarkus-maven-plugin:build` from library modules. These modules are not Quarkus applications; they don't need the build goal. `@QuarkusTest` in downstream modules handles bootstrapping through the test lifecycle.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus build goal datasource error
quarkus extension runtime mvn install
hibernate orm configuration exception

entries.title: quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache as <optional>true</optional> dep still activates Hibernate Reactive extension in the module's own tests
entries.body:
quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache as <optional>true</optional> dep still activates Hibernate Reactive extension in the module's own tests

## Symptom

Adding `quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache` with `<optional>true</optional>` to `pom.xml` causes `@QuarkusTest` tests to fail with:

```
ConfigurationException: Unable to find datasource '<default>' for persistence unit '<default>':
No pool has been defined for persistence unit <default>
```

Tests that were passing before now fail to start the Quarkus application.

## Context

Occurs when:
1. A library/extension module adds `quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache` as an optional dep (to support reactive consumers without forcing the dep on everyone)
2. The same module has `@QuarkusTest` integration tests using H2 JDBC

## Root Cause

Maven `<optional>true</optional>` prevents the dep from being transitively propagated to downstream consumers — but it does **not** remove the dep from the current module's own test classpath. The dep is still fully present during `mvn test`.

With the reactive Panache extension on the classpath, Quarkus's build-time bootstrap activates the Hibernate Reactive extension. That extension requires a Vert.x reactive datasource — not a JDBC pool. H2 has no Vert.x reactive driver, so no pool can be created and Quarkus fails to start.

`quarkus.arc.exclude-types` does NOT fix this — it only affects CDI bean scan, not Quarkus extension activation.

## Fix

Remove `quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache` from the module's `pom.xml` entirely. Provide only the SPI interface (which only needs `io.smallrye.mutiny.Uni`, already on the Quarkus classpath). Consumers who want reactive add the dep to their own module.

```xml
<!-- DON'T add this to a module with @QuarkusTest using H2 -->
<!-- <dependency>
  <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-hibernate-reactive-panache</artifactId>
  <optional>true</optional>
</dependency> -->
```

If a pre-built reactive implementation is needed, put it in a **separate Maven module** (e.g. `quarkus-mylib-reactive`) so the reactive dep never lands on the blocking test classpath.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The Maven `optional` flag is commonly understood to mean "this dep won't bother consumers" — developers assume it also means "won't cause problems in my own tests." The Quarkus extension activation is a build-time concern triggered by classpath presence, not by CDI bean wiring or config. The error message (`No pool has been defined for persistence unit <default>`) doesn't mention reactive or optional dependencies at all.

**See also:** GE-20260420-33b95f (fix: %test.quarkus.datasource.reactive=false), GE-20260420-45d53b (general mechanism), GE-20260420-dcec35 (extension-level variant)

**See also:** GE-20260420-cbd0fa (H2 cannot be used as reactive datasource, vertx-jdbc-client not enough)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus hibernate reactive panache test failure
quarkus optional dep test error
hibernate reactive datasource h2

entries.title: @QuarkusIntegrationTest must live in a separate module from the extension runtime
entries.body:
@QuarkusIntegrationTest must live in a separate module from the extension runtime

## Symptom

Adding `quarkus-maven-plugin` with the `build` goal to a Quarkus extension runtime module to enable `@QuarkusIntegrationTest` fails at the package phase:

```
ConfigurationException: Datasource '<default>' is not configured.
To solve this, configure datasource '<default>'.
```

The build succeeds in the `test` phase (normal `@QuarkusTest` works fine) but fails in `package` when the plugin tries to produce a deployable artifact.

## Context

Quarkus extensions intentionally omit datasource configuration — consuming applications provide their own. The `quarkus-maven-plugin build` goal performs Quarkus augmentation, which validates that all required configuration is present. Since the extension's `application.properties` has no datasource, augmentation fails.

## What Was Tried

Adding `quarkus-maven-plugin` with build/generate-code/generate-code-tests goals directly to the extension runtime module's `pom.xml`.

## Root Cause

Quarkus augmentation (the build phase) requires a fully configured application. An extension module is not an application — it's a library. The augmentation validation for Hibernate ORM requires a datasource to be present.

## Fix

Create a separate `integration-tests` Maven module that:
1. Depends on the extension runtime (`quarkus-tarkus` etc.)
2. Provides its own `src/main/resources/application.properties` with datasource config (H2 for tests)
3. Contains the `quarkus-maven-plugin` build goal and `maven-failsafe-plugin`
4. Contains `*IT.java` tests annotated `@QuarkusIntegrationTest`

```xml
<!-- integration-tests/pom.xml -->
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.quarkiverse.myext</groupId>
    <artifactId>quarkus-myext</artifactId>
    <version>${project.version}</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
    <artifactId>quarkus-jdbc-h2</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

```properties
# integration-tests/src/main/resources/application.properties
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=true
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The `@QuarkusTest` tests in the extension runtime module work perfectly — they start a full Quarkus app including the extension in the same JVM without requiring a packaged artifact. So it seems like `@QuarkusIntegrationTest` should "just work" the same way by adding the plugin. The distinction between "test-phase app boot" and "package-phase augmentation" is not surfaced clearly in the error message.

### Why this fix

The separation keeps the extension module pure (no app-specific config) while enabling native image testing in the integration-tests module where full app configuration is appropriate.

**See also:** GE-0065 — quarkus:dev silently skips if build goal missing; GE-20260417-a405a4 — quarkus-maven-plugin build goal in extension runtime pom breaks mvn install

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus integration test package failure
quarkus augmentation datasource configuration
@QuarkusIntegrationTest build failure error

entries.title: Named Hibernate ORM persistence unit requires both @PersistenceUnit qualifier AND packages config for entity discovery
entries.body:
Named Hibernate ORM persistence unit requires both @PersistenceUnit qualifier AND packages config for entity discovery

### Symptom

JPA queries return empty results or `em.find()` returns null for entities that exist in the database. No error, no warning — Hibernate simply doesn't see the entity class.

### Context

Adding a JPA entity to an application that shares a foundation module's named persistence unit (e.g. Qhorus's `qhorus` PU). The entity is in a different package than the foundation module's entities.

### Root cause

Two independent configuration points must both be set:

1. `@PersistenceUnit("qhorus")` on the EntityManager injection — without it, the default PU is used, which has no datasource configured
2. `quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages` must include the new entity's package — Hibernate only scans packages listed in this config for the named PU

Missing either one causes silent failure. The compound nature is what makes this non-obvious — setting only the annotation or only the packages config both appear correct in isolation but produce empty results.

### Fix

Both changes are required:

```java
@Inject
@PersistenceUnit("qhorus")
EntityManager em;
```

```properties
# application.properties — extend the existing packages list
quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages=io.casehub.qhorus.runtime,io.casehub.ledger.runtime,io.casehub.drafthouse
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Each configuration point has its own diagnostic blind spot:
- Missing `@PersistenceUnit`: the default PU has no datasource, so Quarkus may fail at startup with an opaque CDI error OR silently use a different (empty) schema
- Missing packages config: the entity class exists on the classpath and the PU is correct, but Hibernate's entity scan doesn't find it — no warning, just empty results
- Both missing: you get the compound failure of both above

Related entries cover individual aspects — GE-20260422-334eb8 covers the annotation import (`io.quarkus.hibernate.orm.PersistenceUnit` not `jakarta.persistence.PersistenceUnit`), GE-20260424-6b88a0 covers datasource routing. This entry covers the compound requirement.

**See also:** [GE-20260612-8e925b](GE-20260612-8e925b.md) — Quarkus quarkus.hibernate-orm.<pu-name>.sql-load-script for named PU | [GE-20260512-ea776c](GE-20260512-ea776c.md) — Quarkus named persistence units silently skip schema generation | [GE-20260521-2b82e7](GE-20260521-2b82e7.md) — Panache.withTransaction() uses the default persistence unit | [GE-20260530-da427e](GE-20260530-da427e.md) — Quarkus multi-PU sub-package matching assigns entities to wrong PU | [GE-20260423-fce720](GE-20260423-fce720.md) — quarkus-work-core FilterRule JPA entity requires datasource | [GE-20260429-21e6cf](GE-20260429-21e6cf.md) — JPA entity in dependency forces datasource config on all downstream consumers

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
