JpaWorkItemStore.scan() with assigneeId also matches candidateUsers LIKE '%actorId%'
entries.body:
JpaWorkItemStore.scan() with assigneeId also matches candidateUsers LIKE '%actorId%'

## Symptom

Calling `WorkItemStore.scan()` with an `assigneeId` filter to count active WorkItems for a
specific actor returns more items than expected — items that are in the open pool (PENDING,
`assigneeId = null`) but list the actor in `candidateUsers` are incorrectly included.

This caused least-loaded routing (`LeastLoadedStrategy`) to bias against actors who appeared
in any pool's `candidateUsers` field, making them appear busier than they were.

## Context

When building `countActive(actorId)` using `WorkItemStore.scan(query)` with `.assigneeId(actorId)`,
the JPA store generates a WHERE clause with OR semantics:

```sql
WHERE assigneeId = :assigneeId
   OR candidateUsers LIKE :assigneeIdLike
```

The `LIKE` branch exists to support inbox queries ("show me everything I can claim"),
but it also fires when you intend exact-match-only assignment semantics.

## What was tried

Using `workItemStore.scan(WorkItemQuery.builder().assigneeId(actorId).statusIn(ACTIVE_STATUSES).build())`
appeared correct from the query API but produced inflated counts.

## Root cause

`WorkItemStore.scan()` is designed for inbox queries, which are broader: an item appears
in your inbox if you're the assignee OR if you're eligible to claim it via candidateGroups/candidateUsers.
There is no `exactAssigneeId` method that generates only `assigneeId = :x` without the LIKE branch.

## Fix

Post-filter the scan result in memory:

```java
private int countActive(final String actorId) {
    return workItemStore.scan(WorkItemQuery.builder()
            .assigneeId(actorId)
            .statusIn(List.of(WorkItemStatus.ASSIGNED,
                              WorkItemStatus.IN_PROGRESS,
                              WorkItemStatus.SUSPENDED))
            .build())
            .stream()
            .filter(wi -> actorId.equals(wi.assigneeId))  // exact match only
            .count();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The method is named `assigneeId(actorId)` which strongly implies exact-match semantics.
The OR/LIKE behaviour is an implementation detail of the inbox-query model not surfaced
in the API. The bug only appears in routing scenarios where workload counts matter;
in normal inbox use the broader semantics are correct.

### Why this fix

The post-filter is cheap (in-memory, no extra DB round-trip) and makes intent explicit.
A `WorkItemQuery.Builder.exactAssigneeId()` method would be cleaner long-term but
requires changing the query API; the post-filter is the minimal correct fix.

### Alternatives considered

- Adding `exactAssigneeId(String)` to `WorkItemQuery.Builder` to emit only `assigneeId = :x` — cleaner but requires API change
- Querying Panache directly (`WorkItem.count("assigneeId = ?1 AND status IN ?2", ...)`) — bypasses the abstraction layer

**See also:** GE-20260421-9498ff — WorkItemService.delegate() must run strategy BEFORE clearing assigneeId or Hibernate auto-flush corrupts workload counts

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
assigneeId LIKE '%actorId%'
WorkItemQuery.builder().assigneeId()
countActive(actorId)

entries.title: Full pre-push PR QA — scope scan + deletion review catches unrelated inclusions and accidental removals
entries.body:
Full pre-push PR QA — scope scan + deletion review catches unrelated inclusions and accidental removals

### What

Two distinct failure modes corrupt PRs after rebase or squash. Run both checks before every push.

**Step 1 — Scope scan (accidental inclusions)**

```bash
git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only
```

Review every file. Any file outside the expected directories is an unintended inclusion — catch it here, not in code review. Automate with a global pre-push hook (see Enforcement section below).

**Step 2 — Deletion review (accidental removals and modifications)**

```bash
git diff origin/main..HEAD | grep "^-" | grep -v "^---"
```

Scan every removed line. Look for:
- Methods, classes, or constants removed without reason
- Visibility changes (`public` → `private`) without justification
- Modifications to shared files outside the PR's core module — each needs explicit justification

This is judgement, not automation. It must be a conscious act.

### Why this is non-obvious

Developers check `git diff` for content correctness but not for *what was silently lost*. Two failure modes exist and are independent:

- **Inclusions**: rebase replays commits in sequence; a commit that touched a CI workflow file lands silently in the squashed result
- **Deletions**: an edit to a shared file drops a method, constant, or registration that compiled fine but silently broke behaviour at runtime — no warning, no error, reviewers catch it expensively

Both happened in the same PR: a CI workflow regression slipped in, and `toString()`, `JsonAnyOfSchemaObjectSubstitution`, and `SkipToolBoxProcessingBuildItem` were silently removed.

### Root cause

Rebase and squash both replay and compress history. The developer's mental model is "my changes" but the actual diff is "everything between origin/main and HEAD" — which includes more than intended when branches share history.

### Enforcement — global pre-push hook

Discipline fails under pressure. Automate it instead with a global `pre-push` hook that blocks the push when always-suspicious files (`.github/`, `.gitignore`, `LICENSE`, `CODEOWNERS`, `.editorconfig`, `.mvn/`) appear in the diff:

```sh
# ~/.config/git/hooks/pre-push  (global via git config --global core.hooksPath)
#!/bin/sh
SUSPICIOUS=$(git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only 2>/dev/null | grep -E \
  "^\.github/|^\.gitignore$|^\.gitattributes$|^LICENSE|^CODEOWNERS$|^\.editorconfig$|^\.mvn/")

if [ -n "$SUSPICIOUS" ]; then
  echo "⚠ Out-of-scope files detected:"
  echo "$SUSPICIOUS"
  exit 1
fi
```

Register globally:
```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/git/hooks
chmod +x ~/.config/git/hooks/pre-push
git config --global core.hooksPath ~/.config/git/hooks
```

Use `--no-verify` only when the out-of-scope file is genuinely intentional (e.g. a PR that actually updates CI).

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only
git diff origin/main..HEAD | grep "^-"
JsonAnyOfSchemaObjectSubstitution

entries.title: Hibernate 6 JPQL arithmetic on MIN/MAX aggregates in HAVING is silently accepted by H2 but rejected by PostgreSQL
entries.body:
Hibernate 6 JPQL arithmetic on MIN/MAX aggregates in HAVING is silently accepted by H2 but rejected by PostgreSQL

## Hibernate 6 JPQL arithmetic on MIN/MAX aggregates in HAVING is silently accepted by H2 but rejected by PostgreSQL

### Symptom

A JPQL query using arithmetic on `MIN()` / `MAX()` aggregate results in a `HAVING` clause
throws at runtime on PostgreSQL:

```
org.hibernate.query.SemanticException: Operand of - is of type 'java.lang.Object'
which is not a numeric type (it is not an instance of 'java.lang.Number',
'java.time.Temporal', or 'java.time.TemporalAmount')
```

The same query works silently on H2 — all H2-backed `@QuarkusTest` pass green, giving
false confidence. The failure only appears when the query executes against PostgreSQL.

### Context

Typical pattern in a health-check or audit job:

```jpql
SELECT e.subjectId, e.tenancyId, COUNT(e), MIN(e.sequenceNumber), MAX(e.sequenceNumber)
FROM LedgerEntry e
GROUP BY e.subjectId, e.tenancyId
HAVING COUNT(e) != MAX(e.sequenceNumber) - MIN(e.sequenceNumber) + 1
```

`sequenceNumber` is declared as `int` (Java primitive). Hibernate 6's semantic checker
classifies `MIN(int field)` and `MAX(int field)` as `Object` rather than a numeric type
when they appear as arithmetic operands in a `HAVING` clause — but only when the
PostgreSQL dialect is active.

The query executes at job runtime (e.g. on a 1h scheduler interval), not at startup,
so the failure surfaces hours into production operation.

### Root cause

Hibernate 6 rewrote JPQL type resolution. Aggregate functions in `HAVING` arithmetic
are typed differently depending on the active dialect's type resolution path. The H2
dialect resolves `MIN`/`MAX` return types as numeric for arithmetic, while the
PostgreSQL dialect's path leaves them as `Object` — triggering the semantic checker.

This is a regression from Hibernate 5 where both dialects accepted the arithmetic.

### Fix

**Remove the arithmetic from HAVING. Filter in Java.**

Drop the `HAVING` clause entirely and filter in the result loop:

```jpql
-- Query (no HAVING):
SELECT e.subjectId, e.tenancyId, COUNT(e), MIN(e.sequenceNumber), MAX(e.sequenceNumber)
FROM LedgerEntry e
GROUP BY e.subjectId, e.tenancyId
```

```java
// Filter in Java — arithmetic is safe here:
for (SubjectSequenceStats s : repo.findSequenceStats()) {
    final long expected = (long) s.max() - s.min() + 1;
    if (s.count() == expected) continue;
    // anomaly detected
}
```

**Also: convert to `@NamedQuery` for startup validation.**

The query that failed did so at runtime. Had it been a `@NamedQuery` on the entity class,
Hibernate would have thrown the `SemanticException` at startup — not after the first
scheduler firing. Converting inline `em.createQuery()` calls to `@NamedQuery` turns a
1-hour-delayed runtime failure into an immediate boot failure:

```java
@NamedQuery(
    name = "LedgerEntry.findSequenceStats",
    query = """
        SELECT NEW com.example.SubjectSequenceStats(
            e.subjectId, e.tenancyId, COUNT(e), MIN(e.sequenceNumber), MAX(e.sequenceNumber)
        )
        FROM LedgerEntry e
        GROUP BY e.subjectId, e.tenancyId
        """)
@Entity
public abstract class LedgerEntry { ... }
```

The `NEW` constructor expression passes aggregate values as constructor arguments — no
arithmetic in the query — so the type checker does not fire.

### Why this is non-obvious

JPQL semantic analysis is supposed to be dialect-independent — it validates the JPQL
AST before any SQL is generated. The natural assumption is that if H2 tests pass, the
query is semantically valid. This assumption breaks here: H2's dialect contributes to
the type resolution path, and H2 resolves aggregate arithmetic types differently than
PostgreSQL does.

The failure mode is also severe: with a 1h scheduler interval and H2 tests giving a
false green, the bug can reach production undetected and remain invisible until the
first health-check execution.

### Why this fix

Removing HAVING arithmetic is preferable to using JPQL `CAST()` because:
1. It eliminates the type-resolution dependency entirely — no arithmetic means no type checking issue
2. The arithmetic is usually already computed in Java for display/logging purposes
3. It is universally portable across all Hibernate dialects

`CAST(MAX(e.sequenceNumber) AS Long)` would also work for the PostgreSQL dialect, but
it introduces a dialect-specific JPQL extension that may not be supported in all versions
of H2 or future dialects.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
MIN MAX aggregate HAVING PostgreSQL error
sequenceNumber int Hibernate 6 semanticException
JPQL arithmetic type resolution

entries.title: quarkus.arc.exclude-types on a non-indexed JAR triggers full JAR scan — activating beans instead of suppressing them
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.exclude-types on a non-indexed JAR triggers full JAR scan — activating beans instead of suppressing them

## Symptom

Adding `quarkus.arc.exclude-types=com.example.SomeBean` causes *new* CDI failures to appear — unsatisfied dependencies, scheduler errors, or ambiguity errors for beans that were never a problem before.

## Context

You have a production dependency (e.g. `casehub-engine`) whose JAR has no Jandex index and no `beans.xml`. Adding an entry to `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` that names a class from that JAR causes Quarkus to scan the entire JAR to locate the target class.

## Root cause

Quarkus ARC must physically find the class to exclude it. For JARs without a Jandex index, ARC falls back to scanning the whole JAR. During that scan it discovers every `@ApplicationScoped`, `@Singleton`, etc. class — registering all of them as CDI beans. The net effect is the opposite of what the exclusion intended: the JAR gains full CDI discovery while one bean is removed.

## Fix

**Option 1 — Use a production-profile prefix** so the exclusion only applies during `quarkus:build`, not during `@QuarkusTest`:

```properties
%prod.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=com.example.SomeBean
```

**Option 2 — Add `quarkus.index-dependency`** explicitly for the JAR so ARC uses the Jandex index instead of scanning:

```properties
quarkus.index-dependency.mylib.group-id=com.example
quarkus.index-dependency.mylib.artifact-id=mylib
```

Then the exclude-types works as documented.

**Option 3 — Fix the upstream library** to ship a Jandex index (`io.smallrye:jandex-maven-plugin`) so ARC never needs to scan.

## Why this is non-obvious

Exclusion is supposed to reduce beans — not add them. The documentation for `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` says nothing about triggering a full JAR scan. The symptom (new unsatisfied dependencies or scheduler failures) points away from the exclusion entry as the cause.

### Why this fix

Using `%prod.` is the lightest fix — it scopes the exclusion to the context where the ambiguity actually exists, and keeps the test ARC context clean.

**See also:** [GE-20260523-afab1d](GE-20260523-afab1d.md) — Jandex index required for CDI bean discovery | [GE-20260516-2805b7](GE-20260516-2805b7.md) — abstract superclasses indexed by Jandex treated as CDI candidates | [GE-20260523-20046c](GE-20260523-20046c.md) — %prod. prefix to limit indexing to production

**See also:** [GE-20260524-c1e573](GE-20260524-c1e573.md) — exclude-types silently fails for beans registered by a Quarkus extension

**See also:** [GE-20260516-8375d5](GE-20260516-8375d5.md) — jar with application.properties at root causes Quarkus to scan all its classes

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-9d91f9](GE-20260604-9d91f9.md) — propagate inherited interceptor bindings to synthetic CDI beans via AnnotationsTransformerBuildItem

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: CorpusIngestionService checkpointCursors overwrites failed-scan cursor — corpus appears fully indexed when nothing was ingested
entries.body:
CorpusIngestionService checkpointCursors overwrites failed-scan cursor — corpus appears fully indexed when nothing was ingested

### Symptom

Engine starts, reports "No cursor — bootstrapping with fullScan", the scan fails (e.g. Qdrant collection doesn't exist yet, or embedding API returns 400). Log says "Cursor NOT advanced due to processing failures." On restart, the engine does NOT retry the fullScan — instead it runs `changesSince(cursor)` which finds no changes, and no documents are indexed. The corpus appears fully indexed (cursor file exists, 500KB) but Qdrant has 0 points.

### Context

`CorpusIngestionService` has two cursor-saving paths:

1. **`doProcessBinding`** — saves cursor only if `!anyFailure` (correct)
2. **`checkpointCursors`** — 5-minute scheduled timer that saves the filesystem watcher's current state as the cursor (unconditional)

When the initial scan fails, `doProcessBinding` correctly does NOT advance the cursor. But the filesystem watcher was started during `onStart()` and recorded the full file state. After 5 minutes, `checkpointCursors` fires and saves the watcher's state — which includes all files — as the cursor. On next restart, `changesSince(saved_cursor)` sees no changes.

### Root cause

`checkpointCursors` does not check whether the initial scan succeeded. It unconditionally saves the watcher's in-memory file state, which reflects what's on disk — not what was successfully ingested. The scheduled poll (`poll()`) also cannot retry because it explicitly skips `WatchableChangeSource` bindings.

### Fix

None known — this is a design issue in `casehub-rag`. Workaround: delete the cursor file and restart.

```bash
# Find and delete the stale cursor
rm /var/folders/.../casehub-ingestion-cursors/garden.cursor
# Also delete the Qdrant collection if it exists but is empty
curl -X DELETE 'http://localhost:6333/collections/hortora_garden'
# Restart the engine — fullScan will run from scratch
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The cursor file's existence and size (500KB) suggests successful indexing. The engine logs "No cursor — bootstrapping with fullScan" on first start, but on second start it silently runs `changesSince` and finds nothing. There is no log message saying "cursor loaded, N entries already indexed" — the developer has to check Qdrant directly to discover the corpus is empty despite the cursor being present.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
CorpusIngestionService checkpointCursors overwrites failed-scan cursor
`changesSince(cursor)` fails when no changes are present
Qdrant collection empty after ingestion failure

entries.body:
Panache entities cannot be scanned by two Quarkus persistence units simultaneously

### Symptom

Build-time `IllegalStateException: Panache entities do not support being attached to several persistence units: io.example.MyEntity is attached to: <default>,qhorus`

### Context

Quarkus project with two named persistence units configured via `quarkus.hibernate-orm.packages` and `quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages`. Occurs when the same Java package appears in both lists — even if you intended only a subset of entities in that package to be managed by the second PU.

### What was tried

Added a `LedgerEntry` subclass to `io.casehub.clinical.entity` (alongside regular Panache entities), then listed `io.casehub.clinical.entity` in both `hibernate-orm.packages` and `hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages` so both entity types would be visible to their respective PUs.

### Root cause

Quarkus scans the entire package for all entity classes when a package is listed in a PU's `packages` config. Panache entities found in both scans are flagged as "belonging to two PUs" at build time — Panache's proxy mechanism cannot support this.

### Fix

Put JPA entities managed by the second PU in a **separate package** not listed under the default PU:

```properties
# Default PU — Panache entities only
quarkus.hibernate-orm.packages=io.casehub.clinical.entity

# Second PU — separate package for non-Panache JPA entities
quarkus.hibernate-orm.qhorus.packages=io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model,io.casehub.clinical.ledger
```

Create the new package (`io.casehub.clinical.ledger` or similar) and place the non-Panache JPA entities there.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural instinct is to put a new entity subclass alongside related entities. The error appears at build time (not runtime), but the message doesn't explain that the fix requires a separate package — it just says the entity is "attached to" two PUs.

**See also:** [GE-20260423-4aa1e0](GE-20260423-4aa1e0.md) — JPA InheritanceType.JOINED forces all hierarchy entities into one persistence unit

**See also:** [GE-20260422-334eb8](GE-20260422-334eb8.md) — Quarkus named persistence unit EntityManager injection uses io.quarkus.hibernate.orm.PersistenceUnit qualifier

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: Adapter router must call all adapters even with empty filtered graph — orphan detection requires it for deprovision
entries.body:
Adapter router must call all adapters even with empty filtered graph — orphan detection requires it for deprovision

### Symptom

Nodes that exist in actual state but are removed from the desired graph are never deprovisioned. The reconciliation loop sees an empty plan and takes no action. No error is logged — the orphaned nodes silently persist.

### Context

`DefaultActualStateAdapterRouter` dispatches `readActual()` to domain-specific `ActualStateAdapter` implementations based on `NodeType`. When the desired graph is updated to remove all nodes of a particular type (or set to empty), the router has no nodes to route and skips calling the adapter entirely.

### What was tried (didn't work)

Initial implementation partitioned desired graph nodes by adapter type and only called adapters that had matching nodes in the partition. This worked for provision (adapters always have nodes to read) but silently broke deprovision.

### Root cause

Adapters serve a dual purpose: they report the status of desired nodes AND detect orphaned nodes (present in actual state but absent from desired graph). The `PipelineActualStateAdapter` and `DungeonActualStateAdapter` both scan their world state for nodes not in the desired graph and report them as `PRESENT`. When the adapter is never called, this orphan scan never runs. The planner sees `desired={empty}, actual={empty}` instead of `desired={empty}, actual={n1: PRESENT}` — no diff, no removal plan.

### Fix

Always call every registered adapter, regardless of whether the filtered subgraph has matching nodes:

```java
Set<ActualStateAdapter> allAdapters = new LinkedHashSet<>(routing.values());

for (ActualStateAdapter adapter : allAdapters) {
    DesiredStateGraph filtered = desired.filterByTypes(adapter.handledTypes());
    ActualState partial = adapter.readActual(filtered, tenancyId);
    merged.putAll(partial.statuses());
}
```

The adapter receives an empty (or reduced) graph and still scans its backing store for orphans. The router merges all partial results — orphaned nodes appear in the merged `ActualState` and the planner generates removal steps.

### Why this is non-obvious

The partitioning optimisation (skip adapters with no matching nodes) is the natural implementation — it avoids unnecessary adapter calls and matches how `NodeProvisionerRouter` works (provisioners genuinely have nothing to do when no nodes match). The asymmetry is that provisioners are *write* operations (nothing to write = skip) while adapters are *read* operations that may discover state beyond the input set. The "always call" requirement only becomes visible when a deprovision test fails with a timeout — the symptom (infinite provision cycle or silent orphan) doesn't point to the router.

### Alternatives considered

- Adding a separate `scanForOrphans()` method to the adapter SPI — rejected because it splits a single concern (reading actual state) across two methods and requires callers to remember to call both.
- Making orphan detection a ReconciliationLoop responsibility — rejected because only the domain adapter knows how to discover orphans in its backing store.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`DefaultActualStateAdapterRouter` orphan detection
`DesiredStateGraph filterByTypes`
`PipelineActualStateAdapter PRESENT`

entries.title: Flyway scans classpath:db/migration recursively — subdirectory db/migration/<module>/ is visible to any datasource scanning the parent path
entries.body:
Flyway scans classpath:db/migration recursively — subdirectory db/migration/<module>/ is visible to any datasource scanning the parent path

### Symptom
`FlywayException: Found more than one migration with version 1` at startup when two datasources are both configured with Flyway — one scanning `classpath:db/migration` (default datasource) and another scanning `classpath:db/migration/<module>/` (named datasource). Flyway's recursive scan on the parent path finds ALL files in `db/migration/` including those in subdirectories, producing duplicate V-number errors.

### Context
A multi-datasource Quarkus app where:
1. The default datasource uses Flyway and scans `classpath:db/migration` (the default location)
2. A named datasource (e.g. `qhorus`) uses Flyway and scans `classpath:db/migration/qhorus/`
3. Both sets of migration files share some V-numbers (e.g. both have V1)

The intent was to isolate the named datasource's migrations in a subdirectory. This works for *which datasource applies which migration*, but not for *which datasource discovers which files*.

### Root cause
Flyway scans classpath locations recursively by default. Configuring `quarkus.flyway.<datasource>.locations=classpath:db/migration/qhorus` scopes which migrations that datasource *runs*, but it does not prevent the default datasource (configured for `classpath:db/migration`) from *discovering* files in `db/migration/qhorus/` during its own recursive scan. Both datasources see the qhorus migrations; the default datasource then finds V1 in both `db/migration/` (its own) and `db/migration/qhorus/` (qhorus's), and Flyway rejects the duplicate.

### Fix
Move the module's migrations completely outside the `db/migration/` namespace:

```
db/qhorus/migration/V1__initial_schema.sql   ← was db/migration/qhorus/V1__initial_schema.sql
```

Configure accordingly:
```properties
quarkus.flyway.qhorus.locations=classpath:db/qhorus/migration
```

Any path that does not start with `db/migration/` avoids the recursive scan overlap.

### Why this is non-obvious
The "scoped subdirectory" pattern (`db/migration/<module>/`) appears to solve the isolation problem and is even described in Flyway documentation and some Quarkus guides as the recommended approach for named datasources. The failure only manifests when *another* Flyway datasource is configured with the parent path — which is the default Quarkus/Flyway setup. The error message ("Found more than one migration with version 1") gives no indication that two datasource scanners are involved; it looks like a duplicate file problem within a single scan.

**See also:** [GE-20260427-59ea5d](../quarkus/GE-20260427-59ea5d.md) — Flyway version collision when optional Quarkus module shares classpath

**See also:** [GE-20260531-e5a1aa](../casehub-engine/GE-20260531-e5a1aa.md) — casehub-engine YAML Binding schema reference

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Flyway duplicate migration version error
classpath recursive scan datasource
db/migration qhorus migration subdirectory

entries.title: MemoryQuery default 20-item CHRONOLOGICAL limit silently truncates time-window post-filters
entries.body:
MemoryQuery default 20-item CHRONOLOGICAL limit silently truncates time-window post-filters

## Symptom

A time-windowed aggregate (`recentTimelineBreachCount()`, last-N-days counts) returns 0
or unexpectedly low values even though recent entries exist in the store. The bug is
intermittent — it appears only once an entity has accumulated more than 20 memory entries.

## Context

`MemoryQuery.forEntity(entityId, domain, tenantId)` creates a query with:
- `limit: 20` (default)
- `order: CHRONOLOGICAL` (oldest first)

When you apply the time-window filter in Java after the query returns, you are filtering
the 20 **oldest** entries — not the most recent ones. Recent entries at positions 21+
are invisible to the filter.

```java
// ❌ BUG: filters 20 oldest, misses recent entries beyond position 20
List<Memory> events = store.query(MemoryQuery.forEntity(entityId, domain, tenantId));
long breaches = events.stream()
    .filter(e -> e.createdAt().isAfter(Instant.now().minus(180, DAYS)))
    .filter(e -> "TIMELINE_BREACH".equals(e.attributes().get("outcome")))
    .count();
// Returns 0 even if there are 3 breaches in the last 6 months — they're at positions 21-23
```

## Root cause

The default query applies the 20-item limit **before** returning results to the caller.
`CHRONOLOGICAL` order means oldest-first, so the 20 results are the 20 oldest entries.
Any recent entry beyond the 20th position is simply not returned.

## Fix

Push the time-window filter into the store query using `.withSince(Instant)`. Apply
`.withLimit(N)` appropriate for the window size:

```java
// ✅ FIX: time window applied in the store, not in Java
MemoryQuery query = MemoryQuery.forEntity("site:" + siteId, ClinicalMemoryDomains.SITE, tenantId)
    .withSince(Instant.now().minus(180, ChronoUnit.DAYS))
    .withLimit(50);
List<Memory> events = store.query(query);
long breaches = events.stream()
    .filter(e -> "TIMELINE_BREACH".equals(e.attributes().get("outcome")))
    .count();
```

`withSince()` instructs the store to return only entries created after the threshold.
The limit of 50 is then applied to the already-filtered result set, not to all historical entries.

## Why this is non-obvious

The natural approach is: query → get entries → filter in Java. This works perfectly until
the entity accumulates more than `limit` total entries, at which point the results silently
become wrong. No error, no warning — just a lower count than the real number. The bug is
intermittent in development (few entries per entity in tests) and emerges only in production
once data accumulates.

Additionally, `MemoryOrder.CHRONOLOGICAL` sounds like it would return "all entries in order" —
the word "chronological" doesn't signal that it means "starting from the oldest." The combination
of CHRONOLOGICAL + limit = 20 is the trap: you always get the 20 oldest, which is rarely what
you want for a recency-based query.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
MemoryQuery limit 20 chronological time window filter
MemoryQuery entityId recentTimelineBreachCount
MemoryQuery CHRONOLOGICAL time-window post-filter

GitHub Packages REST API silently truncates org package listing — no pagination indicator
entries.body:
GitHub Packages REST API silently truncates org package listing — no pagination indicator

### Symptom
`gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven'` returns a subset of packages.
Packages known to exist and be published do not appear in the results. No error,
no warning, no indication that results are truncated.

### Context
Auditing whether all Maven modules in a multi-repo build are published to GitHub
Packages. The org has 200+ packages. Default page size is 30.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Single API call to list all packages — returned only ~30, missing entire repos
- Assumed packages were not published and began investigating CI workflows

### Root cause
The GitHub REST API `/orgs/{org}/packages` endpoint paginates at 30 items by
default. Unlike most GitHub API endpoints, the `gh` CLI does not auto-paginate
this one. There is no `total_count` field or obvious truncation marker in the
response — the caller gets a valid JSON array that simply stops early.

### Fix
Use `per_page=100` and iterate pages until an empty page is returned:
```bash
# Page through all packages
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven&per_page=100&page=1' --jq '.[].name'
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven&per_page=100&page=2' --jq '.[].name'
# ... until empty result
```

Or check specific packages by name (O(1), no pagination):
```bash
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages/maven/{groupId}.{artifactId}/versions' \
  --jq '.[0].name' 2>/dev/null || echo "NOT FOUND"
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Most GitHub API endpoints either return all results or include clear pagination
indicators (Link headers, total_count). This endpoint silently returns a partial
list. The natural debugging path is to investigate CI/CD publishing, not API
pagination — especially when the first page contains packages from other repos
in the org, making the response look complete.

### Why this fix
Checking specific packages by name avoids pagination entirely and is O(1) per
package. Use the paginated listing only when you need the full inventory.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven'` pagination
`org packages api truncation`
`github packages per_page 100`

entries.title: Quarkus ARC @Alternative @Priority(1) subclass not injected when injection point uses concrete superclass type
entries.body:
Quarkus ARC @Alternative @Priority(1) subclass not injected when injection point uses concrete superclass type

### Symptom
Consumer `@QuarkusTest` integration tests fail with `CaseInstance not found or wrong tenant` — 34 of 228 tests. The reactive repository and blocking repository maintain separate in-memory stores despite both being `@ApplicationScoped` singletons.

### Context
Dual-stack persistence pattern: blocking repo is canonical, reactive repo delegates to it via `@Inject`. Both have `@Alternative` test wrappers with `@Priority(1)` in an `engine-testing` module.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Checked all event bus handlers for tenant context propagation — all correct
- Checked `CurrentPrincipal` thread safety — `@ApplicationScoped`, consistent
- Traced `save()` → `update()` flow — tenancyId parameters matched
- Assumed CDI would resolve `@Inject InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository delegate` to `TestCaseInstanceRepository extends InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` via assignability

### Root cause
`InMemoryReactiveCaseInstanceRepository` declared its delegate as:
```java
@Inject InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository delegate;  // concrete class
```
`TestCaseInstanceRepository extends InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` with `@Alternative @Priority(1)` was NOT substituted as the delegate. ARC resolved the injection point to a separate `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` instance — creating two stores with independent state.

### Fix
Inject by SPI interface instead of concrete class:
```java
@Inject CaseInstanceRepository delegate;  // SPI interface
```
ARC correctly resolves `@Alternative @Priority(1)` candidates when the injection point is the interface type. Applied to all 5 reactive in-memory repos.

### Why this is non-obvious
CDI spec says `@Alternative` beans are eligible for any injection point they satisfy by type. The expectation is that `TestCaseInstanceRepository extends InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` satisfies `@Inject InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository`. The failure is silent — no CDI ambiguity error, no deployment failure. Two separate bean instances are created, and the symptom (tenant mismatch) gives no hint about the CDI root cause.

### Alternatives considered
- Making `TestCaseInstanceRepository` a `@Specializes` bean — rejected: Quarkus ARC has limited `@Specializes` support
- Using `@Produces` method to bridge — rejected: adds unnecessary complexity when interface injection works

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`Quarkus ARC injection delegate`
`ARC @Alternative substitution`
`CaseInstanceRepository SPI inject`

InMemoryWorkItemStore.scan() filters by currentPrincipal.tenancyId() — explicit tenancyId on request makes WorkItems invisible
entries.body:
InMemoryWorkItemStore.scan() filters by currentPrincipal.tenancyId() — explicit tenancyId on request makes WorkItems invisible

### Symptom
WorkItem is created successfully (handler logs confirm creation) but `workItemStore.scanAll()` returns an empty list. No error, no warning — the WorkItem silently vanishes from query results.

### Context
Occurs in `@QuarkusTest` suites using `InMemoryWorkItemStore` (the `@Alternative @Priority(1)` test implementation). The test creates a WorkItem via `WorkItemCreator.create(request)` with `tenancyId` set explicitly on the `WorkItemCreateRequest`, then queries with `workItemStore.scanAll()`.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Verified the WorkItem was created (handler log confirmed)
- Checked CDI wiring (WorkItemSpiAdapter correctly resolved)
- Verified InMemoryWorkItemStore was the active alternative

### Root cause
`InMemoryWorkItemStore` has an asymmetry between `put()` and `scan()`:

- `put()` stamps `tenancyId` from `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` **only when the WorkItem's tenancyId is null**
- `scan()` (and therefore `scanAll()`) filters results by `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` **always**

When the `WorkItemCreateRequest` sets `tenancyId` explicitly (e.g. `"test-tenant"`), the value flows through `WorkItemService.create()` to the entity. `put()` sees a non-null tenancyId and does not override it. But `scan()` filters by whatever `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` returns — which may be a different value (e.g. the platform default tenant).

Result: the WorkItem is in the store's `ConcurrentHashMap` but filtered out by every query.

### Fix
Do not set `tenancyId` on the `WorkItemCreateRequest` in test contexts. Let `InMemoryWorkItemStore.put()` stamp it from `currentPrincipal`. This ensures `put()` and `scan()` use the same tenant value.

```java
// BAD — tenancyId may not match currentPrincipal
WorkItemCreateRequest.builder()
    .title("Review")
    .tenancyId(event.tenancyId())  // explicit — bypasses put() stamp
    .build();

// GOOD — let the store stamp tenancyId from currentPrincipal
WorkItemCreateRequest.builder()
    .title("Review")
    // no .tenancyId() — put() stamps from currentPrincipal
    .build();
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The old code path (direct entity mutation + `workItem.persist()`) never hit this because `persist()` goes to JPA/Panache, not `InMemoryWorkItemStore.put()`. The tenancy filtering only matters when both creation and querying go through the in-memory store — which happens when migrating from runtime service calls to SPI calls (`WorkItemCreator`).

### Alternatives considered
- Setting `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` to match the explicit value — possible but requires test infrastructure changes and couples tests to tenant identity
- Removing the tenancy filter from `InMemoryWorkItemStore.scan()` — would break multi-tenant test isolation

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
scanAll() returns empty list
tenancyId filtering InMemoryWorkItemStore
WorkItem visibility currentPrincipal

entries.title: Quarkus CDI does not scan @Alternative beans in third-party test jars without explicit index config
entries.body:
Quarkus CDI does not scan @Alternative beans in third-party test jars without explicit index config

## Symptom

`@Alternative @Priority(1)` beans from a `test`-scoped dependency are not selected by CDI in `@QuarkusTest` runs. The default (non-alternative) beans are used instead. No error is thrown — the wrong beans silently win.

## Context

Occurs when a library ships a `-testing` artifact (e.g. `quarkus-mylib-testing`) containing `@Alternative` in-memory implementations intended for use in consumer test suites. Adding the artifact as a `<scope>test</scope>` dependency is not sufficient.

## Root Cause

Quarkus CDI only scans jars that are explicitly indexed. Third-party jars without a Jandex index (or without explicit `quarkus.index-dependency` config) are not scanned for CDI beans, even if the jar is on the classpath and the beans are annotated correctly.

## Fix

Add an index-dependency entry in `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.index-dependency.mylib-testing.group-id=io.example
quarkus.index-dependency.mylib-testing.artifact-id=quarkus-mylib-testing
```

Adjust `group-id` and `artifact-id` to match the testing jar's Maven coordinates.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The dependency is on the classpath. The beans have the correct `@Alternative @Priority(1)` annotations. No exception is thrown. The library's documentation typically says "add the testing dependency" without mentioning the index requirement. The failure mode — wrong beans used silently — is identical to not having the dependency at all, which misleads diagnosis toward annotation or scope issues.

**See also:** GE-0133 — CDI silently ignores beans in jars without Jandex index (general case) | GE-20260421-03fa72 — optional module jar missing Jandex index | GE-20260417-c59817 — quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives activates @Alternative beans

**See also:** [GE-20260424-59906a](GE-20260424-59906a.md) — same CDI scanning root cause for non-alternative beans in library JARs
**See also:** [GE-20260427-c2b84f](GE-20260427-c2b84f.md) — @Alternative beans in test-helper jar — producer-side Jandex fix | [GE-20260427-62d3ab](GE-20260427-62d3ab.md) — @Alternative @Priority(1) inner bean spy technique

**See also:** GE-20260427-987198 — quarkus.arc.exclude-types suppresses CDI beans from library JARs

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.body:
quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size controls tools/list pagination — undocumented default of 50 silently truncates large tool sets

## `quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size` controls tools/list pagination — undocumented default of 50 silently truncates large tool sets

### Stack
quarkus-mcp-server 1.11.1 (Quarkiverse)

### What it is
`quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size` is a runtime configuration property in quarkus-mcp-server that controls how many tools are returned per `tools/list` MCP response. It is defined in `McpServerRuntimeConfig.java` as a nested interface:

```java
public interface Tools {
    @WithDefault("50")
    int pageSize();
    // ...
}
```

### How to use it

**Disable pagination** (return all tools in one response):
```properties
quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size=0
```

**Set a custom page size:**
```properties
quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size=100
```

Setting to 0 or any negative number disables pagination entirely — all registered tools are returned in a single `tools/list` response regardless of count.

### Where it's not documented
As of quarkus-mcp-server 1.11.1, this property does not appear in the main Quarkiverse documentation for the extension. It is only discoverable by:
- Reading the `McpServerRuntimeConfig.java` source
- Noticing that `tools/list` returns fewer tools than expected (no warning is emitted)
- Decompiling the deployment JAR

### Discovery path
Found by: diagnosing silent tool truncation (49 Qhorus + 8 Claudony = 57 total tools, response showing exactly 50 alphabetically-sorted tools). Traced through `ToolMessageHandler` → `fetchPage()` → `serverConfig.tools().pageSize()` → `@WithDefault("50")` in `McpServerRuntimeConfig`.

### Related config
The same nested config likely controls pagination for other MCP feature types (prompts, resources) via similar `pageSize()` methods. The naming convention is `quarkus.mcp.server.<feature-type>.page-size`.

**See also:** GE-20260501-50a9f4 — quarkus-mcp-server silently caps tools/list at 50 | GE-20260414-fa6489 — @ToolArg undocumented required and defaultValue attributes

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: WEIGHTED_MAJORITY attestation aggregation silently masks contradicting verdicts on the same entry
entries.body:
WEIGHTED_MAJORITY attestation aggregation silently masks contradicting verdicts on the same entry

### Symptom
Capability trust scores remain unchanged (e.g. 11/12 = 0.917) regardless of how many FLAGGED attestations are written against an actor's decisions. Investigation naturally targets the query layer, computation logic, or score persistence — all of which are correct.

### Context
Bayesian Beta trust scoring with a four-pass pipeline (capability → dimension → cap×dim → global). Attestations are aggregated per (entryId, capabilityTag) group before scoring. An incident feedback system writes a FLAGGED attestation against an existing entry that already holds a SOUND attestation from the original review.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Checked query layer (findAllEvents, findAttestationsForEntries) — fetches all verdicts correctly
- Checked TrustScoreComputer.compute() — handles FLAGGED by incrementing beta correctly
- Checked PerActorTrustComputer delegation — passes data through unchanged
- Checked JPA upsert — updates existing score rows correctly
- Checked TrustScoreSource/TrustGateService — reads directly from repository
- All unit tests with FLAGGED on separate entries pass

### Root cause
`TrustScoreCalculator.computeAll()` runs `buildEffectiveAttestations()` which groups attestations by (entryId, capabilityTag) and aggregates via `AttestationAggregator.weightedMajority()`. When an entry has SOUND(confidence=1.0) + FLAGGED(confidence=0.9):
- positive = 1.0, negative = 0.9
- `positive >= negative` → verdict = SOUND
- confidence = |1.0 - 0.9| / 1.9 ≈ 0.053
- Weight in compute() = decayWeight × 0.053 ≈ 0 → neither alpha nor beta increment meaningfully

The FLAGGED attestation is not ignored — it is aggregated into a near-zero-weight SOUND, which is worse: it cancels the original SOUND's contribution too.

### Fix
Use raw attestations (not aggregated) for the capability pass. Each individual attestation contributes to alpha/beta independently — SOUND increments alpha, FLAGGED increments beta, both on the same entry. The dimension pass already used raw attestations; this brings the capability pass into alignment.

```java
// Before (broken): used effectiveAttestations (pre-aggregated)
final Map<String, Map<UUID, List<LedgerAttestation>>> byCapabilityAndEntry =
        effectiveAttestations.stream()
                .filter(a -> !CapabilityTag.GLOBAL.equals(a.capabilityTag))
                ...

// After (fixed): uses rawAttestations
final Map<String, Map<UUID, List<LedgerAttestation>>> byCapabilityAndEntry =
        rawAttestations.stream()
                .filter(a -> a.capabilityTag != null
                        && !CapabilityTag.GLOBAL.equals(a.capabilityTag))
                ...
```

Note the added null guard on `capabilityTag` — raw attestations don't pass through `buildEffectiveAttestations` which normalizes nulls to GLOBAL.

### Why this is non-obvious
The aggregation step sits between data fetch and computation. Both endpoints work correctly in isolation. The symptom (score unchanged) points at the computation or query layer. The aggregation is designed to reduce noise from multiple attestors — it silently converts the sequential-evidence case (SOUND then FLAGGED over time) into the concurrent-vote case (competing opinions) without any log message or signal.

### Why this fix
Raw attestations are the right model for capability scoring because attestations on the same entry arrive at different times as sequential evidence (review outcome, then incident feedback), not as concurrent competing votes. The aggregation model was designed for the N-attestors-same-time case. Trade-off: N attestors on the same entry now contribute N× weight instead of 1× consensus weight — an idea has been logged to explore a hybrid approach.

### Alternatives considered
- Changing the WEIGHTED_MAJORITY tie-break from `>=` to `>` — still produces SOUND for the 1.0 vs 0.9 case; doesn't fix the core issue
- Adding a temporal-awareness flag to the aggregator — overengineered for the current use case; the raw-attestation approach is simpler and matches the dimension pass
- Processing attestations individually with no aggregation anywhere — would affect the global pass which intentionally uses aggregation via GlobalScoreStrategy SPI

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
findAllEvents FLAGGED attestation
TrustScoreComputer compute() SOUND verdict
weightedMajority attestation aggregation

entries.title: quarkus-ledger sequence_number index is not unique — race yields silent duplicate sequences
entries.body:
quarkus-ledger sequence_number index is not unique — race yields silent duplicate sequences

## quarkus-ledger sequence_number index is not unique — race yields silent duplicate sequences

### Symptom

Two concurrent `@ObservesAsync` handlers for the same `caseId` both compute `sequenceNumber = 1` (or the same N). Both rows insert successfully. No exception is thrown, no constraint is violated — the DB silently accepts duplicate sequence numbers.

### Context

`ledger_entry` has an index named `idx_ledger_entry_subject_seq`:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_ledger_entry_subject_seq ON ledger_entry (subject_id, sequence_number);
```

The name implies ordered, per-subject sequencing — but it is a plain performance index, not a `UNIQUE` constraint. There is no uniqueness guard on `(subject_id, sequence_number)` anywhere in the schema.

### What was tried

Using `MAX(sequenceNumber) + 1` inside a `@Transactional` observer method to compute the next sequence number. Under concurrent writes, two threads read the same `MAX` before either commits — both derive the same next value and both succeed.

### Root cause

The V1000 schema migration creates only an index, not a unique constraint. The `@Transactional` boundary does not prevent the read-then-write race at `READ COMMITTED` isolation because both reads happen before either write commits.

### Fix

Replace the `MAX()` aggregate with `ORDER BY sequenceNumber DESC / setMaxResults(1) / findFirst()` — the same pattern as `casehub-engine`'s `findLatestByCaseId()`. This eliminates the aggregate scan and uses the index, but has the same theoretical race window. For true concurrency safety, add a `UNIQUE` constraint or use a DB-level sequence object upstream.

```java
private int nextSequenceNumber(UUID caseId) {
    return em.createQuery(
                    "SELECT e FROM CaseLedgerEntry e WHERE e.subjectId = :caseId ORDER BY e.sequenceNumber DESC",
                    CaseLedgerEntry.class)
            .setParameter("caseId", caseId)
            .setMaxResults(1)
            .getResultStream()
            .findFirst()
            .map(e -> e.sequenceNumber + 1)
            .orElse(1);
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The index name `idx_ledger_entry_subject_seq` strongly implies that sequence ordering is enforced. Developers familiar with SQL will assume a named index on `(subject_id, sequence_number)` implies a uniqueness guarantee — distinguishing a plain index from a `UNIQUE` constraint requires reading the schema DDL directly. The schema migration comment mentions per-subject ordering but does not flag the absence of a uniqueness guarantee. Duplicate rows are also invisible to consumers unless they explicitly check for non-monotonic sequence numbers.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`sequenceNumber index not unique`
`quarkus-ledger race duplicate`
`@ObservesAsync caseId sequenceNumber`

entries.title: Score-replacing decorators silently discard pre-applied multipliers — temporal decay before cross-encoder reranking has zero effect
entries.body:
Score-replacing decorators silently discard pre-applied multipliers — temporal decay before cross-encoder reranking has zero effect

### Symptom

Temporal decay configured on a CBR query has no effect on the final retrieval ranking. Old cases rank identically to recent cases despite `TemporalDecay.HalfLife` being set. No error, no warning — the decay factor is computed and applied but silently thrown away.

### Context

CDI decorator chain for CBR retrieval:
```
TrendEnrichment@90 → Reranking@75 → OutcomeWeighting@65 → Tracking@50 → Store
```

Temporal decay was applied inside the store (InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore, JpaCbrCaseMemoryStore) as a post-scoring multiplier: `score *= decay.factor(storedAt, now)`.

### Root cause

The reranking decorator at @Priority(75) calls the cross-encoder to independently evaluate semantic relevance for each candidate. It produces a new sigmoid-normalized score that **completely replaces** the input score. Any multiplier applied to the input score (decay, confidence weighting, feature adjustments) is silently discarded — the cross-encoder score has no memory of the pre-applied factor.

Result flow: Store returns `score * decayFactor` → Tracking records it → OutcomeWeighting adjusts → **Reranking replaces with `sigmoid(crossEncoderScore)`** → decay gone.

### Fix

Score modifiers that should affect the final ranking must be applied at a HIGHER priority (outer in the decorator chain) than the score-replacing decorator. Higher CDI @Priority = executes first on the way in, last on the way out (processes results after the inner decorator).

```
TrendEnrichment@90 → Decay@80 → Reranking@75 → OutcomeWeighting@65 → Tracking@50 → Store
```

With decay at @Priority(80), it wraps the reranker and sees the final cross-encoder scores. The final score becomes `crossEncoderScore * decayFactor`.

Remove any store-level decay to avoid double application when the decorator is active.

### Why this is non-obvious

The CDI decorator chain reads left-to-right as "this wraps that", but the score flow is the reverse. A developer adding decay "after scoring" naturally puts it in the store or at a low priority — which is correct when no score-replacing decorator exists. The reranker's score replacement is not documented as "discards all pre-applied multipliers" — it's just "re-evaluates using cross-encoder", which sounds additive.

### Alternatives considered

- Apply decay inside the reranker itself (couples unrelated concerns)
- Add decay as a fusion leg in hybrid retrieval (only works for hybrid mode, complex)
- Apply decay at store level and skip when reranking is enabled (fragile, breaks when decorator config changes)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
TrendEnrichment decorator overwriting multipliers
Cross-encoder replacing input scores silently
Reranking decorator discarding pre-applied decay factors

entries.title: InMemoryReactiveCommitmentStore.delegate missing @Inject — NPE in @QuarkusTest but works in plain unit tests
entries.body:
InMemoryReactiveCommitmentStore.delegate missing @Inject — NPE in @QuarkusTest but works in plain unit tests

### Symptom
`NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "InMemoryCommitmentStore.findByChannel(UUID)" because "this.delegate" is null` when calling any method on `ReactiveCommitmentStore` in a `@QuarkusTest`.

### Context
`InMemoryReactiveCommitmentStore` delegates all operations to an `InMemoryCommitmentStore` via a package-private `delegate` field. The sibling reactive stores (`InMemoryReactiveChannelStore`, `InMemoryReactiveMessageStore`) have `@Inject` on their delegate fields — CDI wires them automatically in Quarkus test contexts. `InMemoryReactiveCommitmentStore` was missing `@Inject`, so CDI left the field null.

### What was tried (didn't work)
Injecting `ReactiveCommitmentStore` in a `@QuarkusTest` and calling `findByChannel()` — NPE with no useful context about the missing wiring.

### Root cause
The `delegate` field on `InMemoryReactiveCommitmentStore` lacked the `@Inject` annotation. In plain unit tests, the delegate is set manually (`store.delegate = blocking`), so the bug never surfaces there. It only appears when CDI manages the bean lifecycle.

### Fix
Add `@Inject` to the delegate field:

```java
@Inject
InMemoryCommitmentStore delegate;
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The field is package-private with no annotation — it looks like it's meant to be set manually. The sibling stores have `@Inject` but you wouldn't check them unless you already suspected a CDI wiring issue. Plain unit tests pass, so CI doesn't catch it. The NPE message says "delegate is null" but doesn't hint at CDI — you'd first suspect a bean resolution issue or missing `@Alternative` priority.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`@QuarkusTest NPE InMemoryReactiveCommitmentStore delegate`
`missing @Inject ReactiveCommitmentStore`
`NPE findByChannel UUID`

entries.title: MessageQueryJpql silently ignores new MessageQuery fields — JPA stores return unfiltered results
entries.body:
MessageQueryJpql silently ignores new MessageQuery fields — JPA stores return unfiltered results

### Symptom
Topic-filtered projections return all messages in JPA-backed stores but correctly filter in in-memory stores. No error, no warning — the results are silently wrong.

### Context
`MessageQuery` is a value object with fields like `channelId`, `sender`, `topic`, etc. Two consumers translate it to queries:
- `MessageQuery.matches(Message)` — in-memory predicate, used by `InMemoryMessageStore`
- `MessageQueryJpql.from(MessageQuery)` — JPQL WHERE clause builder, used by `JpaMessageStore`

When a new field is added to `MessageQuery` (e.g. `topic()`), `matches()` gets the filter automatically (it checks all fields), but `MessageQueryJpql` must be manually updated with the corresponding `AND` clause.

### Root cause
`MessageQueryJpql.from()` is a hand-written JPQL builder that must be kept in sync with `MessageQuery` fields manually. There is no compiler check, no runtime assertion, and no test that verifies field coverage parity between the two paths. A missing predicate silently degrades to "no filter" — the WHERE clause simply omits the condition.

Both `from(MessageQuery)` (tenant-unaware) and `from(MessageQuery, String)` (tenant-scoped) variants must be updated together — they are duplicated code blocks.

### Fix
Add the missing predicate to both `from()` variants in `MessageQueryJpql`:

```java
if (q.topic() != null) {
    where.append(" AND LOWER(topic) = LOWER(?").append(idx++).append(")");
    params.add(q.topic());
}
```

Case-insensitive matching (`LOWER()`) is required to match `MessageQuery.matches()` semantics which uses `equalsIgnoreCase`.

### Why this is non-obvious
The in-memory store tests all pass — `MessageQuery.matches()` handles every field. The bug only manifests through JPA-backed stores, which are typically not exercised in unit tests. A developer adding a field to `MessageQuery` has no signal that `MessageQueryJpql` needs updating — the code compiles, tests pass, and the query silently returns too many results.

### Alternatives considered
- **Criteria API**: Would derive predicates from field metadata, eliminating manual sync. Rejected — heavier abstraction for a record with ~12 fields; the manual builder is readable and fast.
- **Reflection-based parity test**: Could assert that every non-null field in a `MessageQuery` produces a predicate in the JPQL output. Not yet implemented but would catch future regressions.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
MessageQuery JPQL filtering issues
MessageQuery topic() filtering problems
JPA MessageQuery predicate synchronization

entries.title: Quarkus ARC @DefaultBean injection points resolve before @Alternative activation in external JARs
entries.body:
Quarkus ARC @DefaultBean injection points resolve before @Alternative activation in external JARs

### Symptom

A `@DefaultBean` reactive bridge (`BlockingToReactiveCbrBridge`) that injects a blocking SPI interface (`CbrCaseMemoryStore`) silently resolves to the no-op `@DefaultBean` implementation (`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`) instead of the `@Alternative @Priority(2)` in-memory implementation (`InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore`), even when:

- The alternative is listed in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`
- Both JARs are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency`
- Direct injection of the blocking interface in a test class correctly resolves to the alternative

The retrieval returns empty with no error or warning — completely silent.

### Context

This occurs when three beans implement the same interface across two external JARs:

- **JAR A** (`casehub-neocortex-memory`): `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` (`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped`) and `BlockingToReactiveCbrBridge` (`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped`, injects `CbrCaseMemoryStore`)
- **JAR B** (`casehub-neocortex-memory-cbr-inmem`): `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` (`@Alternative @Priority(2) @ApplicationScoped`)

The bridge in JAR A is supposed to delegate to whichever `CbrCaseMemoryStore` is active. When `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` is activated via `selected-alternatives`, direct injection works — but the bridge's own injection point does not.

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Adding `quarkus.index-dependency` for both JARs — no effect on resolution
2. Adding `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in the memory profile — direct injection works, bridge delegation does not
3. Adding `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` for `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` — breaks CDI wiring entirely (the bridge has no delegate)

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC resolves `@DefaultBean` beans' injection points at build time. When the bridge (`@DefaultBean`) is being wired, ARC resolves its `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` using the standard `@DefaultBean` resolution rules — which picks the other `@DefaultBean` (`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`) in the same JAR. The `@Alternative` from the external JAR is not considered for the bridge's injection point even though it would be selected for direct injection sites.

Confirmed via `System.identityHashCode()` tracing: both the test's `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` and the bridge's `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore delegate` resolve to the same `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore_ClientProxy` instance.

### Solution 1 — Bypass the reactive bridge

**Approach:** Inject the blocking interface directly and offload to a worker thread.

**Pros:** No CDI resolution ambiguity. Works with any test profile.

**Cons:** Caller must handle thread offloading explicitly.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyService {
    @Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore cbrStore; // blocking, not reactive

public Uni<List<Result>> retrieve(Query query) {
        return Uni.createFrom()
            .item(() -> cbrStore.retrieveSimilar(query, MyCase.class))
            .runSubscriptionOn(Infrastructure.getDefaultWorkerPool())
            .map(this::mapResults);
    }
}
```

### Solution 2 — Use QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives()

**Approach:** Override alternatives programmatically in the test profile.

**Pros:** Properly activates @Alternative beans for all injection points including bridge delegates.

**Cons:** `getEnabledAlternatives()` REPLACES (not appends to) `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` — ALL alternatives from the base profile must be re-declared. Missing one breaks other tests sharing the profile.

```java
public static class MemoryProfile implements QuarkusTestProfile {
    @Override
    public String getConfigProfile() { return "memory"; }

@Override
    public Set<Class<?>> getEnabledAlternatives() {
        return Set.of(
            InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository.class,
            InMemoryReactiveCaseMetaModelRepository.class,
            // ... ALL other memory profile alternatives ...
            InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore.class);
    }
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The bridge pattern (`@DefaultBean` reactive wrapper delegating to `@DefaultBean` blocking implementation, replaced by `@Alternative` at test time) is a standard Quarkus CDI pattern. Nothing in Quarkus documentation warns that `@DefaultBean` injection points resolve before `@Alternative` activation. The failure is completely silent — no ambiguity error, no warning, just empty results from the no-op. Only `System.identityHashCode()` tracing reveals which implementation was actually injected.

### Why this fix

Solution 1 (bypass the bridge) is preferred because it eliminates the CDI resolution issue entirely and has no test infrastructure side effects. Solution 2 works but creates a maintenance burden — every new alternative added to the memory profile must also be added to every `getEnabledAlternatives()` override.

### Alternatives considered

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` for the no-op: breaks CDI wiring when the bridge needs a delegate and no alternative is available
- Using `Instance<CbrCaseMemoryStore>` with programmatic lookup: adds complexity without addressing the root cause
- Filing a Quarkus ARC bug: may be working as designed (build-time CDI optimisation)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`
`@Alternative @Priority(2)` resolution
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`

entries.title: @Alternative on a CDI bean silently suppresses all @DefaultBean beans of the same type — they vanish from the container entirely
Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException

### Symptom

After removing `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from one CDI bean, a different bean
silently becomes the active implementation. No `AmbiguousResolutionException`, no
warning, no log. Tests that depend on the removed bean's behaviour fail with
unrelated-looking assertion errors.

### Context

Three implementations of the same port interface coexist in the build:

| Bean | Annotations | Role |
|------|------------|------|
| `PrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` | Layer 1 naive baseline |
| `QhorusPrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(1)` | Layer 3 qhorus messaging |
| `PrReviewCaseService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(2)` | Layer 5 engine (active) |

This is the CDI displacement pattern for progressive layer integration — each layer
adds an implementation; CDI priority determines which is active at runtime.

### What was tried (didn't work)

Removed `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from `PrReviewCaseService` to fix an anti-pattern
documented in ARC42STORIES §8 ("CDI priority gymnastics"). Expected: the plain
`@ApplicationScoped` bean would still displace the `@DefaultBean` baseline via
Quarkus's `@DefaultBean` semantics.

### Root cause

CDI resolution rules interact in a non-obvious way:

1. `@DefaultBean` beans are suppressed when any non-`@DefaultBean` bean exists ✅
2. Activated `@Alternative` beans (with `@Priority`) take precedence over regular beans ⚠️
3. After removing `@Alternative` from `PrReviewCaseService`, it becomes a regular bean
4. `QhorusPrReviewService` (`@Alternative @Priority(1)`) is still an activated alternative
5. **Rule 2 applies**: the activated alternative wins over the regular bean
6. `QhorusPrReviewService` becomes the active implementation — silently

The mental model "I'm just removing unnecessary annotations" is wrong. The annotations
are load-bearing: they participate in a priority chain where every bean's annotation
set matters.

### Fix

All implementations in the `@Alternative` chain must be addressed together, not one at
a time. To properly fix the anti-pattern:

- Either make ALL non-baseline implementations use `@DefaultBean` displacement
  (remove `@Alternative @Priority` from all of them and ensure only one non-`@DefaultBean` exists)
- Or keep the `@Alternative @Priority` chain intact and accept it as the mechanism
  for layer coexistence

Do not remove `@Alternative` from one bean without checking what other `@Alternative`
implementations exist for the same interface.

### Why this is non-obvious

Most developers reason about CDI alternatives in pairs: "my bean vs the default."
The three-way interaction (DefaultBean + Alternative(1) + Alternative(2)) is rarely
encountered, and the silent resolution change (no exception, wrong bean) gives no
diagnostic signal. The symptom (test assertion failure on unrelated data) is
completely disconnected from the cause (CDI annotation change).

### Why this fix

The obvious approach — "just remove the anti-pattern annotation" — is wrong because
it treats the annotations as decoration rather than as a load-bearing priority chain.
The fix requires understanding the full set of implementations and their annotation
interactions before changing any single one.

### Alternatives considered

- Remove `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from only the active bean → silently breaks resolution (this gotcha)
- Remove `@Alternative` from ALL implementations and use `@DefaultBean` displacement → requires ensuring exactly one non-`@DefaultBean` impl, and retiring or `@DefaultBean`-ing the intermediate layers
- Keep `@Alternative @Priority` chain as-is → accepted as the working mechanism until a coordinated cleanup addresses all implementations together

**See also:** GE-20260626-c21b02 — @DefaultBean suppression by any Instance<T> peer, a different silent failure in the same CDI displacement space.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`CDI priority resolution ambiguousResolutionException`
`alternative bean suppressionDefaultBean`
`applicationScoped bean displacement`

entries.title: quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives default priority 1 creates tie with @Priority(1) subclass beans — two @ApplicationScoped instances with separate state
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives default priority 1 creates tie with @Priority(1) subclass beans — two @ApplicationScoped instances with separate state

### Symptom
`CaseInstance not found or wrong tenant` (or similar state-not-found error) despite the instance being saved moments earlier. The save and lookup use the same `CaseInstanceRepository` interface, but they resolve to different `@ApplicationScoped` bean instances with separate `ConcurrentHashMap` stores.

### Context
`casehub-engine-testing` provides `TestCaseInstanceRepository extends InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` with `@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped`. This is the standard test harness — it auto-activates without `selected-alternatives`.

A consumer project adds `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in test `application.properties`, thinking it's redundant but harmless.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Checking event bus threading and Vert.x serialization — object identity was intact
- Verifying `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` consistency — MockCurrentPrincipal returns a constant
- Adding more beans to `selected-alternatives` — made it worse

### Root cause
Quarkus Arc assigns a **default priority of 1** to alternatives listed in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` that don't have `@Priority`. This creates a priority tie:

- `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` — priority 1 (from `selected-alternatives` default)
- `TestCaseInstanceRepository` — priority 1 (from `@Priority(1)`)

Both are `@ApplicationScoped`, so CDI creates **two separate bean instances**. Each has its own `ConcurrentHashMap<UUID, CaseInstance> store`. If CDI resolves different injection points to different beans (or resolves non-deterministically), saves go to one store and lookups to another.

### Fix
Do not add parent classes to `selected-alternatives` when the engine-testing module already provides `@Priority(1)` subclasses:

```properties
# WRONG — creates priority tie with TestCaseInstanceRepository
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=...,io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository

# RIGHT — let engine-testing's @Priority(1) beans handle it
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=...
# (omit InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository, InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository, InMemoryEventLogRepository)
```

The engine-testing module exists specifically to provide auto-activating alternatives for test contexts. Adding the parent classes to `selected-alternatives` defeats the purpose.

### Why this is non-obvious
Adding a class to `selected-alternatives` feels like an explicit, high-confidence activation — surely it would "win" over a `@Priority(1)` subclass. But the default priority is also 1, creating an exact tie. The Quarkus docs mention the default priority but don't warn about ties with existing `@Priority(1)` alternatives on the classpath. The symptom (state not found) appears as a threading or serialization bug, not a CDI resolution issue.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`CaseInstance not found or wrong tenant` error
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives priority tie`
`ConcurrentHashMap store`

entries.title: Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied
entries.body:
Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied

## What happened

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI type appeared on the CDI
classpath simultaneously (one from a platform mock library, one from a persistence testing module).
Quarkus reported **"Ambiguous dependencies"** and refused to start — even though both beans
explicitly said "I am a default, defer to anyone else".

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is documented as "yield to any other bean of the same type". With two
`@DefaultBean` beans and no non-default implementation, neither bean yields — the contract
("yield to someone else") cannot resolve because there IS no "someone else" with higher
precedence. The error message is **Ambiguous** (same as two regular `@ApplicationScoped`
beans conflicting), not **Unsatisfied** (what you'd expect if both were supposedly yielding).
Developers often assume two `@DefaultBean` beans resolve cleanly because they both "opt in"
to being overridden.

## Root cause

CDI/ARC `@DefaultBean` semantics: a default bean is only eligible when no other bean at
the same or higher priority is eligible. With two `@DefaultBean` beans and no higher-priority
bean, the tie-break is undefined — ARC treats this as an ambiguous injection point.

## Fix

Exclude the unwanted `@DefaultBean` implementation via `application.properties`:
```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockGroupMembershipProvider,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockPreferenceProvider
```

This removes the conflicting bean from CDI discovery entirely, leaving the desired
`@DefaultBean` as the sole implementation. Prefer excluding the one that returns null or
uninitialized values rather than the one with correct sentinel behaviour.

### Why this fix

`@Alternative @Priority(N)` would also work, but requires activating it via
`selected-alternatives` — that is a heavier configuration change and makes the
intent less clear. `exclude-types` is surgical: "this specific class should not
participate in CDI at all in this context."

### Alternative — use `Instance<T>` with `isUnsatisfied()` to avoid the conflict entirely

Rather than excluding a conflicting bean after the fact, don't provide a competing `@DefaultBean` in the extension at all. Inject `Instance<T>` and check `isUnsatisfied()` at call time:

```java
@Inject Instance<PreferenceProvider> preferenceProviderInstance;

int threshold;
if (preferenceProviderInstance.isUnsatisfied()) {
    threshold = DEFAULT_VALUE;  // no provider on classpath
} else {
    threshold = preferenceProviderInstance.get().resolve(...).getOrDefault(KEY).value();
}
```

`Instance<T>` always satisfies its own injection point (the container injects the `Instance` holder, not `T` directly). When zero beans of type `T` exist, `isUnsatisfied()` returns `true`; when one is active, `.get()` returns it. No `@DefaultBean` is added to the extension, so no conflict can arise.

**Best for:** library/extension authors who control their own code and want to make a platform SPI optional without contributing a competing `@DefaultBean`.

**Limitation:** requires call-site guards (`isUnsatisfied()` before `.get()`); callers that inject `T` directly still get an ambiguous point if two `@DefaultBean` beans exist from other sources.

## Constraints

Applies when both `@DefaultBean` implementations reach the CDI container's scanning phase
(i.e. both are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency` or are in the app's own sources).
In two-repo / multi-module projects, platform library JARs can silently contribute
`@DefaultBean` mocks that conflict with internal no-ops.

## Alternatives considered

- Mark one bean `@Alternative @Priority(1)` instead of `@DefaultBean` — works but changes
  the semantics of the "winning" bean and requires `selected-alternatives` configuration.
- Remove one of the `@DefaultBean` implementations from the classpath entirely — clean, but
  may not be possible if it comes from a third-party dependency.

## Invalidation triggers

Would change if Quarkus ARC adds a deterministic tie-break for two `@DefaultBean` beans
(e.g. favour the one in the current module's sources). Track Quarkus changelog for ARC
`@DefaultBean` resolution changes.

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean must be on @Produces method not on the class | [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException | [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260609-26ffa5](GE-20260609-26ffa5.md) — @ApplicationScoped POJO + @Produces for same type causes CDI ambiguous bean resolution

**See also:** [GE-20260515-99cf39](GE-20260515-99cf39.md) — config-driven @Produces @DefaultBean for engine-internal strategy selection

**See also:** [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel, clashing with @DefaultBean fallback | [GE-20260604-b3d2ef](GE-20260604-b3d2ef.md) — quarkus-flow CDI extension already registers WorkflowApplication — adding @Produces causes ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260615-6c4767](../casehub-engine/GE-20260615-6c4767.md) — adding custom CDI qualifier to @ApplicationScoped removes @Default

**See also:** GE-20260627-51e402 — @Alternative totally suppresses @DefaultBean (not just deprioritized, gone from container)

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException
@DefaultBean application scope
Quarkus ARC ambiguous injection point

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
```
