### Symptom
Claude CLI subprocess appears to time out silently — the `QueryExpandingCaseRetriever` decorator catches a `TimeoutException` and falls back to the original query. Benchmark results are identical to baseline despite the decorator being active in the CDI graph. No error logged by `AgentProviderChatModel` — only the decorator's catch block emits a WARNING.

### Context
The call chain is: `LlmQueryExpander` → `ChatModel.chat()` → `AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` → `agentProvider.invoke()` → `ClaudeAgentProvider` → Claude CLI subprocess. Two separate timeout configurations exist:
- `casehub.platform.agent.claude.default-timeout` (default PT5M) — used by `ClaudeAgentClient` for the subprocess wall-clock timeout
- `casehub.platform.agent.langchain4j.close-timeout` (default PT30S) — used by `AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` when awaiting the Mutiny stream

### What was tried (didn't work)
Setting `casehub.platform.agent.claude.default-timeout=PT3M` — queries still timed out at exactly 30 seconds. The Claude agent timeout was never the bottleneck.

### Root cause
`AgentProviderChatModel.doChat()` calls `.await().atMost(properties.closeTimeout())` where `properties` is `AgentLangchain4jProperties`, not `ClaudeAgentProperties`. The LangChain4j bridge has its own timeout that fires before the Claude agent timeout. The two config prefixes are different packages with no cross-reference in documentation or logging.

### Fix
Set the correct timeout:
```properties
casehub.platform.agent.langchain4j.close-timeout=PT3M
```

Or bypass the ChatModel bridge entirely by using `AgentProvider.openSession()` directly — the session approach avoids both timeouts and provides prompt caching benefits.

### Why this is non-obvious
Two timeout configs (`agent.claude.default-timeout` and `agent.langchain4j.close-timeout`) control the same call chain at different layers. Setting the wrong one has zero effect — no error, no warning, no log indicating which timeout fired. The `TimeoutException` stack trace shows Mutiny internals, not which config governed the timeout.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
langchain4j close-timeout PT30S
AgentProviderChatModel doChat timeout
Claude CLI subprocess timeout

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus ambiguous resolution ChatModel @Default
quarkus @DefaultBean conflicts with @Default SYNTHETIC
Ollama extension ChatModel registration error

entries.title: langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types
entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
DeclarativeUtil chatSupplierParameterResolvers
@ChatModelSupplier CDI resolver hook
CdiBean workaround limitations

LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
JSON response format without schema
Anthropic UnsupportedFeatureException
JSON schema requirement

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-core Quarkus extension stalls @QuarkusTest augmentation when no model provider is configured
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-core Quarkus extension stalls @QuarkusTest augmentation when no model provider is configured

## Symptom

`mvn test` hangs indefinitely during Quarkus augmentation when `quarkus-langchain4j-core` is a compile-scope dependency of a non-extension library module and no AI model provider is configured. No error message, no timeout — the build just blocks.

## Context

Occurs when a library module (Jandex-indexed, not a full Quarkus extension) adds `io.quarkiverse.langchain4j:quarkus-langchain4j-core` as a compile dependency to use the `EmbeddingModel` interface. During `@QuarkusTest` augmentation, the Quarkus extension activates and waits for a model provider that never arrives.

## What was tried

Adding `quarkus-langchain4j-core` as a `provided` scope — still stalls because the extension's deployment artifact is resolved transitively during augmentation.

## Root cause

`quarkus-langchain4j-core` is a Quarkus extension (has both runtime and deployment jars). When it appears on the augmentation classpath, Quarkus activates it and expects at least one model provider (OpenAI, Ollama, etc.) to be configured. Without one, augmentation stalls waiting for the CDI bean to resolve.

## Fix

Use `dev.langchain4j:langchain4j-core` (the plain Java library, **not** the Quarkus extension) as the compile dependency. This provides the `EmbeddingModel` interface for compilation without triggering Quarkus extension activation:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>langchain4j-core</artifactId>
  <version>1.13.0</version>
</dependency>
```

For CDI injection, use `Instance<EmbeddingModel>` instead of `@Inject EmbeddingModel`:

```java
@Inject
public MyBean(final Instance<EmbeddingModel> modelInstance) {
    this.model = modelInstance.isResolvable() ? modelInstance.get() : null;
}
```

When no provider is configured, `instance.isResolvable()` returns `false` gracefully. The consuming app brings `quarkus-langchain4j-openai` (or any other provider extension), which satisfies the CDI bean at their own augmentation time.

## Why this is non-obvious

The symptom is a hang with no error — not a compilation failure or a clear exception. The natural instinct is to add the Quarkus extension for its CDI integration, but the correct separation is: library module uses the plain Java API, consuming application brings the Quarkus extension.

### Why this fix

The plain Java `langchain4j-core` provides the same `EmbeddingModel` interface without triggering extension activation. `Instance<EmbeddingModel>` makes the dependency optional at CDI resolution time, so the library works both with and without a configured provider.

**See also:** GE-20260422-3242bf — Use Instance<T> for optional CDI injection — resolves gracefully when no bean exists

### Alternatives considered

- `provided` scope: still triggers augmentation because the extension's deployment artifact is resolved transitively
- Mocking `EmbeddingModel` via `@InjectMock` in every `@QuarkusTest`: works but requires all existing tests to be updated

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus langchain4j core augmentation stalls without model provider
quarkus test augmentation stalls compile scope langchain4j
embeddingmodel instance isresolvable false error

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache

## Symptom

After adding `quarkus-langchain4j-ollama` as a test-scope dependency inside a Maven profile
(`-Peval-ollama`), the Ollama `ChatModel` bean is not registered. Config keys are logged as
`Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"`, and the
test fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for `ChatModel`.

## Context

The module was previously built without the Ollama extension. Maven resolves the Ollama JAR
when the profile is active, but Quarkus reuses its disk-based augmentation cache from the
prior build — before the Ollama extension was on the classpath. The Ollama extension is
silently absent from augmentation: no beans registered, no config processors active.

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Running `mvn test -Peval,eval-ollama` after the JAR appeared in `~/.m2` — stale augmentation
  cache persisted, config keys still unrecognized.
- Adding `-Dquarkus.test.profile=eval` explicitly — no effect on cache.

## Root cause

Quarkus augmentation is disk-cached in `target/quarkus-app/`. When classpath changes occur
(new extension added via Maven profile), the cache invalidation heuristic does not always
detect the change, especially when the Ollama JAR was already present in `~/.m2` from a
prior `mvn dependency:resolve` call (updating file timestamps). The cache is reused, and
the Ollama extension's CDI beans are never registered.

## Fix

Run `mvn clean` before the first test run with the new profile:

```bash
JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 26) mvn clean test -pl eval -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dtest=PromptEvalTest#evaluateRealWorldScenarios \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name=qwen3:8b" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

Subsequent runs without `clean` work correctly — the Ollama-aware augmentation is now cached.

## Why this is non-obvious

The "unrecognized configuration key" warning does not hint at augmentation caching — it reads
as though the extension was not added at all, not that a stale build artifact is in play.
The Ollama JAR is visible in `mvn dependency:resolve` output, making the missing registration
doubly confusing. The standard fix for missing CDI beans (`check your imports, check your
annotations`) leads nowhere.

**See also:** [GE-20260530-0178fd](GE-20260530-0178fd.md) — Quarkus @QuarkusTest augmentation requires extension deployment JARs in ~/.m2 | [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension @Default ChatModel clashes with @DefaultBean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"
Augmentation cache stale test-scope Ollama ChatModel

entries.title: SPLADE (MS MARCO) has zero Java domain vocabulary — expands ChatModel to hotel/beauty/renovation
entries.body:
SPLADE (MS MARCO) has zero Java domain vocabulary — expands ChatModel to hotel/beauty/renovation

### Symptom
Adding SPLADE sparse embeddings to dense retrieval (RRF fusion) churns result sets without improving quality for Java/CDI domain queries. All 28 queries changed, 3 highly relevant entries were displaced while 40 noise entries were removed — net effect ambiguous.

### Context
Hortora engine hybrid search benchmark (#28). SPLADE (`Splade_PP_en_v1`) added as sparse embedding alongside nomic-embed-text dense vectors. RRF fusion (k=60, denseTopK=40, sparseTopK=40). Tested across 14 real-world scenarios covering Java class names, CDI annotations, JPA patterns, and Quarkus framework terms.

SPLADE vocabulary analysis decoded the activated tokens for each query:

| Query | Top SPLADE Expansions | Expected (Java domain) |
|-------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `DefaultBean\|AmbiguousResolutionException` | ambiguity, groups, unclear | cdi, qualifier, alternative, inject |
| `ChatModel\|AgentSession\|LangChain4j` | agent, talk, beauty, renovation, genre | model, inference, provider, adapter |
| `Priority(100)\|CDI priority` | priorities, cds (music), urgency, precedence | qualifier, scope, alternative, bean |

Zero Tier 1 domain term activations across all 14 KW queries. Not one activation of `panache`, `jandex`, `qualifier`, `interceptor`, `singleton`, `persist`, or any unambiguous Java/CDI term.

### Root cause
Two compounding failures:

1. **BERT WordPiece tokenizer** fragments Java class names into meaningless subwords: `AmbiguousResolutionException` → `["am", "##bi", "##guous", "##reso", "##lution", "##exception"]`. The semantic content is destroyed before SPLADE runs.

2. **MS MARCO training data** contains no Java ecosystem content. SPLADE's learned vocabulary expansion maps "chat" to web-domain associations (hotels, beauty, renovation) — not to software engineering concepts.

This is expected behaviour for this model architecture, not a defect. The same limitation applies to nomic-embed-text (see GE-20260627-4712de) — the difference is that SPLADE actively ADDS noise through irrelevant expansions, whereas nomic-embed-text merely fails to discriminate.

### Fix
Do not use general-purpose (MS MARCO-trained) SPLADE models for Java/CDI domain retrieval. Three alternatives:

1. **BM25 keyword matching** (casehubio/neural-text#47/#48) — exact token matching via Qdrant full-text index. Directly addresses the vocabulary gap.
2. **Code-domain SPLADE model** (casehubio/neural-text#49) — if one exists with Java training data.
3. **Code-domain dense embedding model** (casehubio/neural-text#49) — models like CodeBERT, UniXcoder trained on source code.

### Why this is non-obvious
SPLADE is presented as a vocabulary expansion technique that recovers keyword precision lost by dense embeddings. The expectation is that it bridges the gap between semantic search and keyword matching. For general-domain web queries, this is true. For Java class names, it actively makes things worse by introducing irrelevant web-domain associations into the sparse vector.

### Why this fix
BM25 is the highest-leverage fix because it directly solves the failure mode (exact token matching for Java identifiers) without requiring model training or fine-tuning. Code-domain models are the long-term architectural fix but have higher uncertainty and longer timeline.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`AmbiguousResolutionException` Java CDI
`ChatModel\|AgentSession\|LangChain4j` vocabulary
`Priority(100)\|CDI priority` term activations

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs

## What it is

The Quarkus LangChain4j Ollama extension sets a **10-second default REST client timeout**
for all chat requests. This is undocumented. For local LLMs (8B+ parameter models on CPU
or M-series Neural Engine), a single JSON-structured chat request typically takes 15–120
seconds, so the default silently causes every judge call to fail.

## Context

Appears when running eval harness tests with Ollama models as the judge. The `PromptJudge`
call fails with:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Judge LLM call failed — check judge model configuration
Caused by: javax.ws.rs.ProcessingException: The timeout period of 10000ms has been exceeded
  while executing POST /api/chat for server localhost:11434
```

The timeout fires before the model finishes generating the structured JSON response.

## Fix

Pass the timeout override via system property:

```bash
"-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

The property is not documented in the Quarkus LangChain4j extension docs or the
quarkus.io reference (as of 2026-06-14). It's discoverable only by reading the
extension's `OllamaConfig` source.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("check judge model configuration") points to configuration rather
than networking/timeout, leading to checks of model name, format=json flag, and CDI
wiring — none of which are the problem. The 10-second timeout is plausible for
hosted APIs but is impractical for any local model above 3B parameters.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

Ollama REST client timeout default value

SupervisorAgentService bypasses WorkflowAgentsBuilder SPI — setWorkflowAgentsBuilder cannot intercept it

### Symptom

Config override for `@SupervisorAgent(maxAgentsInvocations=10)` does not work even though `AgenticServices.setWorkflowAgentsBuilder()` is correctly set with a config-aware wrapper.

### Context

`WorkflowAgentsBuilder` covers loop, sequence, parallel, conditional, and parallelMapper builders. But `SupervisorAgentService` is NOT created through it.

### Root cause

`buildSupervisorAgent()` in `AgenticServices` creates the builder directly:
```java
var builder = new SupervisorAgentServiceImpl<>(agentServiceClass, agentMethod, chatModel)
    .maxAgentsInvocations(supervisorAgent.maxAgentsInvocations())
```

This bypasses the `WorkflowAgentsBuilder` SPI entirely. There is no interception point.

### Fix

None available in current upstream. Config for `maxAgentsInvocations` can be declared in the config interface but cannot be wired until upstream provides either a supervisor builder SPI or the workflow-level `AgentConfigurator` (langchain4j/langchain4j#5399).

### Why this is non-obvious

All other workflow builders (loop, sequence, parallel, conditional) go through `WorkflowAgentsBuilder`. The supervisor is the exception — and there's no documentation or API design hint that it's different.

@Transactional on @PostConstruct is silently ignored — Arc proxy not created yet
entries.body:
@Transactional on @PostConstruct is silently ignored — Arc proxy not created yet

### Symptom

A `@PostConstruct` method calls an injected service method annotated with `@Transactional`. At runtime:
- No error or exception is thrown
- The transaction is silently never started
- Database operations inside the service method fail with "no EntityManager associated" or run outside a transaction, silently committing or rolling back contrary to expectations
- Annotating `@PostConstruct` itself with `@Transactional` also has no effect

### Context

Occurs in any Quarkus `@ApplicationScoped` (or other normal-scoped) CDI bean whose `@PostConstruct` method invokes a service that requires a JTA transaction. Classic example: bootstrapping a channel or configuration record in a qhorus `ChannelService.create()` call during bean initialisation.

### Root Cause

Quarkus CDI (`Arc`) implements `@Transactional` via a CDI proxy subclass. When `@PostConstruct` executes, the proxy has not yet been created — the bean is being initialised. The call is made directly on the concrete instance, bypassing the proxy entirely. The `@Transactional` interceptor never fires.

This is not a bug in Arc: the CDI specification requires `@PostConstruct` to execute on the bean instance, not through the proxy. `@Transactional` only works through proxy dispatch.

### Fix

Wrap the transactional work in `QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew()`:

```java
import io.quarkus.narayana.jta.QuarkusTransaction;

@PostConstruct
void init() {
    QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew().call(() -> {
        channelService.findByName(CHANNEL_NAME)
            .map(c -> c.id)
            .orElseGet(() -> channelService.create(...).id);
        return null;
    });
    // Other non-transactional init...
    activeTypes = computeActiveTypes(consumers);
}
```

`QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew()` starts a real JTA transaction programmatically on the current thread. The transaction commits (or rolls back on exception) when the lambda returns. This does not require a proxy.

### Why this is non-obvious

Developers naturally annotate `@PostConstruct` with `@Transactional` (it compiles fine), or rely on injected services being `@Transactional` to "just work" when called from `@PostConstruct`. Neither approach produces any error — the annotation is present, the service is injected, the method call executes — but the transaction silently never starts. The symptom only surfaces as unexpected database behaviour (missing data, constraint violations, or EntityManager-not-bound errors) rather than a clear "no transaction" message.

### Why this fix

`QuarkusTransaction.requiringNew()` is the programmatic API specifically designed for contexts where CDI interception is unavailable — tests, listeners, and lifecycle methods. It is unambiguous about starting a new transaction and does not depend on proxy dispatch.

### Alternatives considered

- Annotating `@PostConstruct` with `@Transactional` — no effect; proxy not created yet
- Self-injecting the bean via `@Inject Instance<Self>` and calling through the proxy — works but awkward and misleading in an init method
- Moving init logic to a `@Observes StartupEvent` method — works and the proxy IS active at that point; valid alternative but changes when init runs (after full CDI startup vs during bean creation)

**See also:** [GE-20260512-a9ad9f](GE-20260512-a9ad9f.md) — raw ExecutorService drops CDI context — @Transactional silently broken on background threads | [GE-20260513-a49d06](GE-20260513-a49d06.md) — CDI this.method() call bypasses @Transactional proxy | [GE-20260501-884024](../quarkus/GE-20260501-884024.md) — @Observes(AFTER_SUCCESS) doesn't fire when no JTA transaction

**See also:** [GE-20260518-069f64](GE-20260518-069f64.md) — calling @Transactional method via this inside Mutiny lambda silently bypasses CDI proxy

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`@Transactional @PostConstruct no EntityManager`
`Arc proxy JTA transaction`
`QuarkusTransaction requiringNew`

@LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern

### Context
A Quarkus application ships multiple provider implementations of an SPI (e.g. `DeviceProvider`) in one Docker image. Each provider should be independently enableable via config (`provider.enabled=true/false`). Disabled providers must be invisible to `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration — not just "present but returning empty results."

### What a skilled developer would normally do
Guard in `@PostConstruct`: check `enabled`, skip initialization if false. Make every method return a no-op result (`discover()` → empty list, `dispatch()` → FAILED, `status()` → DISCONNECTED). This is the "inert-bean" pattern — the bean exists but does nothing.

Problems with inert beans:
- The bean IS discovered by `Instance<DeviceProvider>` — callers see a broken provider
- `@PostConstruct` still runs (and may fail if config properties are missing)
- Every method needs guard logic
- SmallRye Config still validates all `@ConfigMapping` properties at startup (see GE-20260626-e0ecaf)

### Technique
Use `@LookupIfProperty` from Quarkus ARC:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@LookupIfProperty(name = "casehub.iot.homeassistant.enabled", stringValue = "true")
public class HomeAssistantProvider implements DeviceProvider { ... }
```

When `enabled` is absent or `false`:
- The bean is never instantiated
- `@PostConstruct` never runs
- `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration skips it entirely
- No guard logic needed in any method

Combined with `Optional<String>` on all `@ConfigMapping` properties (GE-20260626-e0ecaf), this allows disabled providers to exist on the classpath without causing config validation failures or appearing in the provider registry.

### Why this is non-obvious
`@LookupIfProperty` is less well-known than `@IfBuildProperty` (which is build-time only and prevents runtime reconfiguration). The naming — "lookup if" vs "if build" — doesn't clearly convey the difference. Many developers reach for `@IfBuildProperty` first, discover it prevents runtime toggling in Docker images, and then fall back to the inert-bean pattern instead of finding `@LookupIfProperty`.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`@LookupIfProperty` CDI bean activation
`Instance\u003cDeviceProvider\u003e` provider iteration
`inert-bean` pattern disable

entries.body:
Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans

### Symptom
Consumer `@QuarkusTest` fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for a dependency
(`ChatModel`) that only the production bean needs — even though an `@Alternative @Priority(1)`
test stub exists for the same SPI and would be selected.

### Context
`LlmQueryExpander` is `@ApplicationScoped` with `@IfBuildProperty(enableIfMissing=true)` — registered by default.
Its constructor requires `ChatModel`. `InMemoryQueryExpander` is `@Alternative @Priority(1)` implementing
the same `QueryExpander` SPI. In a `@QuarkusTest` without a `ChatModel` bean, the expectation is that
`InMemoryQueryExpander` replaces `LlmQueryExpander` and no `ChatModel` is needed.

### What was tried (didn't work)
Adding `InMemoryQueryExpander` as `@Alternative @Priority(1)` to the test classpath. The alternative
is correctly selected for `QueryExpander` injection points, but `LlmQueryExpander` is still a
registered bean and its `ChatModel` constructor parameter is still validated.

### Root cause
Quarkus Arc validates injection points of ALL registered beans at build time — not just the
selected bean for a given type. `@Alternative` controls which bean is injected at consumer
injection points, but does NOT suppress validation of other registered beans' own injection
points. A registered bean with an unsatisfied dependency causes a build failure regardless
of whether it would ever be instantiated.

### Fix
Two complementary approaches:

1. **Remove `enableIfMissing = true`** from `@IfBuildProperty` — require explicit mode
   selection so the heavy bean is only registered when the consumer explicitly opts in.

2. **Add a `@DefaultBean` no-op** that implements the SPI with zero dependencies.
   `@DefaultBean` is displaced by any `@ApplicationScoped` bean (when mode is set)
   or `@Alternative` (in tests). The no-op ensures a bean always exists without
   dragging in heavy transitive dependencies.

### Why this is non-obvious
The mental model of `@Alternative` suggests it "replaces" the original bean. In standard
CDI (Weld), this is closer to true — alternatives affect typesafe resolution. But Quarkus
Arc performs aggressive build-time validation of ALL registered beans' injection points,
including beans that will never be instantiated because a higher-priority alternative exists.
The distinction between "not selected" and "not registered" is invisible until it breaks.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Quarkus Arc @Alternative injection point validation
`UnsatisfiedResolutionException` ChatModel
`LlmQueryExpander` @IfBuildProperty test stub

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus ambiguous resolution ChatModel @Default
quarkus @DefaultBean conflicts with @Default SYNTHETIC
Ollama extension ChatModel registration error

@All List<T> in Quarkus/ArC gives testable multi-bean injection without Instance<T>
entries.body:
@All List<T> in Quarkus/ArC gives testable multi-bean injection without Instance<T>

## Context
When building a registry or routing layer that needs all CDI beans of a type
(e.g. routing to the right `Connector` by id), the natural CDI approach is
`Instance<T>`. But `Instance<T>` is a CDI interface with many abstract methods
— difficult to stub in plain JUnit tests without a full container.

## What developers normally do
Inject `Instance<T>`, iterate with `.stream()`, or use `@InjectMock` inside a
`@QuarkusTest` — both require a CDI container.

## The technique
Inject `@All List<T>` instead. ArC populates it at startup with all discovered
beans. In tests, pass `List.of(...)` directly to the constructor — no CDI
context, no mocking of `Instance<T>`, no `@QuarkusTest` needed.

```java
// Production: ArC populates this automatically
ConnectorService(@All List<Connector> connectors) {
    this.registry = connectors.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Connector::id, Function.identity()));
}

// Test: plain JUnit, no CDI
new ConnectorService(List.of(new SlackConnector(), new TeamsConnector()));
```

## Why this is non-obvious
`Instance<T>` is the CDI standard; `@All` is ArC-specific and not prominently
documented for this use case. The standard guidance says to use `@QuarkusTest`
for CDI testing. `@All List<T>` sidesteps the container requirement entirely
for patterns where the bean set is static at startup.

## Constraints
Requires `io.quarkus.arc.All`. Only works when the bean set is consumed at
construction time (static registry). Not suitable if beans are added/removed
at runtime.

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean — not as replacements (gotcha when combining these patterns)

**See also:** [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException (related CDI injection gotcha)

**See also:** [GE-20260609-75e00d](GE-20260609-75e00d.md) — package-private test constructor + @PostConstruct null guard technique

**See also:** [GE-20260614-efee3b](GE-20260614-efee3b.md) — SyntheticBeanBuildItem without addInjectionPoint compiles but fails at runtime

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: Two @Startup @ApplicationScoped Quarkus beans have no guaranteed initialization order — @PostConstruct side effects are unreliable across beans
Quarkus Arc resolves CDI cycles between @ApplicationScoped beans via client proxies — even with constructor injection
entries.body:
Quarkus Arc resolves CDI cycles between @ApplicationScoped beans via client proxies — even with constructor injection

### Symptom
Code review flags a CDI cycle between two `@ApplicationScoped` beans as Critical — "application will not start." The cycle exists in the injection graph: `A → B (constructor injection) → A`. But the full build and all `@QuarkusTest` suites pass without any startup error.

### Context
`MessageService` (`@ApplicationScoped`) was given a field-injected `ChannelGateway`. `ChannelGateway` (`@ApplicationScoped`) already constructor-injected `MessageService` for its inbound dispatch paths (`receiveHumanMessage`, `receiveObserverSignal`). The cycle: `MessageService → ChannelGateway → MessageService`.

### What was tried
Code reviewer flagged the cycle as Critical, citing CDI startup failure. Using `Instance<ChannelGateway>` (lazy injection) to break it was considered as a fix.

### Root cause
The concern is correct for **pseudo-scoped** beans (`@Dependent`) which cannot be proxied — CDI cannot create a client proxy for a dependent-scoped bean, so a cycle involving one causes startup failure.

For **normal-scoped** beans (`@ApplicationScoped`, `@RequestScoped`, `@SessionScoped`), CDI mandates that the container MUST be able to create a client proxy. Quarkus Arc honors this: when `ChannelGateway`'s constructor is called, it receives a client proxy for `MessageService` — not the actual instance. The proxy is valid immediately; the actual `MessageService` instance is only resolved on the first method call. Both beans initialize without needing the other to exist first.

### Fix
Ensure all beans in the cycle are normal-scoped. Add a comment explaining the deliberate cycle so reviewers don't flag it:

```java
// Deliberate CDI cycle: MessageService → ChannelGateway → MessageService
// (via ChannelGateway.receiveHumanMessage / receiveObserverSignal).
// Both are @ApplicationScoped (normal scope). Arc resolves via client proxies —
// verified by full build and @QuarkusTest suite.
@Inject
ChannelGateway channelGateway;
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Most developers associate "CDI cycle" with startup failure. The distinction — pseudo-scoped vs normal-scoped — is in the spec but rarely surfaced in error messages or tutorials. The symptom that triggered the concern (a code reviewer calling it Critical) is exactly what skilled developers would say if they didn't know about proxy-based cycle resolution.

### Why this fix
A client proxy is the CDI-correct solution. Using `Instance<T>` (lazy injection) also works but adds indirection and a `.get()` call at every use site. Proxy resolution is transparent — callers don't change. Only use `Instance<T>` when a pseudo-scoped bean is in the cycle and proxy creation isn't possible.

**See also:** [GE-20260422-53d0f7](GE-20260422-53d0f7.md) — JPA @EntityListeners can be @ApplicationScoped CDI beans in Quarkus

**See also:** [GE-20260530-385dbb](GE-20260530-385dbb.md) — @Provider @ApplicationScoped on ClientRequestFilter bypasses CDI injection in Quarkus @RegisterRestClient

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
MessageService constructor injection cycle
CDI proxy resolution @ApplicationScoped
Quarkus Arc client proxy startup failure

entries.body:
Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean

## Context

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` beans from different JARs both implement the same interface. CDI can't resolve which to use and throws `AmbiguousResolutionException`. Standard approaches don't help:

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` is silently ignored for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs (see GE-20260601-848232)
- Marking one as `@Alternative` requires changes to a JAR you don't own
- `@Priority` on `@Alternative` has CDI 2.0 global-scope problems

## Technique

Add a concrete `@ApplicationScoped` bean to your project (production or test sources as appropriate) that implements the conflicting interface:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class ProjectGroupMembershipProvider implements GroupMembershipProvider {
    @Override
    public Set<GroupMember> membersOf(String groupName) {
        return Set.of(); // or delegate to preferred implementation
    }
}
```

CDI selects the most-specific non-default bean. Since your bean is NOT `@DefaultBean`, it wins over both competing `@DefaultBean` implementations and the `AmbiguousResolutionException` is resolved. No changes to any JAR required.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Most developers reach for `exclude-types` first (fails silently for Jandex-indexed JARs), then try `@Priority` on one of the `@DefaultBean` beans (requires modifying third-party JARs), then consider `@Alternative` + `selected-alternatives` (same problem). The CDI suppression rule — "a non-default bean beats all @DefaultBean candidates for the same type" — is the correct lever, and a thin adapter class is the minimal mechanism that activates it without touching any dependency.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex JARs | [GE-20260601-3dbc80](GE-20260601-3dbc80.md) — exclude-types as technique for @DefaultBean ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260601-7a3b38](GE-20260601-7a3b38.md) — @DefaultBean invisible when supertype JAR has no Jandex index

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

entries.title: CDI @Inject silently does nothing on plain Java objects owned by CDI beans — inject into the owning bean instead
CDI @Alternative reactive wrapper with private new Impl() delegate is a separate instance from the CDI bean — @AfterEach clear() silently targets the wrong object
entries.body:
CDI @Alternative reactive wrapper with private new Impl() delegate is a separate instance from the CDI bean — @AfterEach clear() silently targets the wrong object

### Symptom

`@AfterEach` calls `channelStore.clear()` on an injected CDI bean but state leaks between tests — subsequent tests see data from previous test runs despite the cleanup.

### Context

A Quarkus test class has:
```java
@Inject InMemoryChannelStore channelStore;   // CDI @Alternative @Priority(1)

@AfterEach void cleanUp() { channelStore.clear(); }
```
A reactive wrapper bean also exists:
```java
@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped
public class InMemoryReactiveChannelStore implements ReactiveChannelStore {
    private final InMemoryChannelStore delegate = new InMemoryChannelStore();
    ...
}
```

### Root cause

`InMemoryReactiveChannelStore` creates its delegate via `new InMemoryChannelStore()` — plain Java instantiation, not CDI injection (`@Inject`). The CDI container manages:
- One `InMemoryChannelStore` bean (injected into the test)
- One `InMemoryReactiveChannelStore` bean (used by reactive services)

The reactive wrapper's `delegate` field is a **third, separate object** — not the CDI bean. Services injecting `ReactiveChannelStore` write to the wrapper's private delegate. `clear()` on the CDI `InMemoryChannelStore` bean clears the wrong instance.

### Fix

Inject the type that the actual service uses:
```java
// If service uses blockingChannelService → ChannelStore:
@Inject InMemoryChannelStore channelStore;        // correct for blocking path

// If service uses ReactiveChannelStore:
@Inject InMemoryReactiveChannelStore channelStore; // has its own clear()
```

Verify which path the service under test takes by reading its source — field type determines which CDI bean it receives.

### Why this is non-obvious

Both `InMemoryChannelStore` and `InMemoryReactiveChannelStore` are `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(1)` CDI beans — they appear symmetric. The internal `new InMemoryChannelStore()` delegation is an implementation detail only visible in source code. `clear()` returns void and throws no error, so state leakage is the only signal — and that's often masked by test ordering or unique identifiers.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---

reactive wrapper delegate instance

entries.title: @Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection, making bean ordering undefined
entries.body:
@Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection, making bean ordering undefined

## @Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection

### Symptom

Bean iteration order from `Instance<T>` is silently non-deterministic despite
`@Priority` annotations on all implementations. Sorting by
`resolver.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)` returns `null` for every
bean, so all beans get `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and ordering is undefined.

### Context

When iterating CDI beans from `Instance<T>` and sorting by `@Priority` using
Java reflection. Common in composite/pipeline patterns where multiple
implementations of an SPI must execute in a defined order.

### Root cause

`@jakarta.annotation.Priority` is not meta-annotated with `@java.lang.annotation.Inherited`.
CDI proxy classes (e.g. `WebDIDResolver_ClientProxy`) are JDK subclasses of the
real bean class. `proxy.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)` returns `null`
because the JDK only propagates annotations marked `@Inherited` to subclasses.

The proxy class itself carries no annotations — it is a synthetic subclass
generated by the CDI container solely for interception and scoping purposes.

### What was tried (didn't work)

```java
// Natural reflection approach — silently fails for all proxied beans
private static int priorityOf(DIDResolver resolver) {
    var priority = resolver.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class);
    return priority != null ? priority.value() : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    // Always returns MAX_VALUE for proxied beans
}
```

### Fix

Use Quarkus Arc's `Instance.Handle` API to read bean metadata through the
CDI container rather than through reflection on the proxy class:

```java
@Inject
public CompositeDIDResolver(@DIDMethod Instance<DIDResolver> methodResolvers) {
    this.resolvers = methodResolvers.handles().stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(h -> priorityOf(h)))
            .map(Instance.Handle::get)
            .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());
}

private static int priorityOf(Instance.Handle<?> handle) {
    var bean = handle.getBean();
    if (bean instanceof InjectableBean<?> injectable) {
        Integer p = injectable.getPriority();
        if (p != null) return p;
    }
    return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
}
```

Arc stores priority metadata at container build time (augmentation), independent
of proxy reflection. `InjectableBean.getPriority()` reads this stored value.

### Why this is non-obvious

`getClass().getAnnotation()` is the natural Java reflection approach for reading
annotations. It works for many annotations and in many contexts. The `@Inherited`
requirement is a JDK detail that only matters when the object is a subclass of
the annotated class — a situation that is universal in CDI (every injected bean
is potentially proxied) but rarely encountered in direct reflection usage.

The failure is silent: no exception, no warning. The annotation simply isn't
found, and the fallback value (typically `Integer.MAX_VALUE` or a default
priority) is used for every bean, making ordering non-deterministic.

### Alternatives considered

- **Walk superclass chain:** `resolver.getClass().getSuperclass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)`
  — works for single-level proxies but fragile if proxy depth changes or if
  the container uses a different proxy strategy.
- **`@All List<InstanceHandle<T>>`:** Quarkus-specific injection that preserves
  metadata — equivalent to `Instance.handles()` but declared at the injection site.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
What is the effect of @Inherited missing on CDI proxy classes?
How does reflection fail to read @Priority annotations on proxied beans?
Why does sorting CDI beans by @Priority return Integer.MAX_VALUE?

entries.title: CDI @Alternative @Priority on a subclass of a framework-internal @ApplicationScoped bean causes Quarkus augmentation failure
entries.body:
CDI @Alternative @Priority on a subclass of a framework-internal @ApplicationScoped bean causes Quarkus augmentation failure

## Symptom

`ExceptionInInitializerError` → `NoClassDefFoundError` for a class that is NOT directly
referenced by the subclass (e.g. `PostgreSQLAgroalConnectionConfigurer`). The error occurs
during Quarkus augmentation (`quarkus:build` phase), not at runtime.

## Context

Creating a CDI `@Alternative @Priority(1)` subclass of a framework-internal
`@ApplicationScoped` bean to override a single method. The superclass has `@Inject`
fields whose dependency chain includes optional extensions not on the classpath.

Example: subclassing `SchedulerService` (casehub-engine internal) to override
`registerScheduledTriggers()`. The superclass injects `JobScheduler`, whose Quartz
implementation transitively references `PostgreSQLAgroalConnectionConfigurer`. Even
though the subclass overrides the method that uses those dependencies, Quarkus
augmentation resolves the entire dependency chain of the `@Alternative` bean at
build time.

## Root cause

Quarkus Arc CDI resolves all injection points of a bean at augmentation time (build
phase), not lazily at first use. When an `@Alternative` subclass is registered, Arc
resolves ALL inherited `@Inject` fields — including those from the superclass that
the override will never call. If any transitive dependency in that chain is not on
the classpath, augmentation fails with `NoClassDefFoundError`.

## Fix

Do not subclass framework-internal beans with `@Alternative`. Instead:
- Provide a no-op implementation of the SPI the internal bean consumes (if the SPI
  exists and is public)
- Or file an issue on the framework to make the internal behavior configurable
- Or use `@InjectMock` (quarkus-junit5-mockito) for test-only overrides

## Why this is non-obvious

The `@Alternative` subclass compiles cleanly. The superclass is `public`. The method
being overridden is `public`. The failure occurs at augmentation time with a class
name from a completely different module (PostgreSQL JDBC) that appears nowhere in
the subclass code. The connection between "I subclassed SchedulerService" and
"PostgreSQLAgroalConnectionConfigurer not found" is invisible without understanding
Quarkus augmentation's eager dependency resolution.

**See also:** [GE-20260605-e42cc5](GE-20260605-e42cc5.md) — @Blocking on plain @ApplicationScoped method causes Quarkus test classloader failure | [GE-20260529-c4ed43](GE-20260529-c4ed43.md) — shared @ApplicationScoped CDI bean as algorithmic kernel across @Alternative @Priority strategy | [GE-20260513-4f26a7](../quarkus/GE-20260513-4f26a7.md) — @DefaultBean + plain @ApplicationScoped enables CDI layer displacement

entries.title: `@UnlessBuildProfile` on a bean causes "Unsatisfied dependency" in any bean that injects it without a matching profile guard
entries.body:
`@UnlessBuildProfile` on a bean causes "Unsatisfied dependency" in any bean that injects it without a matching profile guard

## `@UnlessBuildProfile` on a bean causes "Unsatisfied dependency" in any bean that injects it without a matching profile guard

**ID:** GE-0066
**Stack:** Quarkus 3.x, Quarkus Arc (all versions with profile-based CDI)
**Symptom:** Adding `@UnlessBuildProfile("X")` to bean `A` causes every other bean that injects `A` directly (not via `Instance<A>`) to fail at startup in profile `X` with: `Unsatisfied dependency for type A and qualifiers [@Default]`. The failure is a CDI build-time error — the application doesn't even start.
**Context:** Any Quarkus application using profile-based CDI exclusion where the excluded bean is injected by profile-unguarded consumers.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Added `@UnlessBuildProfile("sc2")` to `SimulatedGame`
- `CaseFileResource` and `IntentResource` still injected `SimulatedGame` directly
- Application failed to start in `%sc2` profile with "Unsatisfied dependency"

### Root cause

Quarkus Arc resolves CDI injection points at build time. When a bean is excluded via `@UnlessBuildProfile`, it disappears from the CDI graph entirely in that profile. Any other bean with a direct `@Inject SimulatedGame` field becomes invalid — the injection point has no candidate. Unlike Spring's conditional beans (which produce null), Quarkus treats this as a deployment error.

### Fix

Two options depending on intent:

**Option 1 — Also guard the consumer** (if the consumer is also profile-specific):
```java
@UnlessBuildProfile("sc2")  // same guard as the dependency
@ApplicationScoped
public class CaseFileResource { ... }
```

**Option 2 — Switch to `Instance<T>` injection** (if the consumer must exist in all profiles):
```java
@Inject Instance<SimulatedGame> simulatedGame;  // optional injection

public void doWork() {
    if (simulatedGame.isResolvable()) {
        simulatedGame.get().tick();
    }
}
```

`Instance<T>` is CDI's optional injection mechanism — `isResolvable()` returns false when the bean doesn't exist in the current profile. The injection point itself is always valid.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error looks like a misconfiguration ("why can't it find SimulatedGame?") rather than a profile design issue. Developers familiar with Spring's `@ConditionalOnProfile` expect null or a default fallback, not a hard startup failure. The `Instance<T>` pattern is the correct CDI solution but requires knowing it exists.

*Score: 13/15 · Included because: hard startup failure with a misleading error message, combined with wrong mental model from Spring experience · Reservation: none identified*

**See also:** [GE-20260424-e9df70](GE-20260424-e9df70.md) — library JPA repository without @ApplicationScoped causes same UnsatisfiedResolutionException symptom

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`@UnlessBuildProfile("sc2")` causes "Unsatisfied dependency"
`Unsatisfied dependency for type A and qualifiers [@Default]`
`profile-based CDI exclusion`

entries.title: Multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException for the bean itself, not a constructor
entries.body:
Multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException for the bean itself, not a constructor

### Symptom
Quarkus startup fails with:
```
UnsatisfiedResolutionException: Unsatisfied dependency for type io.example.MyBean and qualifiers [@Default]
```
The bean class exists on the classpath, all its constructor parameter types exist, and it is annotated with `@ApplicationScoped`. No warning about constructors appears.

### Context
The bean has two constructors: one for CDI injection (using `@All List<X>` or `Event<Y>`) and one package-private constructor for unit tests (accepting simpler types). Neither constructor is annotated with `@Inject`.

### Root cause
CDI requires exactly one constructor annotated with `@Inject` when a class has multiple constructors. If none is annotated, CDI falls back to looking for a no-arg constructor. When no no-arg constructor exists, CDI reports the failure as "Unsatisfied dependency for the bean type" — not as "no suitable constructor found." The error message points at the injection point in the *caller*, not at the bean's constructor, making it look like the bean is absent from the CDI context.

### Fix
Annotate exactly one constructor with `@Inject` — the one intended for CDI use:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class InboundConnectorService {

@Inject  // ← required when multiple constructors exist
    InboundConnectorService(@All List<InboundConnector> connectors,
                            Event<InboundMessage> messageEvent) {
        this(connectors, messageEvent::fire);
    }

// Test constructor — no @Inject
    InboundConnectorService(List<InboundConnector> connectors,
                            Consumer<InboundMessage> eventBus) { ... }
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The error message says the *bean* is unsatisfied, not that its constructor is unusable. A developer familiar with the technology checks: Is the bean annotated? Is it on the classpath? Is Jandex indexing it? All answers are yes. The actual cause — no `@Inject` on the right constructor — is invisible in the error. Debugging time is wasted checking classpath, module boundaries, and Jandex configuration before the constructor annotation is noticed.

### Why this fix
CDI's fallback to no-arg when `@Inject` is absent is documented behaviour, but the error emitted when no no-arg exists is a bean-level "unsatisfied dependency" rather than a constructor-level error. Adding `@Inject` is the minimal fix; the alternative (providing a no-arg constructor) would require CDI-unfriendly field injection or a proxy-unsafe no-op default.

### Alternatives considered
- Using field injection with `@Inject` — avoids the constructor problem but breaks testability (can't use constructor injection in pure JUnit tests without CDI)
- Adding a no-arg constructor — CDI would use it, but then there is no way to inject dependencies without field injection

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for same type → AmbiguousResolutionException

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260607-3611a2](GE-20260607-3611a2.md) — Preferences is not a CDI bean — inject PreferenceProvider

**See also:** [GE-20260604-4bfd2c](GE-20260604-4bfd2c.md) — adding package-private test constructor to CDI field-injected bean removes implicit no-arg

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`UnsatisfiedResolutionException MyBean @Inject`
`CDI multiple constructors no @Inject`
`ApplicationScoped constructor @Inject`

casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409
entries.body:
casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409

### Symptom

REST endpoint returns HTTP 409 Conflict instead of the expected 500 Internal Server Error.
Happens when application code throws `IllegalStateException` for an infrastructure failure
(poll timeout, misconfiguration, unresolvable dependency).

### Context

Any application that depends on `casehub-work` and throws `IllegalStateException` from a
REST-invoked code path.

### Root cause

`casehub-work` JAR ships `io.casehub.work.runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper` — a
`jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper<IllegalStateException>` that maps every
`IllegalStateException` to HTTP 409 Conflict. The mapper is registered globally via CDI
and affects any `IllegalStateException` thrown during a REST request in the application,
not just ones thrown from casehub-work code itself.

### Fix

Use a different exception type for infrastructure failures that should produce 500:

```java
// ❌ Produces HTTP 409 — mapped by casehub-work's IllegalStateExceptionMapper
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);

// ✅ Produces HTTP 500 — no mapper for generic RuntimeException
throw new RuntimeException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);
```

Alternatively, register a `@Priority(1)` exception mapper that overrides casehub-work's
for specific exception subtypes, or use a custom exception class that extends
`RuntimeException` directly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The mapper is shipped inside a transitive JAR (`casehub-work-0.2-SNAPSHOT.jar`) and is
nowhere documented. The symptom (409 instead of 500) gives no hint that an exception
mapper is involved — 409 Conflict is semantically about resource state, so developers
naturally investigate their domain logic rather than exception infrastructure. The 5-second
delay before the 409 (from a poll timeout) makes the connection even harder to spot.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`IllegalStateExceptionMapper` `jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper`
`casehub-work` `HTTP 409`
`runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper`

entries.title: static new ObjectMapper() silently fails to serialize Instant in Quarkus — use @Inject ObjectMapper
entries.body:
static new ObjectMapper() silently fails to serialize Instant in Quarkus — use @Inject ObjectMapper

## Symptom

An SSE endpoint (or any endpoint) that serialises `SessionResponse` objects silently returns `[]` (empty array) instead of the actual workers. No exception is visible to the caller — the exception is caught internally and the fallback value is returned. The server logs may show a `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.exc.InvalidDefinitionException` at DEBUG level.

## Context

`SessionResource` in Claudony had:
```java
private static final ObjectMapper MAPPER = new ObjectMapper();
```

`SessionResponse` contains `Instant createdAt` and `Instant lastActive`. Serializing a `List<SessionResponse>` through this `MAPPER` threw:
```
com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.exc.InvalidDefinitionException:
Java 8 date/time type `java.time.Instant` not supported by default:
add Module "com.fasterxml.jackson.datatype:jackson-datatype-jsr310"
```

The exception was caught in the `buildCaseSnapshot` helper and the fallback `"data: []"` was returned silently.

## Root Cause

`new ObjectMapper()` creates a bare instance with no modules registered. Quarkus configures its CDI-managed `ObjectMapper` bean with `JavaTimeModule` (and other modules like `Jdk8Module`) automatically. A static field bypasses this configuration.

## Fix

Replace the static field with CDI injection:

```java
// WRONG — no JavaTimeModule
private static final ObjectMapper MAPPER = new ObjectMapper();

// CORRECT — uses Quarkus-configured instance with all modules
@Inject
ObjectMapper MAPPER;
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The class had a `static final` `ObjectMapper` that worked fine for other uses (simple POJOs without time fields). The failure only surfaced when the snapshot function started serialising `SessionResponse` with `Instant` fields. Because the exception was caught with a fallback, the endpoint returned valid JSON (`[]`) — not an error — making it very hard to notice.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`Jackson InvalidDefinitionException Instant`
`Quarkus ObjectMapper JavaTimeModule`
`static ObjectMapper serialization failure`

entries.title: Maven child POM missing snapshotRepository causes SNAPSHOT deploy to parent's registry (403)
entries.body:
Maven child POM missing snapshotRepository causes SNAPSHOT deploy to parent's registry (403)

## Symptom

`mvn deploy` on a SNAPSHOT version fails with `403 Forbidden` when deploying a child module. The error URL points to the *parent* POM's registry, not the child's. CI succeeds for release versions but fails for SNAPSHOTs.

```
Could not transfer artifact io.example:child-parent:pom:0.2-20260427.144117-1
  from/to github (https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/parent-repo): 403 Forbidden
```

## Context

Child POM has a `distributionManagement` block with `<repository>` (releases) but no `<snapshotRepository>`. Parent POM has both pointing to the parent's registry. The CI token only has write access to the child's registry.

## Root cause

Maven uses `<repository>` for release versions and `<snapshotRepository>` for SNAPSHOT versions. When `<snapshotRepository>` is absent from the child POM, Maven inherits it from the parent — which points to a different registry (the parent's). The token cannot write there → 403.

## Fix

Explicitly declare both elements in the child's `distributionManagement`:

```xml
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>github</id>
    <url>https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/child-repo</url>
  </repository>
  <snapshotRepository>
    <id>github</id>
    <url>https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/child-repo</url>
  </snapshotRepository>
</distributionManagement>
```

## Why this is non-obvious

Maven's `<repository>` and `<snapshotRepository>` are independent settings that inherit separately. A child POM that defines `<repository>` still inherits `<snapshotRepository>` from the parent. The 403 error message shows the wrong URL (the parent's), which points to a permissions problem rather than a configuration problem — leading developers to investigate token scopes first.

**See also:** [GE-20260426-840309](GE-20260426-840309.md) — mvn deploy fails on first SNAPSHOT publish to GitHub Packages | [GE-20260426-ad8f5a](GE-20260426-ad8f5a.md) — root parent POM must be deployed even when maven.deploy.skip=true

**See also:** GE-20260428-1ad5c4 "GitHub Actions fork CI deploys to upstream registry using GITHUB_TOKEN — unconditional mvn deploy fails"
**See also:** GE-20260426-d58530 — GitHub Packages silently accepts uploads to non-existent repository paths
**See also:** [GE-20260426-3e6b29 — maven-deploy-plugin retryFailedDeploymentCount retries with zero delay — useless for GitHub Packages first-upload](GE-20260426-3e6b29.md)

**See also:** [GE-20260428-f94886](GE-20260428-f94886.md) — setup-java server-id only wires credentials for exact repository id | [GE-20260619-31e6e4](GE-20260619-31e6e4.md) — GitHub Packages Maven registry does not follow repo name redirects

entries.title: GitHub Packages npm private visibility returns 403 — looks like auth but is a visibility setting
entries.body:
GitHub Packages npm private visibility returns 403 — looks like auth but is a visibility setting

### Symptom
`yarn install` in CI returns 403 Forbidden when resolving `@casehubio/pages-primitives@^0.2.2`
from `npm.pkg.github.com`. The `GH_PACKAGES_TOKEN` is set (shows `***` in logs). Error looks
identical to an auth failure.

### Context
Cross-repo npm consumption: `casehubio/blocks-ui` consumes packages published by
`casehubio/casehub-pages`. Both repos in the same GitHub org. CI uses `GITHUB_TOKEN`
(repo-scoped) for npm auth.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Verified token was set and masked in CI logs — confirmed present
- Changed `GH_PACKAGES_TOKEN` from `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` to `secrets.GH_PACKAGES_TOKEN || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` — still 403
- Assumed it was a cross-org token scope issue

### Root cause
GitHub Packages npm packages default to **private** visibility. A private package cannot be
read by `GITHUB_TOKEN` from another repository, even within the same org. The 403 is not an
auth failure — it's a visibility restriction.

### Fix
Check package visibility:
```bash
gh api '/orgs/<org>/packages?package_type=npm' --jq '.[] | "\(.name): \(.visibility)"'
```

Two options:
1. **Make packages public** via GitHub UI (Settings page per package) — no API exists
2. **Use a classic PAT** with `read:packages` scope, stored as a repo secret

### Why this is non-obvious
The 403 response is indistinguishable from an authentication failure. Nothing in the error
message, response headers, or CI logs indicates visibility is the cause. The GitHub docs
mention visibility settings but don't connect them to the cross-repo 403 symptom. You can
spend hours checking token scopes, registry URLs, and workflow permissions before discovering
the packages are simply private.

### Why this fix
Making packages public is simplest for open-source repos. The PAT approach works for private
repos but adds secret management overhead. There is no API to change visibility — it must be
done per-package in the GitHub UI.

### Alternatives considered
- Using `GITHUB_TOKEN` with elevated permissions — doesn't work; repo-scoped tokens cannot
  read private packages from other repos regardless of permissions
- Organization-level secrets — helps with secret distribution but still needs a PAT value

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`yarn install` 403 private visibility
`GH_PACKAGES_TOKEN` npm package scope
GitHub Packages npm private package

With `.whenComplete()`: exception preserved on the stage → `thenCompose` skips its lambda
→ exception surfaces to SmallRye → message nacked → retried or dead-lettered.

Rule 3 applies **only in pure fire-and-forget dispatch** (the `CompletionStage` is not
returned or chained further).

CDI `@ObservesAsync` adapters are always fire-and-forget.
