entries.title: Jackson readValue() silently accepts trailing content unless FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS is enabled
entries.body:
Jackson readValue() silently accepts trailing content unless FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS is enabled

## Context

When using `ObjectMapper.readValue()` to parse a JSON string, Jackson does NOT reject trailing non-JSON content by default. The parse succeeds and the trailing content is silently discarded.

```java
// This succeeds silently — "extra text" is ignored
Map<String, Object> result = mapper.readValue(
    "{\"key\": \"value\"} extra text here",
    Map.class
);
// result = {"key": "value"}
```

## Symptom

A detection method intended to reject `{"type":"DONE","content":"ok"} explanatory text` accepts it as valid JSON and extracts `{"type":"DONE","content":"ok"}` — the trailing text never causes an error.

The practical failure: an LLM output like `{"type":"DONE","content":"Task complete"} I've now finished the task.` is silently classified as a JSON speech act rather than falling through to bracket-prefix detection, producing unexpected DONE classification when the agent was narrating.

## Root Cause

Jackson's `JsonParser` stops at the end of the first complete JSON value and considers the parse successful. `readValue()` wraps this and makes the trailing content invisible. This is the specified behaviour — Jackson is designed for streaming contexts where trailing content is normal.

## Fix

Enable `DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS` on the `ObjectMapper`:

```java
private static final ObjectMapper MAPPER = new ObjectMapper()
        .enable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS);
```

With this flag set, `readValue("{\"key\":\"val\"} extra", Map.class)` throws `JsonParseException: Trailing token (of type START_OBJECT) found after value`. Catching the exception and falling through to the next detection tier is then correct.

## Why this is non-obvious

Jackson's docs describe `FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS` as an option to opt into, not a default-off footgun. The lenient default exists for good reasons (streaming, multi-value streams), but it's invisible when you have a one-shot string parse and expect strict behaviour. The feature was added in Jackson 2.9 — older documentation doesn't mention it. Without knowing to look for it, the obvious assumption is that `readValue()` of a complete JSON string validates the full input.

### Why this fix

`FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS` is the canonical solution — it targets exactly this behaviour without affecting normal parsing. Alternative: use `JsonParser` directly and check `parser.nextToken() == null` after parse, but this requires more boilerplate and is less obvious to readers.

### Alternatives considered

- **Use `JsonParser` directly** — check `parser.nextToken() == null` after reading the value. More boilerplate; requires try-with-resources pattern and is less discoverable.
- **Check `input.trim().endsWith("}")` before parsing** — fragile; fails for arrays, nested objects, and JSON with trailing whitespace.
- **Regex pre-check** — would reject valid multi-line JSON. Not viable.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
readValue extra text
FAIL_ON_TRAILING_TOKENS error
JsonParseException trailing token

entries.title: Probe delete permission with a nonexistent resource ID — 404 means authorised, 403 means denied
entries.body:
Probe delete permission with a nonexistent resource ID — 404 means authorised, 403 means denied

## What It Is

To test whether a token has delete permission on a resource without actually deleting anything, send a DELETE request to a known-nonexistent resource ID. The response reveals the permission check result:

- **404 Not Found** — the API checked authorisation first, passed, then looked up the resource and couldn't find it. **Permission confirmed.**
- **403 Forbidden** — the API rejected the request at the authorisation layer before even looking up the resource. **Permission denied.**

## Context

Useful when writing diagnostic scripts that need to verify delete scope on a token without side effects, and when no safe "list my permissions" endpoint exists. Works for any REST API that performs authorisation before existence checks (GitHub, most well-designed APIs).

## Example — GitHub Packages

```bash
http_code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  -X DELETE \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GH_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  "https://api.github.com/orgs/$ORG/packages/maven/__probe_nonexistent__/versions/0")

if [ "$http_code" = "404" ]; then
  echo "✓ delete:packages — permission confirmed"
elif [ "$http_code" = "403" ] || [ "$http_code" = "401" ]; then
  echo "✗ delete:packages — permission denied"
fi
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Most developers either (a) check permissions by trying a real delete and accepting the risk, (b) look for a permissions endpoint that often doesn't exist, or (c) inspect the token's OAuth scopes via response headers. This approach requires knowing that well-designed APIs check auth before existence — and that 404 therefore implies authorisation was granted.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $GH_TOKEN" "https://api.github.com/orgs/$ORG/packages/maven/__probe_nonexistent__/versions/0" http_code
404 Not Found permission check
403 Forbidden permission denied

entries.title: Maven Central 403 from GitHub Actions resolved by forcing BOM download before GitHub Packages auth
entries.body:
Maven Central 403 from GitHub Actions resolved by forcing BOM download before GitHub Packages auth

### What happened

`casehubio/aml` CI failed with `403 Forbidden` from Maven Central when downloading the Quarkus platform BOM:

```
Could not transfer artifact io.quarkus.platform:quarkus-bom:pom:3.32.2 from/to central
(https://repo.maven.apache.org/maven2): status code: 403
```

The artifact exists on Maven Central (200 from curl on any residential IP). Other repos in the same org (engine, ledger) were green simultaneously.

### Root cause

The AML repo had no `<dependencyManagement>` in its own `pom.xml` — it relied entirely on the parent POM (in GitHub Packages) for the Quarkus BOM import. Maven's resolution order was:

1. Download `casehub-parent` from GitHub Packages (Bearer token sent)
2. Parent POM imports `quarkus-bom` — Maven tries Maven Central **while the GitHub auth session is live**

Peer repos (engine, ledger) defined their own `<dependencyManagement>` with a local version property, so Maven resolved `quarkus-bom` from Central **before** contacting GitHub Packages — no auth header contamination.

The hypothesis: Maven's HTTP connection pool or CloudFlare's bot detection caused the Central request to receive the GitHub Bearer token, resulting in a 403. Evidence: 100ms failure vs 150ms success, identical workflows, simultaneous green on other repos.

### Fix

Add the BOM import directly to the consuming module's root `pom.xml` with a **locally-defined** version property:

```xml
<properties>
  <!-- Pinned locally so Maven resolves quarkus-bom from central BEFORE
       contacting GitHub Packages for casehub-parent. Without this, Maven
       downloads GitHub Packages first (with Bearer token), then hits Central
       while the auth session is live — causing 403. -->
  <quarkus.platform.version>3.32.2</quarkus.platform.version>
</properties>

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.quarkus.platform</groupId>
      <artifactId>quarkus-bom</artifactId>
      <version>${quarkus.platform.version}</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

Using a **local** property (not inherited from parent) means Maven can resolve the BOM version without downloading the parent first, so the Central download happens cold — before any GitHub Packages connection.

### Why this is non-obvious

The symptom looks like a Maven Central outage or IP ban. Other repos with identical workflows pass. The fix requires understanding Maven's resolution ordering with parent POM inheritance vs local property resolution — a distinction that rarely matters in single-repo projects.

### Constraints

Applies when: repo uses GitHub Packages wildcard URL (`https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/*`) requiring Bearer auth, AND parent POM (in GitHub Packages) contains the BOM import, AND child module has no local BOM import. The local property creates a maintenance burden: must stay in sync with the parent's version when bumping Quarkus.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus-bom:pom:3.32.2
casehubio/aml 403 Forbidden
dependencyManagement quarkus-bom version

entries.title: GitHub Actions GITHUB_TOKEN for fork PRs gets packages:read regardless of workflow permissions declaration
entries.body:
GitHub Actions GITHUB_TOKEN for fork PRs gets packages:read regardless of workflow permissions declaration

### Symptom
`mvn deploy` to GitHub Packages fails with `403 Forbidden` on a merged PR. The workflow declares `permissions: packages: write`. Previous PRs published successfully.

### Context
PR is from a fork (`user/repo` → `org/repo`). The workflow uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` for the deploy step. The publish step is conditioned on `pull_request && merged == true`.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Verifying workflow permissions block — correctly declares `packages: write`
- Checking GitHub Packages settings — repository allows publishing

### Root cause
GitHub silently downgrades `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions for `pull_request` events originating from forks. The token gets `packages: read` regardless of the workflow's `permissions` declaration. This is a documented GitHub security measure to prevent fork PRs from publishing malicious packages. The CI job log shows the actual permissions under "GITHUB_TOKEN Permissions" in the "Set up job" step.

Previous PRs worked because they were from same-repo branches (not forks), which get the full declared permissions.

### Fix
Use `push` trigger instead of `pull_request closed+merged` for the publish step. When a PR is merged, GitHub fires both a `pull_request(closed)` event AND a `push` event to the target branch. The `push` event gets full declared permissions including `packages: write`.

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]    # fires on merge — full permissions
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]  # removed 'closed'
    branches: [main]
```

Publish/downstream steps condition on `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`.

### Why this is non-obvious
The 403 appears only for fork PRs. Same-repo PRs work fine, creating a false sense that the workflow is correct. The permission downgrade is silent — no warning before the deploy step fails.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`GITHUB_TOKEN packages:read fork PR`
`mvn deploy 403 GITHUB_TOKEN`
`GitHub Packages permission downgrade`

entries.title: ConcurrentHashMap.put() rejects null values — breaks fault-tolerance catch blocks that use e.getMessage()
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.put() rejects null values — breaks fault-tolerance catch blocks that use e.getMessage()

## What Happened

A cross-backend aggregator catches all contributor exceptions to return partial results (HTTP 200 always). The catch block stores the error reason in a `ConcurrentHashMap<String, String>`. For any exception type with no message string (`new NullPointerException()`, `new UnsupportedOperationException()`), `e.getMessage()` returns null. `ConcurrentHashMap.put(key, null)` throws `NullPointerException`. The very exception handler designed to prevent failures now causes one, breaking the "always return 200" contract.

## Why This Is Non-obvious

The code reads as defensive: it catches `Exception`, logs, and stores the reason. The bug is that `ConcurrentHashMap` is one of the few `Map` implementations that rejects both null keys AND null values (unlike `HashMap`, which accepts both). Developers familiar with `HashMap` don't expect this. The NPE stack trace points at the `warnings.put()` call, not at `e.getMessage()`, which further misleads.

## Fix

```java
// In the catch block:
final String reason = e.getMessage() != null
    ? e.getMessage()
    : e.getClass().getSimpleName();
accumulator.markFailed(sourceName, reason);
```

Or guard at the `put` site:
```java
map.put(key, Objects.requireNonNullElse(e.getMessage(), e.getClass().getSimpleName()));
```

## Constraints

Applies to any `ConcurrentHashMap` (and `Hashtable`). `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeMap` all accept null values and would silently succeed.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
ConcurrentHashMap null value rejection
ConcurrentHashMap put null key exception
NullPointerException e.getMessage() ConcurrentHashMap

quarkus.http.auth.permission.*.policy=deny on /* blocks ALL requests — @RolesAllowed becomes unreachable dead code
entries.body:
quarkus.http.auth.permission.*.policy=deny on /* blocks ALL requests — @RolesAllowed becomes unreachable dead code

### Symptom
Every endpoint returns 403. Always. Regardless of authentication status, role, or `@RolesAllowed` annotation. The application is completely non-functional.

### Context
When adding OIDC + `@RolesAllowed` to a Quarkus application, a natural instinct is to add a catch-all deny policy so missing annotations fail closed:
```properties
quarkus.http.auth.permission.default.paths=/*
quarkus.http.auth.permission.default.policy=deny
```

### What was tried (didn't work)
The above configuration. Also tried adding `/q/*` health exemptions — the deny policy still blocks all application endpoints.

### Root cause
`quarkus.http.auth.permission.*` policies operate at the **Vert.x HTTP filter layer** — before the JAX-RS container processes the request and before CDI security interceptors run. A `deny` policy on `/*` rejects all requests at that filter, regardless of authentication status, role, or any `@RolesAllowed` annotation. `@RolesAllowed` is never evaluated — it is unreachable dead code.

Additionally, `quarkus.security.auth.enabled-in-dev-mode=false` (which suppresses `@RolesAllowed` evaluation in dev mode) does **not** suppress HTTP permission policies — those are at the `io.quarkus.vertx.http.runtime.security` layer, not the CDI authorization controller layer. Dev mode is also completely broken.

### Fix
Do not use `quarkus.http.auth.permission.*.policy=deny` as a catch-all. Use the JAX-RS-layer mechanism instead:
```properties
quarkus.security.deny-unannotated-members=true
```
This operates inside the JAX-RS container after authentication. `@RolesAllowed` annotations remain fully functional. It is suppressed in dev mode by `auth.enabled-in-dev-mode=false` (same CDI authorization controller layer).

### Why this is non-obvious
The two security layers (Vert.x HTTP filter vs CDI/JAX-RS interceptor) are not clearly distinguished in the Quarkus documentation. Both use `quarkus.` config prefixes. The HTTP permission approach looks like a standard deny-by-default pattern and produces no startup warning — the 403s only appear at runtime.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
quarkus http permission deny all requests
quarkus http auth permission policy deny /*
@RolesAllowed annotation unreachable dead code

JAX-RS @QueryParam endpoint silently ignores JSON request body — body field name is irrelevant
entries.body:
JAX-RS @QueryParam endpoint silently ignores JSON request body — body field name is irrelevant

### Symptom
REST endpoint returns 400 with "claimantId is required" even when the request body contains `{"claimantId":"alice"}`. Changing the body field name from `assigneeId` to `claimantId` has no effect — error persists.

### Context
JAX-RS endpoint uses `@QueryParam("claimant")` to read the caller identity — no `@RequestBody` or `@Body` annotation. A RestAssured test sends the value as a JSON body instead of a query parameter.

### What was tried
Changed the JSON body field name from `"assigneeId"` to `"claimantId"` — still failed with the same error.

### Root cause
`@QueryParam` reads exclusively from the URL query string. Any JSON body is silently discarded with no warning. The service receives `null` for the query param, triggering the "is required" validation — making the error message point to the field name rather than the mechanism.

### Fix

```java
// Wrong — body is ignored regardless of field name:
given().contentType(ContentType.JSON)
    .body("{\"claimantId\":\"alice\"}")
    .put("/workitems/" + id + "/claim")
    .then().statusCode(200);

// Correct:
given().queryParam("claimant", "alice")
    .put("/workitems/" + id + "/claim")
    .then().statusCode(200);
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The error message "claimantId is required" implicates the field name — not the transport mechanism. JAX-RS gives no indication that a body was sent and ignored. The natural fix (correcting the field name) fails silently, making the root cause opaque.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
JAX-RS @QueryParam ignores JSON body
JAX-RS query parameter vs body annotation
"claimantId is required" JAX-RS error

entries.title: java.net.http.HttpClient.send() does NOT throw for 4xx/5xx — returns HttpResponse with statusCode()
entries.body:
java.net.http.HttpClient.send() does NOT throw for 4xx/5xx — returns HttpResponse with statusCode()

## Symptom

HTTP GET responses with 4xx or 5xx status codes are processed as if they were successful. No exception is thrown. Error body bytes (HTML error pages, JSON error responses) are silently treated as valid response data.

## Context

Polling arbitrary URLs with `java.net.http.HttpClient` and using the response body as data. The code has a `try/catch (IOException e)` block around the `send()` call expecting to catch failed requests.

## Root Cause

`HttpClient.send()` signature:
```java
public abstract <T> HttpResponse<T> send(HttpRequest request, HttpResponse.BodyHandler<T> handler)
    throws IOException, InterruptedException;
```

`IOException` is thrown only for **connection-level failures**: DNS resolution failure, TCP connection errors, connection timeout, SSL handshake failure. A 4xx or 5xx HTTP response is a **successful HTTP exchange** from the network perspective — the server received the request and returned a response. `send()` returns the response with `response.statusCode()` set to the error code; no exception is thrown.

## Fix

Always check the status code explicitly after `send()`:

```java
HttpResponse<byte[]> response = httpClient.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofByteArray());
if (response.statusCode() < 200 || response.statusCode() >= 300) {
    throw new IOException("HTTP " + response.statusCode() + " for " + url);
}
// 2xx: use response.body() safely
byte[] data = response.body();
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

`java.net.http.HttpClient` differs from many older HTTP client libraries (Apache HttpClient, OkHttp) that DO throw exceptions for 4xx/5xx by default. Developers migrating from those libraries or relying on exception-based error handling will miss error responses entirely. The consequence — error body bytes silently processed as valid data — can corrupt downstream pipelines with no log entry or observable failure.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
java.net.http.HttpClient send 4xx
HttpClient response statusCode()
IOException HttpClient send()

entries.title: Quarkus REST client interface with @Path at class level silently registers as a server resource — shadows the real endpoint
entries.body:
Quarkus REST client interface with @Path at class level silently registers as a server resource — shadows the real endpoint

## Quarkus REST client interface with @Path at class level silently registers as a server resource — shadows the real endpoint

**Stack:** Quarkus 3.36.x, RESTEasy Reactive

**Symptom:** After adding a REST client interface (for programmatic use with `QuarkusRestClientBuilder`), existing REST endpoint tests break with wrong HTTP status codes. Endpoints that should return 400 return 200 with empty arrays. Domain-filtered searches return no results. No error messages, no warnings in logs.

**Context:** Creating a JAX-RS interface for use as a programmatic REST client (not `@RegisterRestClient`). The interface has `@Path("/search")` at the class level and `@GET` on the method — identical annotations to the server resource.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Checked CDI wiring, federation config parsing, SearchResource code — all correct
- Verified the blank-query check was still in the `search()` method — it was
- Checked whether `quarkus-rest-client-jackson` dependency caused a conflict — it didn't

### Root cause

Quarkus REST discovers **any class or interface** annotated with `@Path` at the class level as a JAX-RS resource — including interfaces intended for client use only. When `RemoteGardenClient` (a public interface with `@Path("/search")` and `@GET`) was on the classpath, Quarkus generated a no-op implementation and registered it as a resource alongside the real `SearchResource`. The no-op implementation matched first for some requests, returning 200 with empty results instead of delegating to the real resource.

### Fix

Make the client interface **package-private** (not `public`) and move `@Path` to the method level:

```java
@Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
interface RemoteGardenClient {  // package-private — not discovered as a resource

@GET
    @Path("/search")  // method-level only
    List<SearchResult> search(
            @QueryParam("q") String query,
            @QueryParam("limit") int limit
    );
}
```

The `QuarkusRestClientBuilder.build(RemoteGardenClient.class)` still works — the builder reads method-level annotations for client-side request construction. It does not require class-level `@Path`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The symptom appears on the **real** endpoint, not the client interface. Nothing in the logs mentions a duplicate resource registration. The failure mode — wrong HTTP status codes on endpoints you didn't touch — gives zero indication that a client interface is involved. The natural debugging path (inspect SearchResource, check CDI, verify query parameter handling) leads nowhere.

### Why this fix

Making the interface package-private is cleaner than `@RegisterRestClient` (which would require CDI and config for a single-URL client) or removing class-level annotations entirely (which would require base URI to include the path). Package-private interfaces are invisible to Quarkus resource scanning while still usable by the programmatic client builder.

### Alternatives considered

- **`@RegisterRestClient`** — rejected because it creates a single CDI bean per interface, requiring `application.properties` config per URL. Programmatic creation via `QuarkusRestClientBuilder` is needed for N dynamic upstream URLs.
- **Removing all `@Path` annotations** — rejected because `QuarkusRestClientBuilder.build()` needs at least a method-level `@Path` to construct the request URL.

*Score: 12/15 · Included because: the symptom (wrong HTTP status on unrelated endpoints) is completely disconnected from the cause (a client interface being discovered as a server resource). Multiple debugging approaches fail before the root cause surfaces.*

**See also:** [GE-20260616-e15321](GE-20260616-e15321.md) — JAX-RS @Path annotation shadows io.casehub.platform.api.path.Path

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
RemoteGardenClient @Path("/search") class-level
Quarkus REST client @Path conflict
REST client interface no-op implementation

casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409
entries.body:
casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409

### Symptom

REST endpoint returns HTTP 409 Conflict instead of the expected 500 Internal Server Error.
Happens when application code throws `IllegalStateException` for an infrastructure failure
(poll timeout, misconfiguration, unresolvable dependency).

### Context

Any application that depends on `casehub-work` and throws `IllegalStateException` from a
REST-invoked code path.

### Root cause

`casehub-work` JAR ships `io.casehub.work.runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper` — a
`jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper<IllegalStateException>` that maps every
`IllegalStateException` to HTTP 409 Conflict. The mapper is registered globally via CDI
and affects any `IllegalStateException` thrown during a REST request in the application,
not just ones thrown from casehub-work code itself.

### Fix

Use a different exception type for infrastructure failures that should produce 500:

```java
// ❌ Produces HTTP 409 — mapped by casehub-work's IllegalStateExceptionMapper
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);

// ✅ Produces HTTP 500 — no mapper for generic RuntimeException
throw new RuntimeException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);
```

Alternatively, register a `@Priority(1)` exception mapper that overrides casehub-work's
for specific exception subtypes, or use a custom exception class that extends
`RuntimeException` directly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The mapper is shipped inside a transitive JAR (`casehub-work-0.2-SNAPSHOT.jar`) and is
nowhere documented. The symptom (409 instead of 500) gives no hint that an exception
mapper is involved — 409 Conflict is semantically about resource state, so developers
naturally investigate their domain logic rather than exception infrastructure. The 5-second
delay before the 409 (from a poll timeout) makes the connection even harder to spot.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`IllegalStateExceptionMapper` `jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper`
`casehub-work` `HTTP 409`
`runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper`

RestAssured percent-encodes `:` in URL paths, breaking JAX-RS routes like `/a2a/message:send`
entries.body:
RestAssured percent-encodes `:` in URL paths, breaking JAX-RS routes like `/a2a/message:send`

## Symptom

`given().when().post("/a2a/message:send").then().statusCode(501)` receives a 404 instead. The endpoint exists and starts correctly. Adding logging shows the request URL is `http://localhost:8081/a2a/message%3Asend`.

## Context

RestAssured's `.post(path)` and `.get(path)` methods apply percent-encoding to the path string by default. A literal `:` (colon) in a path segment is encoded to `%3A`. JAX-RS route matching is case-sensitive and literal — `@Path("/a2a/message:send")` does not match the inbound URI `/a2a/message%3Asend`.

This affects any A2A-style API path following Google's `collection:method` convention, RPC-over-REST patterns, or any path with a colon.

## What was tried

Quoting the colon, double-encoding, `given().baseUri(...)` — all still encode.

## Root cause

RFC 3986 §3.3 permits `:` (colon) in path segments after the first segment — it is not a reserved character in that position. RestAssured misapplies percent-encoding to it anyway.

## Fix

```java
given()
    .urlEncodingEnabled(false)   // ← suppress percent-encoding
    .contentType("application/json")
    .body(requestBody)
    .when().post("/a2a/message:send")
    .then().statusCode(200);
```

Apply `urlEncodingEnabled(false)` to every RestAssured call that hits a path containing a literal colon.

## Why this is non-obvious

The default assumption is that RestAssured handles URL construction correctly per RFC. The RFC explicitly permits the colon here, so the encoding is a RestAssured over-approximation. The symptom (404) gives no indication the URL is being rewritten — you only see it if you inspect RestAssured's request log.

### Why this fix

`urlEncodingEnabled(false)` disables all percent-encoding globally for that request. The alternative of pre-encoding the colon as `%3A` in the path string would cause double-encoding (`%253A`). The flag is the only clean option.

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
RestAssured percent-encode colon in URL
RestAssured JAX-RS route matching issue
`urlEncodingEnabled(false)` RestAssured fix

# REST Adapter Module

## Rule

When a library exposes HTTP endpoints, the REST layer lives in a separate
opt-in module — never in the core library module. Consumers include it by
adding a dependency; consumers who only need the Java SPI pay no JAX-RS
coupling cost.

```
my-library/
  api/              ← SPIs, domain types (Tier 1 — no framework deps)
  runtime/           ← services, entities (Tier 2/3 — no JAX-RS)
  rest/              ← JAX-RS resources, DTOs, exception mappers (opt-in)
```

The REST module is a plain JAR with CDI beans that carry JAX-RS annotations.
It is not a Quarkus extension — no deployment module is needed. Quarkus
auto-discovers the resources via Jandex indexing.

## Rationale

REST is a transport adapter, not part of the domain. Embedding it in the
core module forces every consumer to accept auto-registered endpoints,
pulls JAX-RS into the dependency graph, and makes suppression awkward
(build-time exclusions, `@IfBuildProperty` gates). A separate module
inverts the default: REST is opt-in, not opt-out.

This is Ports & Adapters (Hexagonal Architecture) applied to HTTP: the
library's SPI is the port; the REST module is one possible adapter.

## What belongs in the REST module

- **JAX-RS resource classes** — `@Path`, `@GET`, `@POST`, etc.
- **DTOs** — request/response representations, decoupled from domain entities.
- **Exception mappers** — `@Provider` classes translating domain exceptions to HTTP responses.
- **OpenAPI annotations** — `@Tag`, `@Operation`, `@APIResponse` on resource methods.

## What stays in the core module

- SPIs, domain types, entities, repositories, services, CDI events — everything
  that works without an HTTP boundary.

## Conventions

### Dependency direction

The REST module depends on the core library. The core library never
references the REST module.

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-library</artifactId>
  <version>${project.version}</version>
</dependency>
```

### Path prefix

Each REST module owns a path namespace. Use a consistent prefix across
modules so composed applications have a predictable URL space.

### DTOs vs domain types

REST resources return DTOs (records), not domain entities. The DTO is the
API contract; the domain entity is an implementation detail. This allows
the domain model to evolve without breaking HTTP clients.

### Versioning

The REST module versions alongside the core library — same multi-module
build, same release. Use `${project.version}` to keep them locked.

## Composition pattern

A deployable application composes libraries and their REST modules:

```xml
<dependency>my-engine</dependency>
<dependency>my-engine-rest</dependency>      <!-- opt-in -->
<dependency>my-ledger</dependency>
<dependency>my-ledger-rest</dependency>      <!-- opt-in -->
<dependency>my-work</dependency>
<!-- skip work-rest — this app writes its own domain-specific endpoints -->
```

A reference deployment (starter app, scaffold) is simply the full
composition: all libraries + all REST modules + persistence + config.
It is the canonical runnable artifact, not the only place REST exists.

## Anti-patterns

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| REST in core runtime | Auto-registers on every consumer; can't suppress without build-time exclusion | Separate module |
| Consumer reimplements generic REST | Duplicated boilerplate, inconsistent API surfaces, no shared tooling | Include the library's REST module |
| Scaffold as sole REST provider | Non-scaffold deployments get zero REST for the library | REST module in the library build; scaffold depends on it |
| DTOs that expose JPA entities directly | Hibernate proxies, lazy-load exceptions, schema leaks | Dedicated DTO records in the REST module |

## Relationship to module-tier-structure

This protocol extends the three-tier module structure
(`pure-Java SPI / core library / full extension`). The REST module is a
fourth tier — a transport adapter that depends on Tier 2/3 but is never
required by it. The tiers remain:

1. **Tier 1** — `api/` (pure Java, no framework)
2. **Tier 2/3** — `runtime/` (services, JPA, CDI)
3. **Adapter** — `rest/` (JAX-RS, opt-in)
4. **Adapter** — other transport adapters (gRPC, MCP, CLI) follow the same pattern

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`JAX-RS resource classes @Path`
`DTOs exception mappers @Provider`
`OpenAPI annotations @Tag @Operation`

Quarkus JAX-RS duplicate endpoint error when an interrupted agent leaves a stale resource file
entries.body:
Quarkus JAX-RS duplicate endpoint error when an interrupted agent leaves a stale resource file

### Symptom
`@QuarkusTest` augmentation fails with:

```
jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.DeploymentException:
POST /examples/spawn is declared by:
  io.quarkiverse.work.examples.spawn.SpawnScenario#run consumes *, produces application/json
  io.quarkiverse.work.examples.spawn.SpawnScenarioResource#run consumes *, produces application/json
```

Two classes declare the same JAX-RS path and method with identical media types. No obvious reason for the duplicate — you only wrote one.

### Context
An agent running in a git worktree was interrupted mid-task after creating `SpawnScenarioResource.java`. When the main session resumed and created `SpawnScenario.java` at the same `@Path("/examples/spawn")`, both files were on disk. Quarkus discovered both during augmentation.

### Root cause
Interrupted agents (worktree agents, subagents, or cancelled tasks) can leave uncommitted or committed files in the working tree that the next session doesn't know about. If a new file is created at the same JAX-RS path as an existing file from a prior interrupted task, Quarkus reports a duplicate endpoint at augmentation time — not at compile time.

### Fix
Search for all `@Path` declarations that match the conflicting path:

```bash
grep -rn '"/examples/spawn"' --include="*.java" src/
```

Identify the stale file (usually the one from the interrupted session) and delete it:

```bash
git rm quarkus-work-examples/src/main/java/.../SpawnScenarioResource.java
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The error message names both classes clearly, but when working with agents and worktrees it's non-obvious that a prior interrupted session left a file behind. The fix is trivial once identified; the confusion is in not knowing a second file exists.

**See also:** [GE-20260529-636a36](../jvm/GE-20260529-636a36.md) — JAX-RS @Provider exception mapper bypassed when exception extends a type caught by a generic resource handler

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
`quarkus jax-rs duplicate endpoint`
`@QuarkusTest deploymentexception`
`worktree agent stale resource file`

entries.title: jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response does not implement AutoCloseable — try-with-resources fails to compile
entries.body:
jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response does not implement AutoCloseable — try-with-resources fails to compile

## Symptom

Compiler error when wrapping a REST client Response in try-with-resources:

```
incompatible types: Response cannot be converted to AutoCloseable
```

## Context

Using `jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response` as a return type from a `@RegisterRestClient`
method and attempting to auto-close it to avoid HTTP connection pool leaks:

```java
try (Response response = gatewayClient.invokeAgent(request)) {  // ← compile error
    ...
}
```

## Root cause

`jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response` declares `close()` (added in JAX-RS 2.0) but does **not**
implement `java.lang.AutoCloseable`. The concrete Quarkus/RESTEasy implementation
(`ClientResponse`) does implement `Closeable`, but the declared return type from a
`@RegisterRestClient` method is the abstract `Response` — so the compiler rejects the
try-with-resources block.

## Fix

Use `try-finally` with explicit `response.close()`:

```java
Response response = gatewayClient.invokeAgent(request);
try {
    // use response
} finally {
    response.close();
}
```

`response.close()` is safe to call — it is declared on the abstract `Response` class.
The method releases the connection back to the HTTP connection pool.

## Why this is non-obvious

`close()` is declared on `Response` since JAX-RS 2.0, which strongly implies try-with-resources
should work — that is exactly why `AutoCloseable` exists. Nearly every Java resource type that
declares `close()` implements `AutoCloseable`. The gap is intentional (the JAX-RS spec authors
chose not to add `AutoCloseable` to `Response`) but invisible from the API surface. A developer
who sees `close()` naturally reaches for try-with-resources and gets a compile error with no
hint about why.

**See also:** [GE-20260607-9cef08](GE-20260607-9cef08.md) — sequential try-catch for must-not-throw close() with multiple resources

---HYPOTHETICAL-QUERIES---
Response AutoCloseable compile error
jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response try-with-resources
Response close() not AutoCloseable
